upon his second visit, a single shout left Baizhang’s ears deaf for three days. Its reversal and conformity are unfathomable, and this style has become the common practice throughout all quarters; it does not value mere conformity.
The essence is to cease and rest; it simply requires that one grasp [the truth] by following conditions. This is another transformation.

Thus, one should investigate where one meets the other after death and cremation. In the lineage transmitted from Xueyan to Gao Feng, the focus was exclusively on thoroughly penetrating the "true host" during moments when there are no dreams or thoughts;
they investigated minutely and searched with precision, attaining profound mastery of the innermost depths.

The three roots [of faith, understanding, and practice] are universally encompassed; the single mind penetrates through and through, leaving no further room for regret. This is yet another transformation. As the *I Ching* says:

"When one reaches the limit, there is change; when there is change, there is penetration. I have compiled this work, *Zongfan* (Models of the School), which spans from the stage of initial study to the ultimate attainment of freedom from defilement.

It systematically arranges the methods for self-benefit and benefiting others, encompassing the various rules and models for research and cultivation established by the ancients. Drawing extensively from the *Po-ch'an* (Baozhi’s *Chanmen Zhixin*), I have exerted every effort to penetrate their depths, revealing them without concealment.
Whether one possesses shallow roots or meager faculties, anyone who peruses this work can rely upon its practices to give rise to awakening. Only...

therefore, one should exclusively raise the phrase concerning the "host" during the state of dreamless sleep to lead people into the gateway.
To penetrate to the subtlest point is no mere reckless stratagem of a young master. As I, this patch-robed monk, read and contemplate it, I mirror his diligent toil and rejoice in his universal vow.

Written by the junior disciple of Dongchuan, Nuo-an Pan-tan, on the full moon of the twelfth month of the Yiwei year of the Daoguang era.
General Principles:

First, within the state of thorough penetration, there is no subject of dreams, thoughts, sights, or sounds; yet there are many who vaguely follow the path of intellectual understanding. One friend [asked]: "Regarding the phrase 'like firing a cannon'..."

"There is sound and there is touch. I said, "The neighbor is firing off firecrackers; what connection does that have with you? What relevance does it have to the master of your dreams? At this, he was speechless.
Therefore, for those who possess a point of realization, someone might ask: "At that time, was the sound of the firecrackers the same as or different from the present conversation?
Or one might ask: "Where is the sound of the firecrackers at this very moment? Or one might ask: "After the sound of the firecrackers has passed..."
"When you are fast asleep and have no dreams, where else could we meet? This is a test using a 'grass-cutting' [direct] approach.
Those who respond with such "mechanisms" as raising their fists or shouting downward, or with such words as "the nose straight and the eyebrows arched," are all cleared away.
What is required is that they provide a single word of the true path from the very place of realization at that moment; only if there is truly a seal of verification will it be accepted.
The mind has a "itching sinew" that must be grasped; this is where the final stroke is applied. Otherwise, one must be commanded to investigate further.
Within a single thread of the fundamental school, the principles established by the five houses are more than sufficient for testing and discerning later practitioners;
there is no need to add further terminology or conceptual marks.

After the First Patriarch (Dongshan) crossed the water and attained thorough enlightenment upon beholding his reflection, who knows that he might not have once again encountered Yunyan and received the transmission of the Precious Mirror?
It is simply that this was not recorded in the extant texts.
First, regarding the "Discernment of the Middle" (*Zhongbian*), the words of the various patriarchs are now excerpted according to the original texts; I have not dared to alter them arbitrarily.
However, concerning the matter of Master Mi’s (Mazu Daoyi) "brushing away" [the staff], the *Huisheng jue* records that his transmission of the Dharma-treasury was not handled with sufficient care;

this can be inferred from the fact that he first gave his seal of approval before Master Ren (Nanyue Huairang) and subsequently engaged in debate with him. As for the two patriarchs, Mazu and Nanyue, they were beyond the reach of ordinary Chan practitioners.
Furthermore, do not become dismissive or negligent because of my eloquent discourse.
The *Zhenzhi Zu* (Master Zhenzhi) states in his *Zhengzi Song*: "The four elements have no self; my mind is like the wind. Within this, who is the true host?
Vastly open and suddenly falling away, originally there is nothing at all. Only now do I regret that previously I labored in error. I have had this recorded here for your reference.

such as Shushan who died from vomiting blood due to abdominal distension and Dahui who suffered a toxic reaction— shared the same karmic retribution regarding their deaths.
Do not, because your views differ, recklessly maintain a sense of superiority or inferiority.

Within the One Vehicle teaching, both the Chan school is sudden and perfect, and the Tiantai school is wondrous and perfect; thus, one must know that after [attaining] this, one must also harmonize and integrate the Tiantai school.

I prostrate to the Honored Śākyamuni, To the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, And to all the noble Bodhisattvas.
The great assembly of Śrāvakas, the successive patriarchs of the East and West— I rely upon the foremost masters of the Supreme Vehicle of the present age;
I have investigated the mind with the Lord of No-Dream. After a hundred days of cessation, I was revived;
through the narrow tube, a single gap was opened. Having visited and studied under various Bodhisattvas, Their compassion has served as the tongs and hammer for me.
The religious principles of the Buddhas and Patriarchs I have searched extensively; yet with meager faith, I drifted for thirty-five years until death was suddenly upon me.
Deeply ashamed that I have failed the kindness of my teachers, I see my own shallow practice has grown heavy once more.
Furthermore, reflecting on those who engage in worldly affairs, we all harbor the same ailment: our intellectual understanding cannot withstand the power of karma.
At the end of the year, I was filled with empty anxiety and distress; for this reason, I have compiled these models of the school.
Day and night, I urge myself on in pain, praying that the Triple Gem grant their protection. May all who see this rejoice.
This "Separate Transmission of the Wondrous Mind" consists of ten chapters.
1. The Source of Dhyāna; 2. Thorough Investigation; 3. Cultivation and Training; 4. Entry into the Holy State;
5. Benefiting Others; 6. Manifesting Similes; 7. Functional Mechanisms; 8. Fundamental Tenets; 9. Demonstrating Eloquence; 10. Integrating the Teachings.

Originally, since the Buddhadharma flowed eastward from the Han through the Liang dynasties, the scriptures and teachings were widely disseminated, and there was never a lack of individuals in successive generations who practiced in accordance with them.
Bodhidharma, however, transmitted solely the wondrous mind of the separate tradition, pointing directly to each person so they might see their nature and become Buddha.
Ultimately, what constitutes this wondrous mind? Therefore, he begins with the "Source of Zen" (*Canyuan*). Once the source is established, from where does the student proceed?

To accord with the wondrous mind and follow the ancient regulations, nothing short of diligent investigation (*canchou*) will suffice; therefore, this is followed by "thorough investigation" (*chechan*).

Through investigation comes awakening, whereby one shares the same nostrils as the Buddhas and Patriarchs. However, because beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been eliminated, this is further supplemented by "cultivation and training" (*tiaoxi*).

When these tendencies are exhausted and one's power is vast, one achieves profound resonance with True Suchness (*tathatā*). As the Sixth Patriarch said: "Those who do not regress for the rest of their lives..."

One enters the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). Therefore, this is symbolized by "entering the noble. As in the four preceding chapters, one's own practice is stable and secret; however, one must exercise compassion that is identical in essence (*samatā-karuṇā*).
How could one possibly sever the seeds of the Buddha? Therefore, one is exhorted to benefit others. Regarding the benefit of others, ancient masters have spoken of two paths:

the path of words and the path of expedient application (*upāya*). Thus, they are distinguished into two sections: the section on manifest metaphors and the section on expedient application. Manifest Metaphors.

Regarding the preceding [section]: when the First Patriarch engaged with students, he also manifested the truth through words. By the time of the third and fourth generations, these words began to be transformed into "active function" (*jìngyòng*).

Therefore, "active function" follows next. As the Dharma endured for a long time, corruptions arose; many clever views emerged, and thus the fundamental tenets were established to protect the True Eye.
Therefore, "the Essential Tenets" (*gāngzōng*) follows. Public cases (*gōng'àn*) became numerous, and later venerable masters each produced their own.
I have used my own hand and eye to provide commentaries upon them. Within these, there are manifestations of the provisional and the real, the shallow and the deep, the partial and the complete;

while it is not that they are entirely identical, there are differences among them. Nevertheless, they all equally serve to bring about the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision in those who come to study them;

therefore, I have expanded upon them here to demonstrate their distinctions, as in the nine chapters above. All of these are the fundamental provisions of the Chan school, yet they must not be left unconnected with the various scriptural teachings.

Therefore, I conclude with the "Pervading Teaching" (Guànjiào). From the eighth to the tenth stages, although they are listed after the "Benefiting Others" (Lìrén), self-benefit likewise requires extensive study across these ten categories.
I laugh at myself for being so restless and hurried, appearing like a limping practitioner; my face is full of shame, for while I can speak of it, I cannot put it into practice.
Nevertheless, if those of keen faculties can rely on this and suddenly rise up to act upon it, [they will succeed].
He never retreated throughout his life; in this world he was a teacher of men, and in future lives he shall become a Buddha or a Patriarch.
He must surely be the second great hero of our time. — *Canyuan* (The Source of Zen)
The *Denglu* begins with the verses of the Seven Buddhas and the transmission from the Original Teacher;

it then briefly extracts various sūtras and *gong'an*, followed by a listing of the causes and conditions of the transmission between the twenty-eight patriarchs, tracing back the source and stream. Such is the appropriate literary form. For now, I have no leisure to provide a comprehensive account.
Pointing directly to the Buddha’s birth as non-duality, the separate transmission of the wondrous mind is the source of Chan.

This fundamental principle was established in meaning by Bodhidharma and has flowed down through the various patriarchs. Observing how the First Patriarch received Huiké, as well as Emperor Wu of Liang and Yang Xuanzhi, all of whom were shown the Way through words and phrases, yet it is called "not establishing written texts" and a "separate transmission outside the teachings"—this is truly because of [the limitations of] learning.
People were mired in scriptural teachings and were ultimately unable to seal their realization in accord with the wondrous mind (*miaoxin*) to achieve Buddhahood in this very place.

Therefore, he came at this opportune time to proclaim the Sudden Teaching; this is the source of Chan. What is the wondrous mind? All sentient beings, down to the crawling insects, possess Buddha-nature.
Yet those who have been submerged in the sea of suffering since beginningless time fail to realize that this very mind is, in its essential nature, the Buddha, and thus turn their backs on awakening.
By uniting with sense objects, one completely transforms perfect *bodhi* into ignorance (*avidyā*), becoming deluded and failing to return [to the source].
Although one may cycle through saṃsāra for ten thousand kalpas, the innate Buddha-nature remains forever unchanging. A separate record states that the First Patriarch taught only Master Ke:

"Cease all external conditions; let the internal mind be free from agitation; let the mind be like a wall—it is thus that one may enter the Way. This was the instruction given to the Second Patriarch.

Heshang Moheyan explained the principles of the nature of the mind. Huik'e refuted his errors in general terms but did not explain that the essence of the mind is non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*).
Huik'e suddenly said, "I have already stilled all conditions. Huineng asked, "Does this not result in annihilation? Huik'e replied, "It does not result in annihilation;
it is a constant, lucid awareness. Therefore, words cannot reach it. Huineng said, "This is the mind transmitted by all Buddhas."
As for the essence: when conditions are stilled, external objects are empty; when there is no panting breath, internal discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) ceases.

When it is like a wall, the sphere of mental activity is extinguished; when words fail, the path of language is cut off. When one understands through non-thought, stillness and illumination arise simultaneously;
mind and object are not two, delusion and awakening are not two, and sentient beings and Buddhas are not two. At this point of perfect fitness, even the mind—
It cannot be apprehended. Even "wondrous" cannot be apprehended. Even the two characters for "non-duality" cannot be apprehended. That which cannot be apprehended also cannot be apprehended.
It is neither mind nor non-mind; it is neither wondrous nor non-wondrous. Whether urinating or defecating, laughing, playing, or reviling in anger—all are the manifestation of the wondrous mind.
For now, we provisionally establish the name "wondrous mind" and designate it as *Dharmatā*.
This is the source of the Chan school. You must know that those who settle the mind settle this; those who investigate the mind investigate this;
those who awaken to the mind awaken to this; those who harmonize the mind harmonize this; those who enter the state of sagehood enter this; and those who benefit others benefit this.

Even the manifestations of the various patriarchs, their metaphors, functional applications, guiding principles, and demonstrations of discernment, as well as all the sudden and complete sutras and treatises, do not depart from this.

The mind has a specific referent. In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which the First Patriarch took as the realization of the mind, it is called the "realm of self-awakening" (*svasaṃvedya-gocara*) and "noble wisdom of self-awakening" (*svasaṃvedya-āryajñāna*).
As for "self-awakening," the numinous light shines alone, transcending the sense organs and their objects;

it is eternally quiescent yet illuminating, and is thus termed the "wisdom of self-awakening. It is eternally illuminating yet quiescent, and is thus termed the "realm of self-awakening. The rest is as follows...
The *ālayavijñāna*, "that which is manifested by one's own mind," and the "true consciousness that is neither born nor extinguished" can all be individually resolved [into this].

Therefore, when the First Patriarch cited scriptures to establish the Mind School (*cittamātra*), he would invariably say at the conclusion of his sermons: "Alas! After this sutra has been transmitted four times, it will turn into mere names and characteristics.
Mazu cited the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, saying: "The Buddha’s words take the Mind as their essence; having no gate is the Dharma-gate. (3)
The realms are sealed by the single dharma of mind-only. The Master Hui-man, who was a collateral descendant of the First Patriarch, constantly carried the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as his essential core;
he practiced exactly as it taught. He thoroughly understood that after the awakening of the mind, one must necessarily perform the work of subduing consciousness through the power of cultivation.
These so-called Chan practitioners of today do not merely fail to practice according to the scriptural teachings;
they do not even understand what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says, nor do they know why the First Patriarch uniquely cited this sūtra to certify the Mind.

To place it among those things neither discussed nor debated is truly lamentable. It is simply because the language and meaning of this sūtra are ancient and profound that after several transmissions, it nearly—

This [teaching] fell into silence. In the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) of the Third Patriarch, this wondrous mind is designated by such names as "mysterious principle" (*xuanzhi*) and "true thusness-dharmadhātu" (*tathatā-dharmadhātu*) to manifest it.
The Fourth Patriarch had people recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; the Fifth Patriarch further had them chant the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
When the Sixth Patriarch heard a guest chanting the sutra until the passage: "One should give rise [to the mind] without dwelling anywhere..."
His mind was thereby opened and enlightened. The Fifth Patriarch again questioned him regarding his initial realization. Under the Patriarch’s words, he attained great penetration and said:
"All phenomena do not depart from self-nature; how could I have expected that self-nature is fundamentally pure and fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing?"
It is inherently complete; it is inherently unmoving. Who would have expected that the self-nature could give rise to the myriad dharmas?
Later, when he opened the hall to preach the Dharma, at the very first assembly he expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Dharma, saying: "This must be practiced with the mind."

It does not reside in verbal recitation. It is verbal recitation and mental practice; mind and mouth must correspond. One's original nature is Buddha; apart from this nature, there is no separate Buddha.
"Mahā" means great; the capacity of the mind is as vast as space. It has no boundaries, nor is it square or round, large or small, blue or yellow, angry or joyful, right or wrong, good or evil.
The wondrous nature of worldly people is fundamentally empty; there is not a single dharma that can be grasped. Yet, do not...

Attachment to emptiness: There are those who sit with an empty mind and no thoughts at all, yet claim for themselves to be "Great. They are attached to the emptiness of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Such people as these cannot be spoken to.
Good friend, just as the world’s empty space can contain the myriad images of both the environment and its inhabitants, so too is the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*);
the self-nature can contain the myriad dharmas, which is what constitutes being "Great. These myriad dharmas reside within all people.
Within the nature, if one neither grasps nor rejects any good or evil, and remains unstained by them, the mind is like empty space;
therefore, it is called "Mahā. When functioning, it is clearly and distinctly applied, whereby one immediately knows all things; all things are one.

One is all; coming and going are free, and the substance of the mind is unimpeded. This is precisely the wisdom of all *prajñā*, which arises entirely from the self-nature and does not enter from without. This is called the true nature functioning of itself. One is true, and all are true.
Though one may verbally proclaim emptiness, if one does not cultivate this practice, it is like a person falsely claiming to be a king—it can never be attained. As for *prajñā*:

In the language of Tang, it means "wisdom" (*prajñā*). At all times and in all places, to remain free from delusion in every thought-moment and to constantly practice wisdom is the practice of *prajñā*.
A single moment of delusion severs *prajñā*; a single moment of wisdom gives rise to *prajñā*. People of the world speak of *prajñā* with their mouths but do not recognize true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
*Prajñā* has no form or appearance; the mind of wisdom itself is it. If one understands it in this way, [one realizes it].

This is precisely what is called Prajñā-jñāna (Wisdom) and Pāramitā (Perfection). In the language of Tang, it means "reaching the other shore. To explain its meaning: it is free from arising and ceasing.

When one is attached to objects, arising and ceasing occur; this is called "this shore. When one is detached from objects, there is no arising or ceasing; this is called "the other shore. One who awakens to this Dharma is the Dharma of Prajñā;
one who practices this is the practice of Prajñā. Without such practice, one is a common person. Through a single moment of cultivation, one’s own self—
Ordinary beings are themselves Buddhas; afflictions are themselves bodhi. When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being;
when the succeeding thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, it is affliction; when the succeeding thought is detached from objects, it is bodhi.

The Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the most honored, the most supreme, and the foremost. It is without abiding, without departing, and without coming. Thus have the Buddhas of the three periods of time [taught].
Emerging from this, one should employ great wisdom to shatter the afflictions and defilements of the five aggregates.
Practicing in this manner, one will certainly attain the Way of Buddhahood, transforming the three poisons into precept, concentration, and wisdom.

This Dharma-gate of mine gives rise to eighty-four thousand forms of wisdom from a single prajñā, because human beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions; were there no afflictions, there would be no wisdom.

Wisdom is ever-present and never departs from its own nature. One who awakens to this Dharma is one of non-thought, free from recollection and attachment, and does not give rise to deception or delusion.

From the written word comes the functional application; from the functional application comes the *huatou*. Shifting once, shifting twice, it accords with the occasion as the time demands.

The conditioned is the function of the unconditioned; the unconditioned is the basis of the conditioned. Because one does not abide in that basis, it is said to be like space, having no support.

How does one face external objects so that the mind becomes like wood or stone? The Master said: "All phenomena originally do not say they are empty, nor do they say they are form. Nor do they say..."
This is neither defilement nor purity, nor does the mind bind anyone. It is simply that people themselves falsely conceptualize and cling, forming various interpretations, attachments, and fears.
One should merely realize that all phenomena do not arise of themselves, but exist only through the grasping at signs by one's own single thought of deluded inversion.
Knowing that the mind and its objects fundamentally do not reach one another, they are liberated in their very place; each and every thing is quiescent extinction.
One abides at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Furthermore, the fundamental nature is beyond naming or designation;

it is fundamentally neither ordinary person nor sage, neither defilement nor purity, neither emptiness nor existence, and neither good nor evil. If the mind of defilement and purity is exhausted, one dwells neither in bondage nor in liberation.

There is no mental measure (*cittamātra*) of any conditioned or unconditioned states of bondage or liberation. Abiding within birth and death, one’s mind is sovereign and ultimately does not associate with any phenomena.
The false illusions of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, birth and death, and the sense entrances are a mere confluence; they are utterly without locus and entirely ungraspable.
Coming and going through birth and death is like a door opening and closing. When one encounters various circumstances—whether agreeable or disagreeable—the mind remains without retreat or dejection.
One does not crave fame, merit, or gain, nor is one obstructed by worldly dharmas. One maintains an even-minded equanimity toward both suffering and pleasure.

Clothing and food suffice for sustaining life; remain steadfast and simple as if ignorant. If you possess even a slight degree of resonance with the Way, yet you extensively study for intellectual understanding or seek blessings and wisdom, all of it remains within birth and death.
You will instead be tossed by the winds of conceptual objects and drowned in the sea of saṃsāra. The Buddha is one who seeks nothing; the Principle is a principle that cannot be sought.
To seek them is to deviate from them. Yet, if you cling to "seeking nothing" and "non-action," you again become the same as those who have something to seek.

Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*): if one can for a single moment give rise to a mind like wood or stone, not being swept away by the five desires or the eight winds, then the causes of birth and death are severed.
One becomes free in going and staying, no longer bound by the causes and effects of all conditioned things, nor constrained by outflows (*āsrava*).
At another time, one may again take that which was previously unconditioned as a cause, benefiting others through shared activity, responding with a mind free from attachment.

Cutting through all things. With unimpeded wisdom, one unties all bonds. Exert yourself with fierce investigation; do not wait for the suffering of old age, for then you will be unable to control your hands and feet.
One is simply led by the weight of craving and drawn by karmic consciousness to take birth, having no freedom whatsoever.
Question: How can one attain freedom? The Master said: "If you were to attain it now, you would have it. Even when confronted by the five desires and the eight winds,"
Unmoving, their mind is free from grasping or rejecting, stinginess, envy, or craving. The sense of "mine" is exhausted; both defilement and purity have vanished.
Like the sun and moon in the sky, they illuminate without depending on external conditions. Their minds are as firm as wood or stone;

One must be able to internalize it. Indeed, when reading the words of the scriptures and teachings, everything must be digested and returned to oneself.

Sound and form are also free from detachment, and one does not dwell in conceptual understanding. This is the practice of the teachings of the Three Vehicles, all of which treat the maladies of greed, hatred, and the like.

Yet when it is destined to burn or drown us, we are burned or drowned; when it is destined for birth, we are born; when it is destined for death, we die. Our going and staying are determined by ourselves.

Bodhidharma said, "The mind is like wood or stone. The Third Patriarch said, "Utterly forgetting conditions. Caoqi said, "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all.
Mazu said, "It is like a lost person who cannot distinguish directions. Master Zhao said, "Close off wisdom and block the ears; awaken alone in profound stillness. Mañjuśrī said:
Because the mind is like empty space, I pay homage to the profound *sūtra* that has nothing to observe. Not hearing it and not upholding it, there is now only the non-existence of all dharmas;
one perceives neither sound nor form, and the six sense faculties are sealed shut. Only by training in this way does one have the capacity for true practice.
These words are bitter to the palate and harsh to the ear, yet if one can act accordingly, by the second or third life, one will be able to [attain realization].
Go to where there is no Buddha and sit upon the Great Seat of Enlightenment to achieve Equal and Perfect Awakening. It is also said: "It is like a person seeing fire;
simply do not touch it with your hand, and the fire will not burn you. Right now, there are ten phrases that do not exist:

the turbid mind, the greedy mind, the desiring mind, the defiled mind, the angry mind, the grasping mind, the dwelling mind, the relying mind, the attached mind, the seizing mind, and the longing mind. However, each of these is but a single phrase.
The Three Phrases. Each and every one penetrates through these three phrases. Yet, all manifestations of illumination and function are left to proceed freely in every direction;
all movements, speech, silence, weeping, and laughter are entirely the Buddha-wisdom. In each and every circumstance, one is neither deluded nor confused, neither angry nor joyful.

At the gates of the six sense faculties, through diligent scrubbing and refinement, they are brought to purity. Such a person is one who has nothing to do. As for the "three phrases," they are non-abiding.
Neither dwelling in attachment nor dwelling in non-attachment, and having no conceptual understanding of such non-dwelling—this is called *prajñā*.
Huangbo Xiyun said: "Buddhas and sentient beings are but this single mind; there is no other dharma. This mind has, from the beginningless past, never been subject to arising or ceasing.
It has no form or appearance; it does not belong to existence or non-existence, nor to new or old. It is neither long nor short, neither large nor small; it transcends [all categories]."
All limitations, names, words, traces, and dualistic oppositions are, in their very essence, this [mind] itself. Like space, it is boundless and immeasurable;
this mind alone is the Buddha. Sentient beings, clinging to appearances, seek outwardly, causing them to search for the Buddha within the Buddha, yet they can never find him.

They do not know that by ceasing discursive thought and forgetting sensory dust, the Buddha manifests spontaneously before them. This mind does not diminish in sentient beings, nor does the Buddha increase.

The six perfections and myriad practices, the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are fundamentally complete within oneself. When conditions arise, they are manifested; when conditions cease, they are quiescent.
To not believe that this is the Buddha and instead practice while clinging to forms is for all such deluded thoughts to diverge from the Way.

This mind is luminous and pure like space, without a single trace of appearance. To stir a thought is to deviate from the essence of the Dharma and to cling to appearances. There has never been a Buddha who clings to appearances since beginningless time.
Cultivating the six perfections and myriad practices is the sequential path. The Buddha who is without beginning and without sequence merely awakens to the one mind;
there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained. This is the true Buddha, like space: when the sun rises, it does not become bright; when the sun sets, it does not become dark.

Though light and darkness contend with one another, the nature of space remains unchanging. Now, if one does not awaken to this essence of mind, all practice that clings to appearances is [merely delusion].
Regarding evil dharmas: making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions is not as meritorious as making an offering to a single "mindless" (wúxīn) practitioner of the Way.
To be "mindless" means to be without all minds whatsoever. The essence of suchness (rú rú) is, internally, like wood or stone—unmoving; externally, like empty space—unobstructed.
It is devoid of subject and object, appearance and characteristics, gain and loss, or spatial location. Those who rush toward it dare not enter this Dharma, fearing they will fall into emptiness.
Having no place to rest, they look toward the precipice and retreat. As for those like the sands of the Ganges: whether it be precious jewels and fragrant scents, the sand does not crave them;

whether it be excrement and foul stenches, the sand does not loathe them. This is precisely the mind that is no-mind, free from all marks. Between the living and the Buddha, there is no further distinction.
If one can simply be without-mind, this is ultimate realization. If one does not immediately become without-mind, one will not achieve it even through countless eons.
The Way is constrained by the practices and cultivations of the Three Vehicles and thus not liberated. Nevertheless, there are differences in the speed of realization:
some attain the state of no-mind upon hearing the Dharma for a single thought-moment, while others only attain it upon reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).

Whether attained quickly or slowly, once one abides in no-mind, there is nothing further to cultivate or realize; truly, there is nothing to be gained. The attainment in a single thought-moment and the attainment at the tenth stage are equal in their merit.
To apply [this] exactly is merely to have labored in vain throughout kalpas. When the Patriarch came from the West, he pointed directly to your mind, saying that it is originally Buddha.
Because each mind is not different [from this], one is called a Patriarch. By seeing this, one suddenly transcends the various stages of the Three Vehicles.

Question: Presently there are all manner of delusive thoughts; why do you say they do not exist? Answer: Delusion has no inherent substance; it arises from your own mind. If you recognize that the mind is...
The Buddha: "The mind is fundamentally without delusion; how can you give rise to a thought and further recognize it as deluded? If you do not stir your thoughts, naturally there is no delusion.

[Question: "When delusion arises, where is the Buddha? [Answer: "Awakening is precisely the Buddha. If there is no delusion, even awakening does not exist. [Question: "At this moment of realization, where is the Buddha?
[Answer: "From where does the question come? From where does awakening arise? [Observe] speech and silence, movement and stillness."
Sounds and forms are entirely Buddha-activities; one must not add head upon head. Simply do not give rise to divergent thoughts.
Mountains, waters, monks, laypeople, heaven, and earth—none of these transcend your own mind. Question: "If this is so, where is Bodhi? Answer: "Bodhi has no such location.
Buddhas do not attain it, and sentient beings do not lose it. It is simply that all sentient beings are [Bodhi]."
The Characteristics of Bodhi. Question: How does one give rise to the bodhicitta? Answer: Bodhi is non-attainment.

When you hear of giving rise to the bodhicitta, you assume it means studying to become a Buddha. Even if you practice for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you will only obtain a *nirmāṇakāya* or *saṃbhogakāya*;
what connection would that have with the Buddha of the original source, true nature? Seeking externally for a Buddha with form is not like you; this original source is pure.
The mind gives rise to the Buddha-world; whether with form or without form, it is equal, perfectly luminous, and universally illuminating.

Yet worldly people do not awaken to this; they merely take seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to be the mind. Being shrouded by these perceptions, they fail to behold the fundamental essence. Simply, there is directly beneath one no-mind.
The fundamental substance manifests of itself. However, the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor is it separate from seeing and the other faculties.

One should simply not give rise to conceptual interpretations regarding seeing and the rest, nor stir thoughts concerning them. One should not seek the mind apart from seeing and the rest, nor abandon seeing and the rest to grasp at dharmas.
Without grasping or attachment, one is free and sovereign whether moving forward or backward; there is nothing that is not the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The simultaneous forgetting of both mind and objects is the true Dharma. Forgetting objects is relatively easy; forgetting the mind is extremely difficult.

People do not dare to forget their minds, fearing they will fall into emptiness where there is nothing to grasp. They do not realize that emptiness is fundamentally not empty, but is simply the one true Dharma-realm.
Question: Does the Buddha attain ignorance through emptiness? Answer: Ignorance is the place where all Buddhas attain the Way;
therefore, dependent origination is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). The site of enlightenment is that which has nothing to be attained. Question: Is ignorance light or darkness? Answer:
It is neither light nor darkness. Light and darkness are phenomena of alternation; ignorance is neither bright nor dark. Not being bright...
Darkness. It is simply self-luminous from the very beginning. People merely desire to move toward light and do not wish to face darkness; they do not love ignorance or afflictions.
Clearly, the Buddha himself is not luminous, and sentient beings are not dark. Because dharmas have neither light nor darkness, this is the fruit of the śramaṇa.

It is accomplished through the cessation of discursive thought; it is not attained through study. The minds of the ancients were sharp; upon hearing a single word, they immediately ceased their learning.

Therefore, they were called "men of leisure who have transcended learning and reached non-action. Nowadays, people merely desire to possess extensive knowledge and understanding, which instead results in obstruction.

Simply by dissolving all internal and external attachments until they are exhausted, and being entirely free from dependence or clinging, one is a man of no affairs. My school’s tradition is simply this.
Know that when the mind is stilled, there is rest. You need only eliminate ordinary sentiments and holy states; outside of the mind, there is no other Buddha.

The Patriarchs pointed directly to the fact that every person is entirely Buddha. If you do not recognize this now, you will cling to the distinction between ordinary and holy, rushing outward in search, thereby deluding your own mind.
A hundred kinds of extensive knowledge are not equal to the supreme state of having no seeking. A man of the Way is one who has nothing to do.
People, there is nothing at all; it is simply the absence of all mental activity that is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

In daily walking, standing, speaking, and acting, you must only refrain from clinging to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Every word uttered and every blink of an eye is then entirely identical to the outflow-free state.
Why do contemporary practitioners of Chan still cling to all sounds and forms? Why not let the mind become like empty space—like withered wood, a stone, cold ashes, or extinguished fire?
Go! This corresponds to a small portion of the Way. It is simply to remain detached from all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent. The mind is like the solar disk in the sky;
its radiance is spontaneous, illuminating without the act of illuminating. This is not a matter of exerting effort.
Reaching this point where there is no place to rest is precisely walking the path of all Buddhas; it is the arising of the mind while dwelling nowhere. This is your pure *dharmakāya*, named *A*.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. An ancient said: "How can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark? With a single leap, one enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.

If you do not realize this, then even if you study extensively until you possess great knowledge and undergo diligent hardships—wearing grass garments and eating from trees—if you do not recognize your own mind, it all counts as deviant practice.
Now, simply learn to be without-mind; after a long time, you must truly attain it. Because your capacity is small, you cannot achieve it suddenly.
"Chao! Simply within thirty or fifty years, you will find an entrance and naturally understand it. The Dharma-body from antiquity until now is identical to that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
where is there any deficiency? Once you have understood this meaning, exert yourself for the remainder of this life. You cannot guarantee that your next breath will follow your last.
He told Prime Minister Pei: 'The very mind is Buddha; no-mind is the Way. When asked about the Sage, he said: 'There is nothing.'"

"The mind is the Buddha. Since ordinary people have no [fixed] mind, do you not sink into emptiness? The Master said, "The Dharma has neither ordinary nor sage; it is also neither empty nor quiescent.

The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent—do not form the view of non-existence. The Dharma is fundamentally non-non-existent—do not form the view of existence. When both existence and non-existence are exhausted, [this is the truth]."

In the School of the Patriarchs, we speak only of ceasing the workings of the mind and forgetting all views. A question was asked: "If the mind is already Buddha, is there any further need to cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices?
The Master said: "Awakening resides in the mind; it has no concern with the six perfections or myriad practices. Among all the gates of the perfections, the Buddha-mind is foremost.
However, once one is free from the mind of birth-and-death and afflictions, there is no further use for dharmas such as bodhi. Therefore it is said: 'The Buddha...'"
"All dharmas are taught for the sake of transcending all minds. Since I have no mind at all, what use have I for all dharmas? This meaning is difficult to believe.
When the Dharma arrives, you may take only one person as your teacher: trust in secret that your own mind is the Buddha.

When both body and mind are non-existent, this is called the Great Way. Truly, not a single dharma can be obtained; this is called sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). As for the site of enlightenment, it is simply...
"Do not give rise to any views. Question: "What is diligence? The Master said: "When body and mind do not arise, this is called the foremost, firm, and enduring diligence.
Question: "How does one transcend the three realms? The Master said: "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all; you shall transcend the three realms right where you are.
Now, simply to have no dwelling place within the midst [of phenomena] is to walk the path of all Buddhas. This is the wheel of sentient beings."
That which turns back without ceasing is the mind that wanders along its objects; it does not rest within the six realms of existence and thus brings about the experience of various sufferings.

Now, simply by being without-mind, all conditions are suddenly stilled. By merely eliminating the various delusions of self and other, hatred and love, victory and defeat, one’s nature is inherently pure from the beginning.
This is precisely the cultivation of the Dharma of Bodhi and the equality of Buddhas; the mind is like a solid rock, without cracks or fissures.
All dharmas cannot penetrate it; it is utterly unattached. Only then does one respond even slightly. This very body and mind is the person of freedom.
Bodhidharma faced the wall so as not to allow anyone a place for views. It is only said that when the contrivance of the mind is forgotten, the Buddha-way flourishes;
when there is discrimination, the demonic armies blaze. Question: "If one practices this Way without a mind, will it be attained? Answer: "Without a mind, it is already attained."
This is practicing this Way. It is said that one neither attains nor fails to attain it. For instance, the moment a single thought flickers up, that is the realm (*viṣaya*).

If there is not a single thought, then the realm is forgotten and the mind extinguishes of itself; there is nothing further to pursue. Question: How does one avoid falling into stages? The Master said:
"Throughout the day you eat rice, yet you have never bitten into a single grain. Throughout the day you walk the road, yet..."
Once one has trodden upon this ground—at such a time—there are no notions of self or others. Throughout the day, one does not depart from all phenomena, yet is not deluded by various sensory objects;
this is called being a person of mastery. Moment by moment, one does not perceive any marks, sitting serenely and upright, flowing spontaneously without restriction;
this is called liberation. Strive! Strive! Of the thousands and tens of thousands who have entered this gate, only three have truly attained it.
Five points. If you do not take these as your concern, the day will come when you suffer calamity. Therefore it is said: "Exert yourself in this life and must bring it to completion;
do not allow yourself to suffer the remaining calamities for many kalpas. Linji said: "The student must seek authentic insight.
If one attains right view, one is unstained by birth and death, and one is free in going and staying. One need not seek excellence; excellence arrives of its own accord."
I, this mountain monk, instruct people only this: you must simply not be deluded. If you wish to act, act; do not hesitate further. At present, the illness lies in a lack of self-confidence;
you are swayed by myriad circumstances and lack autonomy. If you can bring to rest this mind that incessantly pursues and seeks, then you will be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Do you wish to recognize the Buddhas and Patriarchs? They are none other than those right before you who are listening to the Dharma.
This is so. Because people’s faith does not reach this point, they seek it outwardly. According to my own view, it is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
What is lacking in all these various applications? A single divine radiance has never ceased for a moment. If you can see it thus, you are simply a person who, for a lifetime, has nothing to do.
If you wish to be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, you need only not seek outwardly. At this very thought-moment—
The light of pure clarity within the mind is the Dharmakāya Buddha. The light of non-discrimination within a single thought-moment of the mind is the Sambhogakāya Buddha.
The light of non-distinction within a single thought-moment of the mind is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. These three Buddhas are none other than those listening to the Dharma right before you now;
it is simply because you do not seek outward that this efficacy exists. Your physical body of the four elements—does it not [arise from this]?
It is that which explains the Dharma and hears the Dharma. Space does not explain or hear the Dharma.
This distinct, solitary luminosity right before your eyes—this is what explains and hears the Dharma. If you see it thus, you are no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Only at all times must you never let it be interrupted; it is present everywhere you look. It is only because of the arising of deluded thoughts [that you fail to see it].

Wisdom is partitioned; perceptions transform and their substance diverges. This is why one wanders in saṃsāra and undergoes all manner of suffering. O follower of the Way: the mind-dharma has no form and pervades the ten directions.
When it is in the eye, it is called seeing; when it is in the ear, it is called hearing. Originally it is a single brilliant essence, which divides into the six harmonious combinations.
Since the one mind is fundamentally non-existent, one is liberated wherever one is. It is only because the seeking mind does not cease that you run after the ancients.

When people are free from the machinations of the sensory realm, they are true men of the Way. They simply follow conditions to exhaust their past karma; when it is time to walk, they walk; when it is time to sit, they sit.

Not for a single thought do they harbor the aspiration for the fruit of Buddhahood. As the ancients said: "If you wish to engage in practice to seek Buddhahood, that Buddha is but a great omen of birth and death.
You need only act as the master wherever you are; wherever you stand is the truth. Even if circumstances change and shift, you cannot be replaced by them. Even if...
The five deeds of immediate retribution are all liberated within the great ocean.

If you wish to attain freedom in coming and going, dwelling and departing within birth and death, you must right now recognize the one who listens to the Dharma: formless, rootless, and without a place of abode;
yet vibrantly alive, it is the locus for the application of all manner of provisional arrangements. It simply has no fixed location; this is what is called "the secret. Question: How is this so?
These are the four kinds of signless objects. The Master said: "A single thought of doubt is obstructed by earth; a single thought of attachment is drowned by water;
a single thought of anger is burned by fire; a single thought of joy is blown away by wind. If you are not turned by these objects, you can employ them everywhere.
Realize that the four great elements are like dreams and illusions. You, the listener of the Dharma, are not the four great elements; you are able to employ the four."

Great! When one perceives it thus, one immediately attains freedom in going and staying. As for the Buddha’s six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), he enters the six realms of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) without being deluded;
they are all empty in nature and cannot bind him. This is the person who follows the Way without reliance.

Although this is but the coarse substance of the five aggregates, it is itself the spiritual power that traverses the earth. When the Buddha appears, one feels no joy; when hell appears, one feels no fear.
One perceives the empty nature of all phenomena: they exist when transformed, and do not exist when untransformed. The three realms are but the mind;

they are like dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky—what need is there to grasp at them? Only those who listen to the Dharma will not be burned by fire, nor drowned by water, nor obstructed by the earth.
The hells are like viewing a pleasure garden; entering the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, one does not undergo retribution.

Why is this so? Because there is no dharma that can be found wanting. If you love the holy and hate the ordinary, you will sink and float within the sea of birth and death. It is better to rest and remain in non-action.
Do not continue what has already arisen; do not allow what is yet to come to arise. When the mind rests for a single thought-moment, it is called [enlightenment].
The Bodhi tree: if you cannot bring each thought-moment to rest, you will instead ascend the tree of ignorance and enter the six realms of existence, shedding fur and wearing horns.
If you can bring them to rest, this is the pure realm of the body—the mind-born body of supernatural transformations within the three realms.
Dazhu said: "The mind is the root. [Question: By what method does one cultivate the root? The Master replied: "Sitting meditation."

As for *dhyāna* (meditative concentration): when forgetfulness does not arise, this is *dhyāna*. As for *samādhi* (equipoise): sitting and perceiving one's original nature is *samādhi*. This "original nature" is your unborn mind.
"Sitting" means having no-mind in the face of objects, such that the eight winds cannot move you. One who attains such *samādhi*—

Although one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one immediately enters the rank of the Buddha. This gate of sudden enlightenment takes non-thought (*amanasikāra*) as its essence and the non-arising of the deluded mind as its purpose.
It has purity as its substance and wisdom as its function. As for "non-thought," it means the absence of deviant thoughts; it does not mean the absence of correct mindfulness.

Whether there is thought of good or evil, suffering or pleasure, enemies or kin, love or hatred—all such thoughts are deviant. One should not think of anything at all; rather, [one should maintain] only...

To be mindful of bodhi is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Bodhi is unattainable; there is nothing in bodhi to be mindful of. That which has nothing to be mindful of is, in every respect, mindless.
This state of being without anything to be mindful of is the attainment of non-thought (*amanasikāra*); at the moment of attaining non-thought, one is spontaneously liberated.
Knowing that the two natures are empty is itself liberation. Without emptiness, liberation cannot be attained. What is called "wisdom" is the very essence of the emptiness of the two natures.

Knowing that the two natures are empty is called the liberation of function. As for the emptiness of the two natures, it means not giving rise to love or hatred, existence or non-existence, and so forth.
If one clearly realizes for oneself the state of no-mind and does not abide in any place, this is called clearly seeing the original nature.
This mind that does not abide in any place is the Buddha-mind; it is also called the unborn mind. As a sutra says: "Realizing the unborn."
This is the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). When one has not yet attained this state, one must exert effort and apply oneself diligently;

once this work is accomplished, realization will naturally occur. To be without mind in all circumstances is itself realization. Simply by being free from a mind of love and hatred, the two natures are empty, and one is spontaneously liberated.

Question: What is meant by "always never being apart from the Buddha"? Answer: When the mind is without arising or ceasing and remains tranquil in the face of objects, it is ultimately so at all times.

Emptiness and stillness mean that one is never separated from the Buddha. To attain such a vision is called *nirvāṇa*. It is the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
it is also called the gate of non-duality (*advaya-dvāra*), and it is also called the samādhi of single practice (*ekavyūha-samādhi*).

Why? Because one does not accept love or hatred; these two natures are empty. This state of having nothing to perceive is the principle of true thusness (*tathatā*) beyond attainment. As the treatise says, this is ultimate liberation.
As for "principle" (li): it is simply not receiving when phenomena arise; being mindless in all places, eternally tranquil like space, ultimately pure, and naturally liberated.
Once one loses this human body, it is difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas. Strive! Strive!

Furthermore, the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is both empty and not empty. Because the wondrous essence of True Suchness has no form or characteristics and cannot be apprehended, it is called "empty."

However, within emptiness that lacks substantiality or characteristics, there is fully present a function as vast as the sands of the Ganges; thus, there is no phenomenon that is not applicable, and even names are not empty.
Such meritorious achievements have practice as their foundation. If one does not enter by subduing the mind, there is no possibility of attaining realization.
Not being stained by external sounds and the like, and not giving rise to deluded thoughts within, is called "realization. Not forming the notion that one has realized is called "non-realization.
Furthermore, not forming the notion that there is no realization is called "neither non-realization. This is called ultimate realization. A monk asked Nanyang Zhong:
"How should one apply the mind to attain Buddhahood? He replied, "When there is no mind to be applied, one attains Buddhahood. He asked, "If there is no mind, who attains Buddhahood?
He replied, "Without a mind, one spontaneously attains Buddhahood; even the attainment of Buddhahood is without mind. He asked, "If a person takes another's life with a blade, does it exist or not?
He replied, "It does not exist. He asked, "Is there pain? He replied, "Pain, too, does not exist. He asked, "After death, to which realm is one born? He replied, "There is none."
"In death there is neither birth nor the Way. Question: "Once one has attained mastery over the non-existence of all things, yet is still oppressed by hunger and cold, how should one apply the mind?
The Master said: "When hungry, eat; when cold, wear clothes. Question: "If one knows hunger and cold, one must have a mind. The Master asked:

"What kind of form or substance does your mind have? The disciple replied: "It has no form or substance. The Master said: "Since it has no form or substance, it is originally without mind. How can you say [it exists]?"
He said, "There is. Question: When encountering tigers or wolves, how should one apply the mind? He said: "Seeing them as if not seeing; their coming as if they do not come.
They are then without mind, and the evil beasts cannot inflict harm. Question: What is the name for this solitary liberation and absence of mind?
He said: "Call it the Formless Segment Vajra Mahāsattva. Question: What merit does it possess? He said: "A single thought-moment accords with the Vajra."

It is so. One can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and one shall behold as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

The merit of this Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva is immeasurable; even if one were to speak for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it could not be fully exhausted. Question: How does one achieve "correspondence in a single thought-moment"?

He said, "When both memory and wisdom are forgotten, that is 'correspondence' (xiangying). Question: "When memory and wisdom are forgotten, who sees the Buddhas? He said, "Forgetfulness is itself non-existence;
non-existence is itself the Buddha. Question: "How can non-existence be called the Buddha? He said, "Non-existence is empty, and the Buddha is also empty.
Therefore it is said that non-existence is the Buddha. Question: "Since not even a hair’s breadth can be apprehended, what thing is it named? Is there anything similar to it? He said:
Originally there were no names, nor anything resembling it; the world calls it the Peerless and Sole Honored One. Exert yourself to practice in reliance upon this;

none can destroy it. It is uniquely liberated and fearless, always protected by holy sages as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, revered by devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and guarded by benevolent deities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Forever free from obstacles, where could one not find carefree wandering?
Question: "If one wishes to attain Buddhahood, how should one proceed? Answer: "Cast away both Buddha and sentient beings at once; liberation occurs right where you are. Question:
"How does one achieve resonance with this? Answer: "Do not contemplate good or evil; you will spontaneously see your own Buddha-nature. Question: "Does the mind possess afflictions? Answer:
"The nature of afflictions is itself detached from them. Question: "Since the mind is itself the Buddha, may one still cultivate the myriad practices? Answer: "All..."
The Buddhas are all fully endowed with the two adornments; how could they deny cause and effect? Nanquan said: "Ultimate truth is suchness.
Its hidden movement and subtle function are not perceived by anyone; this is called non-leaking wisdom, also termed inconceivable non-leakage.
It is equal to space, an unmoving nature, and not part of the flow of birth and death. When its wondrous function is self-sufficient, one begins to attain autonomy within all spheres of activity."

Because it abides thus, it is said that within the sphere of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one acts without acting. It is also called the "Pervasive Action Samādhi" (*sarvatraga-samādhi*) or the "Universal Manifestation of the Form Body.
Its functioning leaves no trace; it does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. True principle is spontaneously realized, and wondrous function is spontaneously sufficient.
The Great Way has no form; ultimate truth has no counterpart. Therefore, it does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.

As it is said, "not hearing yet hearing" is the path of Great Nirvana. This very thing is neither hearing nor non-hearing. Question: Since it does not belong to seeing or hearing, how can one realize it? Answer:

One must realize that there is a profound, silent resonance that is spontaneously realized. This is also called the "cause of completion" (*yuan-yin*); it does not arise from seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
There is seeing and knowing that belongs to conditions; it arises only in relation to objects. This spiritual subtlety is inconceivable; it is not something that exists through opposition.
Therefore, it is said that its wondrous function is self-penetrating and does not rely upon external things. Thus, this penetration is not "reliance-penetration" (dependent penetration).

To move is to lose the source; to awaken is to become deluded regarding the ultimate intent. The path of speech and the movements of the mind are utterly cut off.
If it is thus manifest before you, what more is there to doubt? Having no place to dwell, it is free from the past, present, and future;
it is fundamentally true and pure. In its dynamic functioning, nothing is lacking. Failing to awaken to this principle, one vainly involves oneself in worldly affairs and becomes defiled by them.

Even if one were to awaken, the sensory realms would remain in chaotic confusion. If one then attempts to withdraw the mind to break through or suppress these distractions, one falls into the path of the nihilistic outsiders (*ucchedavāda*). Herein, the fundamental...
The realm beyond dust has no stages or positions. To awaken is to move freely in all directions without departing from the fundamental limit (*dharmadhātu*).
There is no place for ordinary beings or sages to stand; movement and stillness, even the raising of an eyebrow, is true liberation. The events of kalpas of dust are all present before one's eyes.

Yet people of this age do not meet virtuous friends and thus cannot distinguish the false from the correct. As an ancient worthy said: "If the mind retains the measure of the holy, one still falls into the dust of dharmas; if one's own views are not yet forgotten..."
This is just like a leak; one cannot maintain the fasts or the precepts, nor can one enter meditative concentration by contemplating emptiness. One must simply depart.

Even the eighty-thousand-kalpa concentrations of the non-Buddhists do not exempt them from saṃsāra, for the root of birth and death has not been severed. A true renunciant is one who possesses genuine clarity and penetration.
Then one is identical to all Buddhas: silent illumination transcends cognition, and the void contains the myriad forms.

By relinquishing idle conditions and bringing the mind and consciousness to rest, one may finally draw near [to the Truth] for a brief moment. Were it not so, one would be entirely carried away by the sentiments of the discriminating consciousness;
what freedom would there be? Now, it is actually no different from insentient wood and stone preaching the Dharma—this is exceedingly true—but few people are able to hear it.
Possessing this true revelation, you will find that within the six realms of existence, it is identical to the pure lands of all Buddhas; what more need you fear of birth and death?
This single gate transcends the causes and effects of both ordinary beings and sages. It is the world-ocean of Vairocana’s wondrous adornment, surpassing the expedient gates of Śākyamuni.
From this very moment until the end of eons, not a single thing shall be taught to you as an object for the eyes to see.

This cannot be attained through your diligent efforts or through adornment; it is simply a matter of recognition. This is the great liberation, the state of one who has reached the pinnacle of thorough penetration.
Do not merely remain long attached to the net of love for birth and death, being bound by good and evil karma and carried away without any freedom.

Even if you could refine your body and mind until they are as empty as space, reaching a state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness that does not waver, you have not yet emerged from the *vijñāna-skandha*.
To call this "stillness" is a delusion; it is like a rushing torrent that one mistakes for tranquility. You will never escape the cycle of birth and death.

How much better it would be to remain an ordinary person on common ground, requiring not even a hair’s breadth of effort, and thus transcend directly. Would you agree? It is like sitting within the ocean... toward [the shore].
When people beg for water, if one’s faculties are dull, one must simply forget weariness day and night and pursue it until the end of one’s life;

only then can one find someone to carry and support them, and by etching this into one’s bones, one may investigate the reality until it is easily attained. There is a certain class who speak of "luminous clarity" and "spiritual awareness," claiming they can see and hear;
this greatly deceives people. Now I ask: why is it that when you are asleep, you are no longer luminous or spiritual? To mistake a thief for one’s own son—this is birth.
The root of death is the breath of deluded thought; it exists only because one discriminates among external objects such as forms, sounds, and other phenomena.
If there were no external objects, your brilliant spirit would be like a hare’s horn. O worthy one, simply recognize your secret adamantine essence:
the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form and emptiness, light and darkness; as well as your own body and mind, and all else.
The Buddha’s attainment of the Way and his benefiting of sentient beings—none of these fail to rely upon the manifestation of the majestic light of your perfect realization.

You possess such a wondrous and extraordinary station for manifesting yourself in the presence of all; why do you not bring this forth? If you do not understand it now, later you shall enter the womb of a donkey and be roasted and boiled.
These afflictions and karmic retributions will not cease after one or two kalpas; they shall endure for as long as your adamantine life span.
It is further said: When people see dangerous beasts, swords, blades, and other such things threatening their lives and bodies, they give rise to boundless fear.
It is like a painter who, having painted a hell for himself, feels terror upon seeing it; this is not the fault of anyone else doing wrong to you.
If you wish to awaken from this illusory delusion, simply recognize your own adamantine eye. If you recognize it, [there is no more fear].
If there were even a speck of dust in the teachings that could be revealed, where else would there be tigers, wolves, swords, or blades to frighten and intimidate you?
Even with the skillful means of Śākyamuni reaching this point, one still cannot find a place to show one's head. Therefore it is said: "The eye of the śramaṇa."
The world is firmly grasped; not even a hair’s breadth is leaked. Where else could there be a single thing for you to perceive or know?
Why do you not urgently investigate and grasp this? Yunmen Wenyan said: "To tell you that there is nothing directly before you already constitutes a burying [of the truth].

To further seek words and look for intellectual understanding is to move further and further away from the Way. Thus we know that all who possess a mind are worlds apart from the truth. However, once attained...
For such a person, the fire of the Way has never burned their mouth. Throughout the day they wear clothes and eat food, yet they have never touched a single grain of rice or a single thread of silk.
This is still merely talk regarding the gateway; one must truly attain it in this way before it is realized. Da Jing said:
"When mental thoughts fly about in confusion, take that very mind which is flying about and investigate the place where it flies. When you investigate and find no place, then..."
Where do these fluttering thoughts abide? If you turn back to investigate the investigating mind itself, where is that very mind capable of investigation?

Furthermore, the wisdom that illuminates is fundamentally empty, and the objects it perceives are likewise quiescent. That which is quiescent yet not-quiescent is because there is no person who knows quiescence;

that which illuminates yet does not illuminate is because there is no object to be illuminated. When both object and wisdom are quiescent, the single nature is serene and at ease; this is "returning."
Yuan Yaodao asked, "Xingchong said that if one wishes to attain realization, one should immediately realize it upon standing in this very place.

However, if one's faculties and thoughts are dull, one must investigate day and night until suddenly seeing [the truth]. Do not consider a small measure sufficient; only then can you reach the ultimate conclusion."
Even to brothels and taverns—whether encountering the pure or the defiled, the good or the evil—exhaustively investigate and instruct yourself regarding what you perceive;

only when this realm is fully mastered can one cultivate with perfection and attain mastery over all transformations. Huizhong said: "That sentient beings cannot achieve liberation is due to the burden of their emotions.
To awaken to the Way is easy; to clarify the Way is difficult. Simply shed emotional attachments and views, and the Way will clarify itself of its own accord. "Clarify" means to have faith.
It is like a snake-handler who, trusting in the power of his incantations and medicines, coils and plays with snakes, even handling them within the folds of his sleeves without difficulty;
yet those who do not know the incantations or medicines are struck with terror and flee. To simply observe one’s own mind closely, conceptual views are immediately shattered.
As for the fact that millions of doubts cannot be resolved now, it is because one has not yet seen one's own mind. Yuantou asked Liangshan: "My..."
"How is it when the difficulty of bandits arises? He said, "Exile them to the realm of non-arising. "Is this not the place where they find rest for their bodies and establish their lives?
He said, "Dead water does not harbor dragons. The questioner asked, "What is the dragon within living water? He said, "It stirs up waves but does not create billows.
The questioner asked, "How is it when the mountain torrents suddenly overturn the peaks and valleys? Liangshan came down from his seat and seized him.
He said, "Preceptor, do not let them beat off the corner of this old monk’s *kāṣāya*. Shendeng raised up Dongshan and said: "Greed, anger, and ignorance—how utterly ignorant they are!
Fortunately, today I have come to recognize them. When they walk, I strike; when they sit, I hammer.
Entrust them to the Mind-King for careful examination. For immeasurable eons they have remained unliberated. I ask you three: do you know or not? Shendeng.

"Not so. Greed, anger, and ignorance are truly without cognition; throughout the twelve periods of the day, they act as they please. When walking, they go; when sitting, they follow. Entrusted to the Mind-King, what can be done?
Since beginningless kalpas, one has been fundamentally liberated; why need one further inquire whether there is knowing or not?
Fayen Yi said: "To see the Way is the eye; to clarify the Way is the merit. Thus, one is able to attain great wisdom."

[This is] power. If you have not yet attained such [a state], then even if you cause all the desirable things of the three realms to vanish entirely, as long as there is even the slightest [attachment] remaining, it is not yet permissible.
Ciming’s song says: "The cowherd boy is truly happy; barefoot and clad in robes, his two horns are broad."
Lying across upon the ox, he sings toward the heavens. When people ask what he is doing, the ox is not yet thirsty.
He turns his head to look; his family’s fields are vast. Let him roam in all four directions without restraint; let him wander freely in all eight directions without confinement.

To bring him back, one need only pull at the end of the rope. Little calf, stroke him gently. His strength is not yet complete, so it is difficult to lift him up. For now, leave him to graze in the small plain.

Slope! Fearing that the four hooves might slip as he ascends the high peak, the sun is already high; stop eating grass. Grip the tip of his nose—no young or old. At once, lead him toward the pen to sleep.
Watch him as he wallows in the mud, falling this way and that. Laughing heartily, "Is it good? Is it not?
He then takes up his cross-flute and plays with the wind, shaking the five lakes, the mountains, and the islands. Riding the ox backward, he sheds his robe.
A padded jacket. Those who know the sound need not seek it on the road. If you ask where the cowherd dwells, his whip points east and west, yet there is no single place.
Fengxian cited an ancient saying: "Cleverness cannot withstand birth and death; dry wisdom cannot escape saṃsāra. Daoqi recounted the words of Bodhidharma:
"The *Laṅkāvatāra* can serve as a seal for the mind. The Sūtra says: "All dharmas have no essence of dharma," yet it speaks...
"It is simply this mind that, failing to see its own nature, gives rise to discrimination. This may be called the Great Compassionate Father’s most authentic and ultimate discourse;
it is only that we ourselves fail to receive it. Question: "Does seeing the cessation of thoughts lead to the severance of discrimination?
The Master said: "It is not so. It is like training a horse: when the horse sees its own reflection, it is not startled, because it knows the reflection has arisen from itself."

Therefore, one knows that by not severing discrimination, one also abandons the characteristics of the mind. Observe right now before you as it truly is; not even a hair’s breadth is to be seen. Question:
"The bell and drum originally have no sound. How can one believe this? The Master said: "Just like that sound, there is no creator and no place of abiding.
Because it is ultimately empty, it merely deceives ordinary people. If the sound of the drum were truly existent," [it would not cease].
When the bells are struck together, their sounds should not interfere with one another; this is why Xuansha said, "The bells and drums do not intersect; every phrase is without before or after.
If one does not realize the quiescence of the essence itself, how could there be no before or after in every phrase?
Jiangshan Yuan answered Wang Pingfu, saying: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs are no different from ordinary people; what differs is that they are able to protect and mind themselves."
The waters that overflow the heavens originate from a mere trickle. Within the pure and tranquil mind, there is no reason for thoughts to stir.
How perilous it is when such stirring exceeds the overflowing of the heavens—how could one allow it? When the Buddhas and Patriarchs transmitted the Dharma, they invariably cautioned:

"Guard and uphold it well yourself. If one asks, "Does the Buddha-Dharma end here? the Master replied: "The ultimate words are not cumbersome; it depends solely on how one practices them. When guests arrive, regardless of their status—

The man was lowly. Ignoring the cold and heat, he spoke no other words; he simply closed his eyes and entered meditative concentration. When a fire broke out in the kitchen and storehouse, the Master continued to eat and drink as usual.

Upon finishing his meal, the man asked nothing further. When the Master came out, the madman entered the monastery, killed a monk, and then committed suicide by cutting his own throat; their corpses lay side by side.

He ran to report this to Master Jiaowu. When the Master returned, he passed by the place where the corpse was, yet he never looked at it. He ascended his quarters and sat upright; his attendants stood to one side, hoping for instructions.
The Master closed his eyes, and they were ultimately unable to request his departure. Furong Daokai said: "Those who leave the household life seek liberation from birth and death.
They must let the mind rest and cease its thoughts, severing all attachments. When encountering sounds and forms, they should be like flowers planted upon a stone. When seeing profit..."
It is called a "name. It is like a speck of dust in the eye. Since beginningless time, there is nothing among these that you have not already experienced;
why must you cling to them with such bitter longing? If you do not cease now, when will you? If you can exhaust this present moment, what further matter remains?
If you attain a state where the mind is free from affairs, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are but enemies; all worldly matters will naturally grow cold and indifferent. Only then—
At first, they were compatible with that [approach]. Yinyang Shan did not show himself even until death, refusing to meet anyone;

Shishuang established a "Hall of Withered Trees" where he would sit and sleep with others, desiring only to kill your mind. Touzi had people prepare rice, which he cooked and shared with them together, wishing to have you realize the matter for yourself.
If these former masters had no superior quality, how could they have endured such things? — Zhenjing Wen.

It is said: "People nowadays mostly attain a state where body and mind are stilled and extinguished, where the past and future are severed, and where they think, 'A single thought lasts ten thousand years;
I shall rest and cease. They settle into a state like a cold, withered incense burner in an ancient temple and consider this to be the ultimate realization.
Little do they know that they are instead obstructed by this sublime and wondrous state; their true knowledge and vision fail to manifest, and their spiritual powers and radiance remain unrevealed."
Some maintain that the ordinary mind is the ultimate Way; they hold that heaven is heaven and earth is earth, that a long month has thirty days and a short month has twenty-nine.
This is merely clinging to grass and attaching to wood—ignorant and unconscious, led straight into delusion.

When asked, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? they immediately say, "It is the Master’s hand. When asked, "How is my foot like a donkey’s foot? they immediately say, "It is the Master’s [hand]."
As for "feet," this refers to the conditions for the Elder's birth. He said, "He was a man from such-and-such a province; do not misunderstand this.
One must simply follow the ordinary path as stable and secure, never daring to take another step elsewhere. Have you not seen Linji say: "What I have here is the living meaning of the Patriarchs.
Take it and use it immediately; wherever you stand is the truth"? He did not say that one phrase is acceptable while another is not.
