This is merely because the eyes are not open, and one harbors a hundredfold taboos and hesitations. Even if one speaks in this manner, to suddenly see with clarity at that very moment is still like staring blankly from within a coffin.
It is further said: "The Buddha-dharma is supremely wondrous and non-dual; yet as long as one has not reached this supreme wonder, there will be mutual variations in length and brevity.
If one truly reaches this wonder, then those who have awakened their minds know their own minds as they really are. To investigate [this] to the end is the ultimate.
Ultimately, one has been a Buddha from the very beginning. One is truly sovereign and at ease; truly liberated and pure.
In daily life, one employs only one’s own mind. This mind manifests transformations; grasp them and employ them without questioning right or wrong.
To deliberate with a calculating mind is not it. Nor is it to have no mind at all. Every moment is authentically free, just as each lotus petal remains unstained by water.

Therefore, by deluding one's own mind, one becomes an ordinary being; by awakening to one's own mind, one becomes a Buddha. Nowadays, many do not believe in their own minds and do not awaken to their own minds;
thus they fail to obtain the wondrous enjoyment, peace, and liberation of their own minds. They falsely seek Chan and the Way outside of the mind.

They falsely establish what is extraordinary and falsely give rise to grasping and rejecting. Even if they practice extensively, they mostly fall into the realms of external paths, the two vehicles, meditative stillness, and nihilistic views.
They practice the "great posture" and sit in "forgetting," ignoring day and night, and severing all social ties, saying, "My path-work is not yet complete.
Yet as the years and months flow like a stream, even those of great capacity such as Yunmen and Zhaozhou would say, "I have only these two times for rice gruel and meals."
This involves a distracted use of the mind. Furthermore, it is said: "How could I have the leisure to apply my efforts in such idle matters?
Moreover, for one whose daily practice increases tenfold over kalpas, how could there be time for refined talk? Sīxin Xin presented the verse of the final word, saying: "The final word."
One must simply cut off the path of the mind. Once the gates of the six sense-faculties are empty, the myriad dharmas are without arising or ceasing.
If one thoroughly penetrates this source, there is no need to seek liberation. Throughout my life, I have loved reviling others; it was only for the sake of long-lasting joy. Lingyuan Qing said:

"When students have not yet escaped birth and death, their illness lies in the fact that their 'thieving mind' has not died. The ancients attained liberation from birth and death through a single word—this is the model.
The thieving mind has already died; yet this is not something the practitioner can achieve by themselves. It is truly due to the subtle and profound skill of the master’s forge.
This is like Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, who faced Hou Jing without shifting his expression or voice, yet the heart of Jing was completely withered and drained.
Hong Juefan quotes the *Zongjing lu* as saying: "Although karma is itself the mind, since it arises from the mind, one must likewise receive its retribution from the mind."
How does one treat the retribution of karma? The original answer is: simply realize non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), and karma will naturally become empty.

Therefore it is said: "If one commits no evil karma, one attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime. It is further stated: "Though there is the performance of action, there is no agent"—this is the secret teaching.
Furthermore, all performed actions are merely the mind's arbitrary conceptualization of external phenomena; one must therefore apply counteractive measures against these very conceptualizations.
Grasping at the unreal constitutes karma. If one realizes that the mind does not grasp at objects, then objects do not arise of themselves;
since no phenomena can be drawn into the heart’s embrace, how could karma be formed? The Master explains: when one offers incense to the Buddha, the mind knows it will obtain merit;

when one wields a blade to slaughter, the mind knows it will enter hell. Whether killing or offering, both are the work of a single hand; why then are the karmic retributions of sin and merit so different? It is all due to one's own deluded projections.
It is calculated that such matters exist; for this reason, one has been wrongly submerged in birth and death from time immemorial.
Just as thunder grows a plantain tree and iron turns toward a magnet, both lack an agent, yet such power exists. Because no object is grasped, the object itself is inherently quiescent;

therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha does not admit the existence of consciousness. Furthermore, it is cited that when Kumārajīva placed his hand atop the Buddha’s alms bowl, he thought the bowl was very large and immediately lowered it.

He said: "My mind possesses discrimination; therefore, the bowl has weight and lightness. I know that all things follow one's thoughts. When thought has not yet arisen, its measure is equal to the great void.
Yet now, when discriminative thoughts manifest, the myriad categories are in turmoil. Why, then, are the spiritual responses not equal?
This is entirely because the power of the mind is dim, faint, slight, and inferior. When Wang Xiang lay upon the ice, the fish leaped up."

When Geng Gong bowed to the well, the spring water became clear and cold. This was because his cultivation was single-minded; thus, the response of spiritual efficacy was as swift as an echo. Furthermore, the *Lingyuan* states:
"A practitioner's cultivation is like a person who is ill and must take medicine; the spiritual efficacy of the medicine is easy to perceive."
One must strictly observe dietary prohibitions; otherwise, what benefit is there in taking medicine? Birth and death are a great illness;
the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are the excellent medicine; a defiled mind is a mixture of poisons. If one cannot avoid these, the disease of birth and death will never be diminished.
I cherish these words and recall the *Nirvana Sutra* (or *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*), which says: "In the final age, sentient beings do not give rise to delusions in their minds."
Delusion. The Buddha said that such a person is a bodhisattva in the present life. The *Dharmapada* says: "If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort, this is delusion, not diligence;
only when the mind is free from delusion is diligence boundless. Miaopu said: "Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city:
by day one wards off the six thieves, and by night one remains alert; the commander-in-chief of the central army can then carry out his orders. Not...
"Brandishing the halberd and spear to establish Great Peace. Yuanwu Keqin said: "Thoroughly pervasive and without interval; stillness and illumination are simultaneous.
As the years and months pass, they are forged into a single whole, and the foundation becomes ever more secure. This subtle, continuous functioning truly does not go beyond this.

One should maintain the absolute reality in every situation, so that wherever one touches, it is all that [the Buddha-nature]. In every moment and every particle of dust, everything exists within one's own great perfect mirror."

The more subtle and dense it becomes, the more capable it is of transformation. Yunmen said: "Even if one attains a state where heaven and earth, the great earth, have not the slightest trace of affliction, this is still a 'turning phrase.
Only when not seeing a single color is it half-raised. One must further know there is a time for the 'total raising' before it is complete.
Therefore, Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout both constitute the thorough realization of non-arising, penetrating to the very peak and through to the bottom.

When the great function manifests before one, only then can one emerge from and submerge into the whole body. Beyond merely wishing for others to shoulder the entire burden, one must retreat to guard the realm of the Great Men, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
Yantou said, "A person who has attained the bottom simply guards a state of leisurely ease;
throughout the two-and-six periods of the day, being without desire and without dependence, they naturally transcend all samādhis. Deshan also said, "But..."
Have no affairs in the mind; when there are no affairs in the mind, it is empty, luminous, and quiescently illuminating.

This having been clarified, one must put it into practice. Simply take a step back; the further you retreat, the more clearly it becomes manifest. The more you do not understand, the more power you possess. As soon as a divergent thought arises—
Immediately sever it with fierce resolve so that it does not continue. Then wisdom will shine through with total clarity, and you will tread upon the solid ground at every step.

How could there be any room for likes and dislikes, aversion or compliance, or discrimination within that state? The habitual tendencies of ignorance arise and vanish in an instant; over time, they lose the power to disturb the person.
The ancients used the metaphor of tending cattle—truly, this requires a person of long-standing perseverance. It is direct and straightforward.

The essential point is this: first, forget the view of self. Allow for emptiness, stillness, tranquility, and harmony, moving spontaneously and freely. Regarding all phenomena, there is nothing to grasp or reject.

Amidst every sense organ and every sensory object, respond with immediate liberation, abiding naturally. Moving alone and shining uniquely, the essence of illumination stands solitary; things and self are as one.
Directly and thoroughly, there is no illumination that can be established—like cutting silk, it is cut in a single stroke.
All is cut off. One then spontaneously engages in making a living. Even the Buddha-view and the Dharma-view are not permitted to arise;
thus, the karmic consciousness of worldly afflictions naturally melts away like ice and crumbles like a fortress. When one has nurtured this to fruition, one is as steadfast as a dull-witted pillar.

Established within the station of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one cannot be constrained or gathered back in. How could such a one be willing to enter the womb of a donkey or a horse? Zhaozhou said: "Even if there were a thousand billion..."

Seeking a person who would become a Buddha—among them, one who would become a bottomless vessel is extremely difficult to find. Xianglin spent forty years before he finally attained a single piece [of realization].
Yongquan spent forty years yet still wandered about aimlessly. Nanquan was able to establish his livelihood at eighteen.

The ancients were all like this, practicing in a subtle and continuous manner. Whenever they encountered conditions or met with circumstances, there was nothing they did not carry within their awareness. How could it stop at this?

Throughout this life, reaching to the limits of the future, one may realize immeasurable saintly bodies; yet even these are not the place of ultimate rest. One must simply retreat with single-minded focus;
by all means, do not harbor any limited conceptions. It is further said: "To penetrate birth and death is no small matter;

one must be as fierce and urgent as if saving one's head from fire, only then will there be a slight resonance with the truth. For those practitioners who rely on worldly wisdom and cleverness, when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives—
One cannot exert even a hair’s breadth of power; this is truly because there was no primary cause from the very beginning, resulting in laborious effort at the end that yields no merit.
When ancient worthies exhorted one to practice the Chan of the "Nirvana Hall," they certainly had a profound purpose. Abiding within birth and death is truly not easy;

only those who have attained great transcendence and realization, exerting their sharp faculties with fierce vigor, can sever the single path directly and find no difficulty. Although this depends upon oneself...

The faculties and powers likewise rely on expedient means to function within the ordinary circumstances of daily life. By striking through to the point where conceptual views no longer remain, the entire reality manifests with a chilling clarity.
One should then put this into practice, cultivating it until it becomes thoroughly matured; thus, when the conditions of this life eventually exhaust themselves, one will be ready.

Naturally free from fear, there is only pure vacuity and translucent clarity; not a single dharma confronts the mind. It is like letting go of one’s hands over a precipice—having cast everything away, there is no lingering attachment.
In a single thought, ten thousand years pass; seeking the beginning of life, it cannot be found. How, then, could there be death?

When the ancients "passed away while sitting" or "perished while standing," or when they performed their transformations and died while walking, they were able to attain such courage and vigor because they had undergone refinement and purification throughout their lives.
One attains purity and cleanliness. For forty years, the forest of incense became a single expanse. Shishuang urged [his disciples] to find rest;

Yongjia said, "The essence is non-arising; realizing the original state is swift. Thus, with constant vigilance and trepidation, keeping this in mind at every moment, one finally attains unimpeded mastery.
Once the physical body is cast off, one attains the "body born of intention" (*manomaya-kāya*), following one's own intent toward future retribution—all of which is achieved through principle.

It is not that one is sent away by the pull of karma—meaning, has one truly transcended birth and death? As long as the conditions of retribution have not yet expired, there will necessarily be such worldly entanglements and interactions.
One must ensure that wherever one goes, there is ample room and leisure; only then can it be achieved. Each person has their own karmic lot;
there is no need to loathe clamor and seek quietude. Provided one is inwardly empty and outwardly compliant, even amidst a bustling marketplace or a boiling cauldron, one remains at ease.
It is likewise tranquil and secure; yet, were there even the slightest hair’s breadth of a perceived thorn, one would immediately be unable to prevail. It is further said:

"For those of keen faculties, it is not difficult to attain a thousand awakenings upon hearing once. What is required, however, is that their footing be firm and solid, that they possess thorough and penetrating faith, and that they maintain steadfast composure."

One who has attained mastery over all circumstances—whether favorable or adverse—and over the diverse causes and conditions, unifies them into a single whole. Like the vast void of space, there is not the slightest obstruction or separation;

it is profoundly still and luminously empty, without change or transformation. Though one passes through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, from beginning to end it remains as one and the same;
only then does one attain stability. I see many who are clever, yet whose faculties are floating and whose foundation is shallow, seeking recognition within the realm of words.

One attains transformation; yet, because one remains within worldly conditions that cannot be transcended, and reaches the point where one is unable to break free from the conditions of objective realms, one consequently experiences progress and retreat—this is truly a pity.
The ancients truly underwent every kind of trial and hardship, experiencing them all completely.

Even when their bodies were cut into seven pieces, they did not stir a single thought; their resolve was as firm as iron and stone, until they finally broke through and attained liberation from birth and death.
It is entirely effortless; is this not the transcendence of a great man? A lay bodhisattva practicing the conduct of one who has left the home-life is like a lotus born from fire.
For fame, status, power, and ambition are ultimately difficult to subdue, let alone amidst the turmoil and scorching heat of the burning house.
Unless one attains immediate, direct awakening to the fundamental reality that is wondrously perfect, one cannot reach the great, tranquil samādhi and find rest.
In the field of rest, one is especially able to let go; vast and ordinary, one thoroughly realizes the state of no-mind.
Viewing all phenomena as dreams, illusions, or bubbles, one remains in a state of open emptiness, dispelling them as they arise according to the moment.

Thus, one shares the same primary cause as Vimalakīrti, Master Fu, Layman Pang, Prime Minister Pei, and Vice Director Yang—these superior laymen who, following their own [nature], [attained liberation].
Through this power, they transform their lack of awakening and together enter the ocean of the *dharmatā*—the state of non-action and non-activity.

Thus, having come once to Jambudvīpa, they will not have failed to realize the fundamental purpose. It is further said: "Recently, those such as Pei Xiu and Yang Shou were able to cast aside their worldly concerns with sincere devotion and seek decisive resolution from a master.
By eradicating superficial, deluded perceptions, they attained great enlightenment and were finally able to transcend and surpass the elder Chan masters."

When one’s virtue is such that one’s conduct and practice reach the point where the final blow is struck at the intersection of the horns, one spontaneously releases and lets go, thereby realizing great liberation.
How could this be a small matter? This alone is the root of all worthies and sages, indestructible and immutable throughout a thousand kalpas.
This shows that one’s past lives have also been permeated by [the Dharma], which manifests when conditions meet.

However, if one can examine oneself and study the Buddha-dharma throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, this is already a state of mixed mental application. Therefore, if one sets aside the Buddha-dharma, one will then walk within the truly pure realm.
Simply by relying on this without any admixture, one becomes purely unified and transparently luminous, free from love and hatred, and detached from grasping and rejecting.
Furthermore, do not distinguish between self and other, nor create notions of gain and loss. All phenomena are level and even;
they are all the inconceivable realm of my own home, the very objects of enjoyment that are still, wondrous, perfect, and luminous.

You must cause this mind to be constantly present before you—neither falling into dullness nor giving rise to cleverness—so that you enter a state of equality, peace, and profound stillness. How could there then be any performance of evil deeds?
When consciousness conditions sensory objects, it interferes with this fundamentally wondrous luminosity.
I fear that when facing the realm of sensory objects, one will completely forget and lose it, falling back into prior confusion and disorder; if that happens, it will be unbearable.

The practice of the ancients was simply to use what they themselves had realized and entered to illuminate and clarify during their time, thereby severing worldly toil and keeping the teaching vividly alive for twenty or thirty years.
When one’s years have matured, it is not difficult to transcend birth and death. The effort must lie in practice; do not value mere talk.

To speak for ten *zhang* is not as good as practicing for even one *chi*. For the power of concentration and wisdom to transform karmic conditions, one must remain alert and maintain a courageous, resolute determination.
This will be constantly utilized throughout a thousand or ten thousand lifetimes. As for the other ancient precedents and机缘 (*jīyuán*), they are as follows: [text continues].
Words and phrases need not be employed; yet, once one point is clearly penetrated, every point will be thus.

Amidst a thousand transformations and myriad shifts, how could they ever alter or change its inherent power and function? With the inner mind already empty and external conditions likewise stilled, one puts on clothes and eats food.
It is inherently natural and true; there is no need for laborious carving or polishing. If one were to establish a superior view or harbor a sense of "I" and "mine," it would be a calamity;
one must be most diligent in guarding against this. Through this, one may enter the field that is truly selfless, equal and suchness, unmoving and unchanging, pure, wondrous, cool, and secure.
Master Zhi said: "Do not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation or study. This is formlessness.
Within this light, one is eternally sovereign. It is further said: "A master of the school permits only the relinquishing of knowledge and views;
not even a hair’s breadth remains within the breast. It is vast and empty like the great void, nurtured for ages until it reaches full maturity.

This is the natural radiance of the original ground, the face as it originally is. Reaching this state that spans from antiquity to the present, one is liberated from birth and death—what more could there be?"
It is difficult. Prime Minister Pei and Layman Pang attained it directly through faith; they immediately gained mastery and enjoyed it with total freedom.
Caoshan said, "Go to the place where there is no change. Yet even going, there is no change. This is because their practice has reached its ultimate depth, arriving at the state of total non-leakage.
Only then can one not be ensnared by any conceptual net. For those who study the Way, if there is even a hair’s breadth of intentional thought, they fall into error.
Amidst the conditions of the mundane world, one’s direct mind is like withered wood or rotten stumps, like a great dead man without the slightest breath.
Heart-mind after heart-mind there is no cognition; thought after thought there is no dwelling. Even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not shift or alter it.

Only then can one cause flowers to bloom upon withered wood, manifesting great functional power, giving rise to compassion and exercising pity—this is the function of non-action, the achievement of non-effort.

How could such action fall into the categories of gain and loss, right and wrong? To retain even a hair’s breadth [of conceptualization] is to encounter resistance within the realm of birth and death;
if one cannot yet cross over oneself, how can one deliver others? It is further said: "If one now illuminates and realizes the original mind, it is perfectly interfused and boundless."
Regarding the objects of form and sound, how could they be made into opposites? One must be far removed and uniquely liberated; empty, still, luminous, and wondrous.
One must grasp this thoroughly from the very bottom and not allow it to become superficial. It must be directly supreme and unsurpassed, vast and limitless.

Pure and naked, perfectly complete and solid—leakless and unconditioned. The thousand sages rely upon it as their foundation; all myriad phenomena are established thereby. You must respond accordingly.

Suddenly turning the light back within, one causes all forms and segments to cease. Clearly and perfectly realized, through ten thousand changes and a thousand transformations, there is no alteration and no shifting;
this is called the Vajra King, and it is called penetrating the Dharmakāya. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is nothing that is not thoroughly permeated.
In every object and at every point, there is no interval or separation. This is termed "dry, white, and pure," a singular clarification of one's own mind. One must not stop merely at this.

To guard it—once you are guarding it, you have already fallen into a conceptual trap. You must instead be courageous and sever it; abandon it completely. The more you abandon it, the more clearly it appears;

the further you distance yourself from it, the closer you come to it. Strive with all your might to settle the mind; only when you are willing to sacrifice your very life will you become one who has cut off the breath of discursive thought.
Only then can one understand how to practice toward the ultimate. This is known only by oneself; even this "knowing" does not stand.
Śākyamuni and Maitreya, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, Deshan and Linji—none dare look directly upon it with their eyes. Is this not a wondrous and extraordinary matter?
Whether it be a staff-blow above or a shout below, whether a single phrase or word, coarse or subtle, form or fragrance—they all penetrate through at once.
This is what is called the realm of no-mind. One nurtures oneself until resembling an infant—purely harmonious and profoundly tranquil.
Though dwelling amidst the toil of the mundane world, one is not defiled by that toil; though residing in places of purity and excellence, those states cannot detain one.

Abiding with the nature as it encounters conditions, one eats when hungry and drinks when thirsty; since even good does not give rise to conceptual thought, how could evil ever be committed again? Therefore it is said: "To follow conditions."
Exhaust old karma and no longer create new calamities. It is further said: "The Way prizes the absence of mind; Chan transcends names and principles.

Only by forgetting the self and reaching total cessation can one advance toward it. Turning the light inward to illuminate, one attains a state of total penetration that admits no room for deliberation."
Suddenly, beneath one’s feet, the bottom of the bucket falls away. One enters this great, perfectly round, quiescent, and illuminating gate of supreme and wondrous liberation.

Having realized all through a single realization, one simply abides in a state of leisurely ease. From the outset, there is no distinction between self and other, nor victory and defeat; were there even the slightest speck of a view or a thorn, it would be immediately apparent.
Immediately uproot it completely. Let it go so that you may attain the sevenfold penetration and the eightfold mastery, moving with ease and freedom.
Nurture this pure density until even a thousand sages cannot see it; even your own self will seem like an enemy. Seek only to distance yourself from it, never leaning toward or dwelling beside it.

Be carefree and pure, empty yet numinous, still yet illuminating. With courageous decisiveness, cut through everything until there is not the slightest hair’s breadth of disturbance remaining in your breast.
Master Wang calls this "making a livelihood. Zhaozhou says that except for the times of eating porridge and rice, it is all "miscellaneous mental activity.
One must practice over a long period until it becomes thoroughly matured; only then will it accord with the mindless embodiment of the Way transmitted from of old.

This is the subtle, continuous functioning where one personally perceives one's own progress. Reaching the final point of culmination, one naturally lets go like a hand released from a precipice—how joyful! Furthermore:
It is said: One must first enter the practice and encounter a person of true substance, directly cutting through to the root.

Retreating to one’s own self, with an iron-like heart, one must at once cast away all prior deluded thoughts and views, worldly wisdom and cleverness, and all notions of self and other, gain and loss.
At this very moment, becoming like a withered tree or extinguished ashes, with emotions exhausted and views eliminated, one suddenly attains realization, following in the footsteps of the ancestors.
The Sages do not shift or alter even a single hair’s breadth. Only when one sees through to this point does it become the gateway for entering the Principle.

Furthermore, you must be taught that in a single thought-moment there are ten thousand years, pure and without admixture. Should there arise even the slightest flicker of arising or ceasing, one falls into the twenty-five realms of existence, with no hope of liberation.
Even at the cost of death, you must stubbornly bite into the teachings until they are severed; only then will your ground be stable and secure.

Within the realms of both the holy and the ordinary, one cannot be confined; this is truly like a bird escaping its cage. It is the place where one rests of one’s own accord and brings all to completion.

Having attained the seat and donned the robe, like pure gold refined a hundred times, every movement and action is effortlessly vast and open. As for the sense bases, the objects of perception, and birth-and-death—[they are all transcended].
The emptiness of object and wisdom is as wondrous as snow melted by hot water. One always knows the proper time for oneself and has nothing beyond this; such a person is called a "mindless wayfarer.
By cultivating oneself through this, one further awakens those who have not yet realized it and causes them to practice in this manner—is this not the essential path?

It is further said: When thoughts have not yet arisen and the hundred [afflictions] do not occupy the mind, one is perfectly interfused and boundless, the entire being is empty and still, and all that is done is free from doubt;

this is called the "manifestation of one's original portion. However, as soon as even a hair’s breadth of intellectual understanding arises, and one desires to take hold of it as a master, one immediately falls into the realm of the five aggregates and is seized by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Losing oneself in the entanglements of right and wrong is like being half-drunk and half-awake.

To penetrate to the very top and bottom and achieve direct, total perfection is to be entirely without form or appearance, yet without ceasing one's effort and without hindering one's activity. Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether arising or falling, it is not another person;
were there even the slightest trace of obstruction, it would all be mere deluded thought. One must simply be free and easy, as vast as empty space.
Emptiness is like a mirror set upon its stand, like the sun shining in the sky; movement and stillness, coming and going, are not obtained from without.
Let them be as they are, free and sovereign, neither bound by dharmas nor seeking liberation through dharmas. From beginning to end, all is forged into a single piece.
Where could there be worldly dharmas outside of Buddha-dharma? Where could there be Buddha-dharma outside of worldly dharmas? Therefore, the Patriarchs directly—
This points to the human mind. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* values the person who is free from signs (*animitta*). It is like a strong man bending his arm: it does not rely on external power.
Such a realization must be cultivated by long-term retreating and investigating within oneself, so as to bring about a place of definitive, true realization.
This is precisely to be constantly and universally studying under boundless and immeasurable great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Furthermore, it is said: "Thoroughly..."

Realizing the state of no-mind, though one responds instantaneously to ten thousand stimuli, how could this disturb the spirit? Though one faces a thousand difficulties with diverse responses, they do not trouble the mind.

In ordinary times, one appears as if dull-witted; yet when facing matters for the sake of sentient beings, one acts with the swiftness of whirling winds and flashing lightning, never failing to meet the occasion.

This is because one has long maintained a fundamental constancy. It is like learning archery: only after a long time does one hit the mark. Awakening occurs in a single kṣaṇa, but the practice of cultivation must rely upon sustained effort.
It is long-lasting. Therefore, those who have attained awakening and clarity must precisely practice subduing.

Just as various sensory objects constantly flow within and create obstructions, for one who has reached the ultimate state, there is nothing that is not empty and penetrating; it is entirely one’s own great gate of liberation.
Though acting all day long, one never truly acts; there is no longing or aversion, nor is there any weariness. Having completely crossed over...

All things are devoid of subject and object; how much less could there be any room for weariness or indolence? If one’s nature is by temperament biased or deficient, one should especially augment those capacities in which one is lacking.

By means of the power of *upāya* (skillful means), one should encompass and transform others while opening the provisional gates; responding to all with grace and composure, one ensures that whether high or low, far or near, there is not the slightest error.
One should constantly practice the conduct of Never-Disparaging and emulate the Immortal of Forbearance, following the tracks of the Buddhas of the past.
He perfected the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and made firm the practice of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Reaching the stage where great function manifests before him, he was equal in both the noisy and the silent, like a boat descending a river that requires no oars or poles. In seamless fusion and all-encompassing inclusion, he fully realized the aspects of Samantabhadra’s conduct;
thus, throughout life after life, he was a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the world. He moved and responded adaptively in all places, yet remained empty within them.
Regarding the awakening to stillness: if one is not bound by that stillness, then wherever one goes, it shall all be one’s livelihood.

One should simply be empty within while conforming to the world without; even if those with a fundamental basis interfere unreasonably, merely retreat and reflect upon yourself, cutting off [the interference] directly on the spot, as if you had never heard or seen it before.
After a long time, demonic activities will naturally dissolve. It is also said: "If days pass..."
It is unchanging. When one has become proficient in seizing, handling, withdrawing, and releasing, all minor realms can be thoroughly illuminated and severed, leaving no trace behind.
At the threshold of birth and death, the patterns are interlaced like a mesh, without mutual confusion; it is limpid and unmoving, transcending with effortless ease.
This is the Chan of the Nirvana Hall on the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month. Dahui Zonggao said: Twelve.
At all times and in whatever circumstances you encounter, do not allow evil thoughts to continue in succession.
Should you fail to maintain mindfulness and a single evil thought arise, you must immediately sharpen your focus and pull your head back around.

If you let it go its way and it continues without interruption, this not only obstructs the Path, but such a person is called one lacking wisdom. Lan’an said: "Once they have entered the weeds, pull them back by the nose; this is how one restrains evil."

You should reflect upon the practice of Nan’an’s “Tending the Ox,” for through long-term cultivation, it will naturally become proficient. This matter is entrusted to those of sharp and keen capacity;

if one relies on mere cleverness, there is no possibility of taking up this burden. Though such a person may enter easily, they find it difficult to maintain, for their entry is not deep and their strength is weak.
The worldly affairs of dust and toil are like a chain of interlocking links that never cease; only when one attains realization can they be severed.

One must be frugal with one's time. Because these habits have been cultivated since beginningless time, if one does not strive to contend against them, one will unknowingly and imperceptibly fall deeper into them over the years.

On the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, when death arrives, one will be unable to manage one’s own affairs. If you wish to avoid being deluded at the moment of death, [you must practice now].
Now, in this place of practice, do not allow things to become inverted. If they are inverted now, there is no possibility that they will not be inverted at the time of death.
Worldly people dwell within the burning house; they take greed, hatred, and delusion as their companions, and everything they see and hear is nothing but evil karma.

Yet, if one can strike through to the bottom within this state, that power is a thousand times superior to that of those who have left the household life. One should [manifest] in the body of a high official.
As for "delivering," it means manifesting in the body of a civil or military official to preach the Dharma; this is precisely how one repays the profound kindness of the Buddha.
One must simply maintain this state of mind without interruption from moment to moment. Do not concern yourself with whether you succeed or fail;

even if you do not attain thorough penetration in this life, at the end of your life you will not be dragged away by evil karma, nor will you be fettered by worldly toil during your daily activities. When you emerge in future lives, you will likewise attain realization as it is.

Regarding its enjoyment: although one may not realize it in this life, one nevertheless plants the seed of *prajñā*. Thus, birth after birth, one will not lose the human body nor fall into the evil realms;
how much more so when the flower of the mind blooms with clarity! It is further said: "Often those of sharp faculties obtain it without expending effort."
If one gives rise to an easygoing mind, one will fail to practice. One will be frequently carried away by present circumstances and unable to maintain mastery over them.
Over time, one becomes deluded and fails to return; when the power of the Way cannot overcome the power of karma, demons find their opportunity and will surely take one under their sway.
If you do not gain strength at the moment of death, remember this well: in principle, there is sudden enlightenment; by means of this awakening, all is simultaneously extinguished.
In practice, however, things are eliminated gradually, coming to an end through successive stages. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must never forget this.

As for the various other distinct sayings of the ancients, they can neither be taken as real nor as unreal. After a long time of pure cultivation, one will naturally attain a silent resonance with the fundamental source.

The mind—there is no need to seek anything else extraordinary or marvelous. It is further said: "To hollow out one's fundamental nature, eliminate auxiliary causes, and oppose manifest karma—this is the man who has completed his task;
among all methods of cultivation and realization, this is the true method and true cultivation. It is further said:

If those of the Daoist school, by means of a mind of deluded thought, are still able to preserve their physical forms and remain in this world, how much more so for one whose mind is entirely within *prajñā*?
When emerging in future lives, it will follow the power of my vows in this life, remaining securely within *prajñā* to be manifest and fully utilized.
This is a certainty. Furthermore, he replied to someone: "Sentient beings are inverted; they take the objects of daily life to be real, not knowing that [they are entirely]..."
The substance is a dream; within it, one further engages in false discrimination, binding the mind with thoughts and taking the spirit-consciousness (*vijñāna*) to be real.

One does not realize that while dreaming, one is speaking of a dream—a perversion upon perversion. Gaofeng once asked his former teacher, who simply pointed his finger and said, "Stop, stop! Cease your false conceptualization.

Gaofeng said, "Before I fell asleep, the Buddha praised following [the teachings]; the Buddha— (Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment, likely from a Zen discourse or commentary. The final sentence is incomplete, as it ends abruptly after "佛" (Buddha).)
He dares not transgress. Whatever he obtains through his teacher’s instruction or by his own minor efforts, he may enjoy it while he is conscious and alert.
However, once he has climbed into bed, he becomes the master no longer; if he dreams of gold and jewels, he rejoices, and if he dreams of swords, blades, or evil scenes, he is distressed.
He thinks, "Once I have fallen fast asleep, I am no longer the master," let alone when the four elements disperse and he finally begins to feel anxious. The Master said, "Wait."
"You say that when so many delusive thoughts cease, you yourself arrive at the state where waking and sleeping are eternally one.
At first, you did not believe this; waking and sleeping were clearly two distinct segments, yet you dared to open your great mouth and speak of Chan.

Later, upon hearing the raising of the question regarding 'the place where all Buddhas emerge'—that 'a fragrant breeze blows from the south'—you cast off the object that had been choking your chest. Only then did you realize that the time of dreaming is precisely the time of waking."
The moment of waking is precisely the moment of dreaming. When the Buddha says that waking and sleeping are always one, only then does one come to know this for oneself;
it cannot be picked up and presented to others. Having received your inquiry, I have unwittingly made a true confession. Your instruction was not wrong, nor was my question on Zen incorrect.
Being pressed to respond, I could not help but disclose what I have long doubted. I pray that you will use the words of Old Pang to stir my mind; I only wish to empty all that is perceived.
"There is. Be careful not to take what does not exist as real. First, take the objects before you and understand them as being like a dream;
then, bring that which was in the dream back to the present moment. Then, the Buddha’s golden drum and Confucius’s collapsing pillars will certainly no longer be dreams. He also said:

"Only when you see the Buddhas and Patriarchs as if they were born enemies will you have a slight measure of response. Practice your work in this way for a long time, and do not let it arise [as a conceptual attachment]."
The mind: the ox is tamed of itself; the monkey dies of itself. As the cited scripture says:

"The mind does not falsely conceptualize past phenomena, nor does it greedily cling to future events, nor does it dwell upon the present. It thoroughly realizes that the three periods of time are entirely empty and quiescent.
One does not reflect upon the past, nor calculate the future, nor direct the mind toward the favorable or adverse in the present. It further states:
Regarding those things that oppose my will, it is sufficient to settle and examine them with the single character "patience" (忍); they will pass away in a short time.
As for favorable conditions, there is simply no place to avoid them; they are like a magnet and iron, which unconsciously draw together as one.
If even insentient objects behave thus, how much more so for active ignorance (無明), whose entire body resides within us? Without wisdom, we remain unaware and unknowing, being led astray by it.
To seek escape from this net—is it not difficult? Thus, to be able to enter the world and yet transcend it without remainder is precisely this principle.

Alas, those who have recently lost their skillful means often mistake active ignorance for "entering the world," and then forcibly manipulate the supramundane teachings to claim they have achieved the state of transcending the world without remainder. How tragic! [Except for...]
Having long possessed a vow, one immediately recognizes and breaks through [delusion], attaining mastery and remaining unobstructed by hindrances. Quoting the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

for those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the Buddha taught that liberation consists in being free from lust, anger, and delusion; yet for those without such pride, the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is itself liberation.
If one avoids this error, then amidst favorable and adverse conditions, there will be no signs of arising or ceasing; only then can one truly enter and attain the world.
There is no world beyond [this]. The above is what Miao-xi experienced in the past; it is the very function of today. Practice in this way alone.
I vow that while my physical strength remains robust, I too shall enter this samādhi. He further said: "A skilled cowherd always holds the rope in his hand;
how could the cattle then damage the crops? If one suddenly lets go of the rope, there will be no place to grasp the cow's nostrils. Compassion.
"Clarifying" means letting [the mind] go in all four directions without obstructing it. When you wish to gather it back, simply pull on the end of the rope.

If you cannot yet do this, you must hold the end of the rope tightly and first practice "combing along" with it. Once your training through prolonged soaking becomes mature, you will naturally no longer need to apply deliberate effort or maintain defensive vigilance.
If you are too hurried, you become restless; if you are too slow, you become dull and lax—both lead to missing the mark. This is Master Puzhao’s secret instruction for cultivating the mind.

It is said: "The mind of emptiness and stillness does not increase for the sage, nor does it decrease for the ordinary person. That which distinguishes Buddhas and patriarchs from other people is their ability to protect and maintain mindfulness.
From beginningless time until now, ordinary beings have been subject to deluded thoughts and inversions; the seeds and habits of ignorance have long since become one with their nature."
Although one may suddenly awaken to fundamental stillness, which is no different from that of a Buddha, habitual tendencies are difficult to sever.

When encountering circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, anger, joy, and the notions of right and wrong arise and cease with blazing intensity. If one does not apply effort toward Prajñā, how can one counteract the signless and reach the ground of great rest?
As it is said: "Though sudden awakening is equal to that of a Buddha, the habitual tendencies of many lifetimes are deep; when the wind ceases, the waves still stir."

[The karmic residue] surges up; though the principle has manifested, habitual thoughts still intrude. Master Gaō said: "Those of sharp faculties dispel [delusions] without expending effort, and thus they easily give rise to a sense of ease.
If they do not further cultivate and refine [their realization], after a long time they will again wander through saṃsāra as before. How, then, can what was realized in a single lifetime suffice?"

Is it that one sets [practice] aside and cultivates only after awakening? Therefore, even after awakening, one must constantly maintain inspection. If delusive thoughts arise, one does not follow them at all.
By diminishing and further diminishing, one reaches the state of non-action (*wuwei*); only then is the practice of "herding the ox" perfected.

Although there is cultivation subsequent to awakening, because one has previously realized that delusive thoughts are fundamentally empty and the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, one neither cuts off evil nor cultivates good.
To practice without practicing is the true cultivation and true severance. Therefore, although one fully cultivates the myriad practices, one takes non-thought as the primary principle.
Caoxi said: "When the mind-ground is free from confusion, it is the self-nature of concentration; when the mind-ground is free from delusion, it is the self-nature of wisdom.

This spontaneous, tranquil awareness—in which cessation and illumination are non-dual—is the simultaneous cultivation of concentration and wisdom characteristic of the Sudden Teaching. Nevertheless, for those whose obstructions are thick and whose habits are heavy...

Observing that the inferior mind is restless, the power of ignorance is great while the power of *prajñā* is small; regarding objects of good and evil, one cannot avoid being moved by the alternation of activity and stillness.
For one whose mind is not tranquil and placid, there are indeed false conditions; thus, the practice of dispelling and purifying them is necessary. As it is said:

"When the six sense organs perceive their objects and the mind does not follow along with conditions, this is called concentration (*samādhi*). When both mind and objects are empty, and the mirror-like reflection is free from delusion, this is called..."

Wisdom: If restlessness (*auddhatya*) is rampant, one first employs the gate of concentration (*samādhi*) to gather the teachings in accordance with principle; the mind does not follow external conditions and accords with primordial stillness (*prakṛti-śānti*).
If dullness (*styāna-middha*) is particularly prevalent, one first employs the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*) to collect phenomena and contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

reflecting clearly without delusion, one accords with primordial knowing (*prakṛti-jñāna*). Use concentration to remedy discursive thoughts and wisdom to remedy indeterminate states (*avyākṛta*); when the mechanisms of movement and stillness have ceased, one faces [reality].

When the work of cultivation is complete, one encounters circumstances and conditions such that every thought accords with the Way; practicing both spontaneously and effortlessly, one finally becomes a person of no affairs. Why is this?

Because the capacities of those in this Sudden Teaching gate vary in superiority and inferiority. Although they have first attained sudden enlightenment, their afflictions may still be thick and their habitual tendencies heavy;

they may be obscured by confusion and lose the clarity of their innate, ever-present awareness. In such cases, one must rely on the meditative concentrations and wisdom of counteractive measures to bring them into balance.

It harmonizes the turbid and chaotic, leading even to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Although it temporarily tames habitual tendencies through the power of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), because one has previously attained sudden awakening to the fact that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure and afflictions are fundamentally empty, this practice—though intended for those of gradual capacity—is, from the perspective of one who has awakened, like "turning iron into gold.
I pray you will examine these words and no longer harbor doubt. Within this direct discourse of the true mind, the authentic is distinguished.

The mind ceases its delusive clouds. One uses the method of "no-mind" (amind) to govern the deluded mind; this is not a state of no-mind as a substantial entity. Rather, when there is nothing within the mind, it is called "no-mind.
Various masters explain the practice of the "no-mind" cultivation differently; ten such approaches will be briefly clarified here. The first is called "vigilant observation":

remaining ordinarily free from discursive thought while remaining on guard against the arising of thoughts. As soon as a thought arises, one perceives and breaks through it, so that subsequent thoughts do not arise, and even the perception [of the thought] vanishes.
Do not employ them. When both false thoughts and awakening are forgotten, it is called "no-mind. This is the cessation of delusion. Second is "resting":

this means not thinking of good or evil; as soon as the mind arises, one rests; when encountering conditions, one simply ceases. Only when one is cool and still, like a dazed or inert person, will there be some slight correspondence with the Way.

This is "resting the deluded mind. Third is "extinguishing the mind while preserving the object": this means that all delusions have ceased together, and one disregards external objects, merely allowing the mind itself to rest.

Since the deluded mind has already ceased, what obstacle could there be to the existence of objects? This is "not taking away the person but taking away the object," wherein one extinguishes delusion by preserving the object while extinguishing the mind.
Fourth is "extinguishing the object while preserving the mind": one contemplates all internal and external objects as entirely empty and quiescent.
When the true mind shines alone, it is "seizing the object but not seizing the person"; this means the object is obliterated while the mind is preserved, thereby quelling delusion.

Fifth, "obliterating both mind and object" means that both the internal mind and the external object are simultaneously stilled; this is "seizing both person and object," whereby the mind and object are both obliterated to quell delusion.
Sixth, the preservation of objects and the preservation of mind: this means that the mind abides in the state of mind and objects abide in the state of objects.

Mind and objects face one another; the mind does not grasp the object, and the object does not confront the mind. Each remains without reaching the other. This is the dharma abiding in its own position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.

This means that both person and environment are not deprived [of their true nature]; it is the preservation of both environment and mind to extinguish delusion. Seventh, the total identity of the internal and external:

this refers to all phenomena—the internal body and the external vessel of the world—being identical to the essence of the True Mind. They are profoundly still, empty, and luminous, without the slightest difference; they are forged into a single whole.
This is the cessation of delusion through the total identity of the internal and external. Eighth, the total function of the internal and external: this refers to the internal and external body...
Regarding all phenomena within the realm of the mental organ and all movements, activities, and functions: observe them all as the wondrous functioning of the true mind.
As soon as a single thought arises, this wondrous functioning manifests before you. This is the complete cessation of delusion through the total functioning of both the internal and external.

Ninth is "the essence is itself the function": within emptiness and stillness there is numinous clarity; the essence is itself the function. Within numinous clarity there is emptiness and stillness; the function is itself the essence. Thus, it is both alert and tranquil.
This is so: "Vigilant conceptualization is not; tranquil vigilance is. "Tranquil non-recording is not.
This is the essence and the function, the stilling of delusion. The tenth is "penetrating through essence and function," which means not distinguishing between essence and function.

Throughout the four quarters and eight directions, there is only a single great gate of liberation. Perfectly round and complete, essence and function are undivided; the entire body is forged into a single piece.
This refers to the essence and function of transcending and penetrating to extinguish delusion. Above, it is not necessary to employ all [methods] completely;
it suffices to achieve mastery in one gate, and delusion will naturally cease. According to one’s faculties and past habits, whatever dharma one has an affinity for, that is what one should practice.
This Dharma-gate of resting the deluded mind is most essential; therefore, it is explained extensively. Regarding the discernment of how the true mind emerges from birth and death, it says:
Birth and death are fundamentally non-existent; they are falsely reckoned as existing, like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky—these are not real.
If one now knows that birth and death are non-existent yet cannot escape them, it is because one's spiritual cultivation has not reached its full measure. The woman Āmrapālī asked:
"If one clearly knows that birth is the dharma of non-birth, why is one still turned by birth and death? Mañjuśrī replied: "Because its power is not yet sufficient."

Regarding his judgment on the true mind and its primary and auxiliary practices: when delusion has not yet ceased, taking the cessation of delusion through non-mind as the primary practice and the cultivation of various virtues as the auxiliary practice;
for while the dharma-body of True Suchness is empty and pure in its essential nature, it is nevertheless defiled by immeasurable afflictions.
Without various kinds of cultivation through skillful means, one will likewise not attain purity; therefore, one must cultivate all wholesome practices as an antidote.
Nowadays, people rely on their own so-called "innate truth" and do not practice various virtues; they cannot even avoid the evil realms, let alone escape birth and death.

Regarding the examination of the true mind and the verification of its function, it is said: "It is like herding oxen; although they have been tamed, one still dares not let go of the whip and the rope. Directly...
Wait until you have entered among the crops without harming them; only then may you dare to let go of your hand. First, bring the objects of attachment before your mind.

If thoughts of love or hatred arise, they are not yet mature; if they do not arise, they are mature. Furthermore, when encountering objects of love or hatred, deliberately arouse the intention to grasp them.
If love or hatred does not arise, this is the mind being unimpeded—like a white ox in an open field that does not damage the crops.
I personally maintain that the fundamental matter of the Chan school is entirely contained within the few words of the Sixth Patriarch:

"Who would have expected that one's own mind is fundamentally pure, fundamentally complete, and fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing. Niu-tou Rong also said: "The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."
All is fundamentally contained within the source of the mind, fully and spontaneously complete. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are, from the beginning, empty and quiescent.
Those of future wisdom must know that the self-nature is naturally authentic, replete with all dharmas, yet inherently extinguished in its very place, ultimately possessing nothing at all.
Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations—this is the inconceivable Sea-Seal Samādhi of Non-characteristic. Mazu said: "It is not the practice of sages or worthies;
it is not the practice of ordinary beings; it is the practice of Bodhisattvas. It does not grasp at good, nor does it reject evil.

One penetrates the emptiness of the nature of offenses, such that they cannot be apprehended in every thought-moment, for they lack self-nature. The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by this single Dharma. Self-...
The nature is originally complete and sufficient; one who does not become obstructed by matters of good or evil is called a practitioner of the Way.

To grasp at good and reject evil, or to encounter emptiness and enter meditative absorption, belongs to the realm of conditioned fabrication. A single thought of delusion is the very root of birth and death within the three realms.
If one simply has no such thoughts, the root of birth and death is eliminated, and one attains the unsurpassed precious treasure of the Dharma King.
Furthermore, one does not pass through successive stages or positions, but awakens suddenly to one's original nature, such that there is nothing remaining.
It is simply because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been ill with the view that all phenomena are substantially real;

moreover, their defiled attachments and habitual tendencies vary in degree, being either light or heavy. Therefore, after attaining realization, the Patriarchs universally instructed people to "know nothing and understand nothing."
Throughout the day, one remains eternally tranquil like space; every thought-moment accords with one's fundamental nature.

After a long time, one’s strength becomes sufficient, and the various concentrations, wisdoms, supernormal powers, and merits inherent in one's original nature will manifest spontaneously without being sought. This occurs without departing from this very life.
One immediately attains liberation. Baizhang said: "Right now, it is like empty space; only when study has begun to bear fruit will one follow the old path at the time of death.
If you fear the confusion and agitation at the moment of death, you must attain freedom right now.
Huangbo said: "Simply leave behind all dharmas of existence and non-existence; the mind is like the sun, ever-present in the void, its light shining forth."
It clarifies that spontaneity illuminates without the act of illuminating. Reaching this point where there is no place to rest is precisely walking the path of all Buddhas;
it is your own pure *dharmakāya*. Because your strength is small, you cannot transcend suddenly. You must simply obtain thirty or fifty years [of practice].
You must first find a point of entry; then you will naturally understand. The Patriarch pointed directly at your mind, saying it is fundamentally Buddha.
Because every thought is no different [from this nature], he was called the Patriarch. Do not deliberate upon good or evil; in that very moment, you shall emerge from the three realms.
As for sentient beings who cycle through existence without ceasing, their mental objects run wild and their minds do not rest within the six paths, thereby causing them to undergo various sufferings.
This plants the seeds of suffering. You should now simply practice being mindless, like a dull-witted person or a stubborn stone.
Only when all phenomena fail to penetrate your mind will you be in accord. When no thoughts arise and all conditions cease to be born, this very body and mind are those of a free person.
Linji said: "Right now, as you listen to the Dharma, the man who relies on nothing is vividly and clearly manifest. Not yet...
There has never been any lack. If you wish to be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, simply see in this way: when mind after mind does not differ, it is called the "Living Patriarch.
All phenomena have no self-nature, nor do they have a nature of arising; there are only empty names, and even those names are empty. To recognize these idle names is to err.
Even if they were to exist, they would all depend on shifting conditions—there is a basis for bodhi and a basis for nirvana.
The reliance on liberation; the reliance on the object and wisdom; the reliance on the Bodhisattva; the reliance on the Buddha. What thing do you seek within these shifting dependencies?
If you seek the Buddhas and patriarchs, you will be bound by the demons of the Buddhas and patriarchs. All seeking is suffering; it is better to have nothing to do.
As cited above, all of this concerns the correct practice for tuning the mind after awakening. This enters through the Gate of Perfect Emptiness within the Sudden and Perfect School.
If one can practice in accordance with this, it constitutes the correspondence between realization and conduct;

furthermore, one will attain the mutual permeation of precepts and practice, such that within this very lifetime, one will surely attain profound realization as swiftly as the wind. However, as spiritual capacities are not uniform, there may be those among the laity who cannot avoid worldly entanglements.
Should their habitual tendencies be thick, even if they achieve a momentary glimpse of awakening, they will repeatedly be obscured by dullness, distraction, greed, and anger.
When such faults recur frequently and you are unable to maintain mastery in every situation, you must bring them up within the perspective of your own fundamental nature and inquire:
"Are this dullness, distraction, greed, and anger originally empty and still? Do they only arise when the mind is deluded by emotions? Or do they truly arise as soon as they manifest?"
When there is thorough illumination, the very essence is quiescent and extinguished; the fundamental state manifests before one, and all delusions of dullness and distraction naturally vanish away.
If you are still unable to find rest, you must further reflect with deep urgency upon your wandering through many lifetimes.

Having fortunately attained clarity regarding this one crucial point in this present life, how could you again follow after [delusions] and fall? You must reproach yourself with bitterness; once you have entered [this state],...

Grass. Pull it back with force. Furthermore, select those afflictive tendencies (*vāsanā*) that are most predominant and treat them first: use loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to treat anger; generosity (*dāna*) to treat stinginess;

meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to treat distraction; wisdom (*prajñā*) to treat dullness; mindfulness of the Buddha to treat delusion; and the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to treat lust.
One should consult spiritual mentors and study the scriptures and teachings to eliminate these obscurations and hindrances, and then practice diligently.
First, eliminate [afflictions]; then residual habits will gradually be exhausted. Baizhang said: "If there are illnesses such as greed and anger, one must first treat them.
If a śramaṇa does not eliminate the illnesses of greed and anger, he must also be taught to practice dhyāna and study wisdom. Nanquan said:
"If you do not practice within this inner realm, how can you subdue the five kinds of greed and the two kinds of desire? Yuanwu said: "Observe..."
The ritual procedures of the former Buddhas bring about the accomplishment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (namely, the seven factors of awakening, the eightfold path, and so forth).

Within the *Heart-Cultivation Instructions*, it is also taught that one must apply remedies to balance concentration and wisdom, thereby harmonizing dullness and agitation. For the individual who has attained awakening, this is like turning iron into gold.
As for the continuous, moment-to-moment awareness and illumination, one must exert diligent effort and take steps within the void; one must exhaustively push the father toward the interior.
Head! Put it down, and put it down again. Throughout the two-and-six periods of the day, struggle against the state of being congealed with emptiness where there is nothing to grasp.
Practice for years, whether walking or sitting, never relaxing for a single moment. Only then may you hope to quickly bring this life to its final resolution.

This must be examined by each person through self-reflection. If, after awakening, the light of the mind is revealed and manifests everywhere, it will not be obstructed by attachment, aversion, dullness, or distraction.
[If you are] obscured, you need only allow things to proceed spontaneously (*yinyun*) while nurturing the holy embryo; thus you become a man of the Way who has nothing to do.

However, if worldly conditions are heavy with toil and past habits are dense, and if you do not rouse your spirit through various skillful means—reproaching and disciplining yourself, speaking of emptiness at every turn while walking in existence at every step, or regarding such remedies as merely matters of the *Śāstra* vehicle—then [you will fail]. Regarding the *Zong* (the Essence):
This is something for which even the sons of noble families would feel disdain. Some, believing that afflictions are themselves bodhi, proceed to pursue them with unrestrained license.

Thus, the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is turned into poison. They fail to reflect upon the instructions regarding the necessity of gradual elimination and sequential exhaustion of causes.
Consequently, their dry wisdom cannot withstand the power of karma; like empty flowers, they yet produce empty fruits. By the time winter arrives...

At the end of the month, there was no sign of efficacy whatsoever. The *He lun* (Compendium) quotes Master Wuye, who said: "Nowadays, those who explain the Way of Chan are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
yet they have not eliminated even a speck of dust, so they cannot avoid the cycle of saṃsāra. They fail to let go of even a single thread of thought, and thus all fall into ruin.

Observing their speech, they disparage the Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles; examining what they practice, they are not even equal to ordinary people who observe the Five Precepts. At the moment of death, [they encounter] the Holy..."
Ordinary sentiments and intellectual measures are not yet exhausted; even the slightest speck of dust or thread of thought has not been forgotten.
Under the weight of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one takes form within the wombs of donkeys and horses, being boiled and scorched in cauldrons of boiling water and glowing embers.

All prior memories and insights are suddenly lost, and one returns once more to be a termite, ant, mosquito, or gadfly. Though the cause was virtuous, one encounters an evil fruit. This is the gathering of the three thousand great...
Even with the iron of a thousand worlds, one could not cast this single great character of error.

Those who have entered the holy and awakened their minds naturally understand how to manage their own livelihood; they turn their fundamental nature into their practice, making use of it throughout the day.
The twelve earthly branches: this constitutes cultivation arising from the fullness of nature, with full cultivation residing within nature.

Within this interval, one undergoes much ripening through successive births, yet without departing from the present life, one realizes the stage of sainthood. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Those who do not regress throughout their lives will certainly enter the stage of sainthood."
Dazhu said: "One who attains sudden enlightenment does not depart from this life but immediately attains liberation. At the very moment of cultivation, one enters the rank of Buddhahood.
One who attains sudden enlightenment does not depart from this life but immediately transcends the three realms. He further said: "Such achievements are rooted in practice.
If one does not subdue the mind before entering [the path], there is no possibility of attaining realization; such a person deceives themselves and deceives others."

Both fall together. Exert yourselves, exert yourselves! However, those who are but guests under the Chan school discuss only the realization of nature (*jìngxìng*), not meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) or liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Within the Tiantai teachings it is also said: "People's understandings differ. Some say that through sudden awakening one is immediately a Buddha, with no further distinction of stages.
Yet other masters say that sudden awakening at the initial stage is itself the ultimate, perfect, and quiescent extinction."
Regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), what stages or positions can there be? For within the equal Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one does not even discuss awakening or non-awakening;
how then could one distinguish between shallow and deep? Once it is possible to discuss awakening and non-awakening, what prevents one from discussing the shallow and the deep?

Furthermore, although the equal Dharma-realm is beyond speech and demonstration, the stages and positions of the Bodhisattva’s practice are nonetheless vividly manifest. *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) asks: "How is the One Mind accomplished?"

Regarding the Way of the Buddha, must one still rely upon traversing the stages and positions (*bhūmi*) for cultivation and realization? Answer: This abiding-free true mind is truly not something that can be cultivated, cannot be realized, and cannot be attained.

It cannot be realized because it is not a fruit to be grasped; it cannot be attained because it is not a dharma to which one can cling; and it cannot be cultivated because it is not a conditioned phenomenon.
If one speaks of stages and positions, these belong to the practice gates of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and even there, [it is not to be found].
This is illogical. For within the state of non-position (*anavasthā*), to discuss sequential positions is to give rise to the fixed attachment that things either exist or do not exist.

The sutras clarify that the distinctions between the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are like the tracks of birds in the sky. If from the perspective of the gate of perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), what sequence could there be in the quiescent true suchness (*tathatā*)?

If from the perspective of the gate of sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), there is indeed progression as one advances by counteracting habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). However, if one attains a direct descent into a mindless state, [all this ceases].
It measures beyond the limits of empty space; what need is there to further traverse the rungs of a ladder?

If one has not yet attained sudden accord with the mindless state, and if even for a single thought there is a discrepancy, one must directly employ the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to rectify it. Only through this can one ultimately realize the perfectly interfused fruit of Buddhahood.

By this, one knows that a follower of the School of the Patriarchs must never cling to a partial view or sweep away the stages of progress, lest they willingly fall into a state of vague and indistinct confusion.

This is indeed the case. For those in the Chan school (*zongmen*), when the water arrives, the channel is formed; they transcend and realize the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the Equal Wondrousness (*samyaksambodhi*) through a principle that occurs spontaneously without being sought.
However, those in the Chan school who realize sainthood in this very life are not easily found. The First Patriarch faced the wall for nine years;
the Second Patriarch said, "I am simply disciplining my own mind"; and the Fourth Patriarch entered the Way at the age of fourteen, never letting his side leave the mat.

(From the *Recorded Sayings of Tianran Yu*): The Sixth Patriarch said, "When one awakens, one saves oneself. The ancestral masters of old never failed to pay close attention to cultivation and refinement, refusing to lay down their practice.

How much more so for us later students! To gain even a fragmentary understanding and then consider ourselves to have attained liberation and finality leads to the inability to take charge on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month; it is nothing but self-deception. [This was] provided by Haogong.
He inquired of Changsha Cen, "Has the world-renowned *kalyāṇamitra* realized the *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues?
Cen said, "Virtuous One, do you ask about *nirvāṇa* on the level of fruition, or *nirvāṇa* within the causal stage? The monk said, "I am asking about *nirvāṇa* on the level of fruition.

Cen said, "The world-renowned *kalyāṇamitra* has not yet realized it; his merit is not yet equal to that of the various sages. The monk asked, "If he is not yet equal [to the sages], why is he called a *kalyāṇamitra*? Cen said, "..."

[The Master] said: "Clearly seeing the Buddha-nature is also called having a 'good spiritual friend' (kalyāṇamitra). [The Questioner] asked: "I do not yet understand to what stage of the path this merit is equal, such that it is named the realization of Great Nirvana. Cen said:
"The illumination of Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the liberation of the most profound Dharma, and the essence of the quiescent Dharmakāya—these three are one in their perfect and eternal principle.
If you wish to know where this merit is equal, it is called the Constantly Quiescent Light (Nityaprabhāsvara). [The Questioner] said: "Regarding the Nirvana of the fruition stage..."

I received this instruction: "What is meant by 'nirvāṇa within the cause'? Ceng replied, "Virtuous One, you must know that when one’s realization of the ground is thoroughly penetrating, one walks hand-in-hand with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Once nirvāṇa within the cause is attained, the burning habits and tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes must be gradually exhausted.
Only when the afflictions of views and thought are completely eliminated will one finally transcend the three realms."
According to the Tiantai teachings, this corresponds to the stage of an Arhat in the Tripitaka (Āgama) teaching, and to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanjiao*).

In our School of the Gate of the Dharma, even the Buddha does not exist, let alone anyone else. Yet, the state where there is neither Buddha nor sentient being is precisely the original self-nature of the Single Honored One, the True and Natural Buddha.
Through gradual cultivation and refinement, the coarse defilements fall away first; suddenly, one arrives at this realm where the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are exhausted.
Having first exhausted [all karmic conditions] and forever transcended the triple world, one is precisely a person at the stage of the seventh faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Baizhang said, "Going and staying are free and spontaneous. Huangbo said, "Arising according to one’s will. Guifeng said, "Regarding the destination of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one may entrust oneself to heaven or the human realm as one pleases;
this is the threefold mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Although this is the mind-made body as categorized within the teachings,"

There are differences in breadth and narrowness. If one follows the enumerations of the Tripiṭaka, this refers to Bodhisattvas of the third, fourth, and fifth stages of the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika-yāna).

Having cultivated samādhi, they attain the bliss of true emptiness and quiescence; they enter universally into Buddha-fields at will without obstruction, and this is called the "Mind-made Body of the Right Reception of the Bliss of Samādhi. As for Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching, they awaken to and realize all...

The essence of the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*) is like an illusion and does not exist [independently]. By means of immeasurable spiritual powers, one enters all Buddha-fields with swiftness as desired, unimpeded and sovereign.
This is called the "Mind-made Body that Awakens to the Self-nature of Phenomena" (*dharmasvabhāvabodhamanomaya-kāya*).

It is attained by Bodhisattvas at the ninth and tenth stages of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), who awaken to the fact that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, and who attain a single body that is simultaneously infinite bodies.
They appear like reflections in a mirror, arising simultaneously with all types of beings. Although they manifest various forms, they are devoid of volitional activity;
thus they are called the "mind-made body that arises simultaneously with all types and is without effortful action.

Regarding these three kinds of mind-made bodies, only the first type—which consists of the bliss of samādhi—has not yet completely severed the afflictions of views and mental states (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*). Nevertheless, it can only be attained by one who is a candidate for the stage of *srotāpanna*.
This is no easy matter. Guifeng said: "Awakening does not depend on emotion; one can transform karma at the moment of death.
