This means that if you feel a desire to act within your emotions but perceive through principle that it is inappropriate, you must stop immediately. If you feel a lack of desire to act within your emotions but perceive through principle that it is appropriate, you must act immediately.
This depends solely on what is right or wrong according to principle, not on feelings of attachment or aversion. Thus, at the time of death—
Karma cannot bind one who acts with sovereign mastery according to their will, whether in the heavens or among humans.
However, if what one does morning and evening is dragged along by the dust of afflictions (*kleśa*), then at the moment of death one will be led away by karma and undergo rebirth.

If, however, one's actions and deeds arise from awakened wisdom rather than the dust of afflictions, then at the moment of death one will undergo rebirth through the sovereignty of the self and not by means of karma.
One should know that to verify whether one possesses mastery over rebirth or not, it is sufficient to examine whether the ordinary mind is free or unfree regarding sensory objects.

In my humble opinion, if one restrains the emotions and accords with principle, practicing secretly and without interruption, such that these [virtuous] thoughts manifest before one at the moment of death, then mastery exists.
However, only those whose power is fully developed can transform karma; for those whose power is not yet full, it seems they likewise cannot.
That they are able to undergo rebirth equally without being subject to karma is the answer Mañjuśrī gave to Āmrapālī; this is the definitive proof.
One must know that for those who have not yet attained awakening, the priority is the correctness of one's vision; once awakened, the emphasis lies entirely upon practice.
This constitutes having both a beginning and an end. If there is a beginning but no end, the ancient masters said it is ultimately not valued. — Yongming.
The Fourfold Discernment says: "When the realm of the aggregates suddenly appears before one, one is instantly carried away by it. This is ten thousand times more dangerous than anything else;
fortunately, do not rely on previously heard words and fail to examine closely, thereby making a 'peace-of-mind' pill.
The *Shan’an zá lù* records that after the monk Moshan had died, he appeared in a dream to the woman Zou, claiming rebirth in her womb. His friend also dreamed of this. When she grew up, although...
He knew of himself that in his previous life he had been a monk; he took no pleasure in associating with monks and was as dull-witted as wood or stone.

When Yidian Ya of Tianmu Mountain saw that Gao Feng had attained the essential meaning [of the Dharma], after Gao Feng died, he appeared in a dream and entrusted his rebirth to the family of a commoner in Wuxing.
He became a monk again, named Ruiying and styled Baotan. There was not a single day that he did not receive the prostrations and offerings of others. I lived in a mountain hermitage.
In the heavenly realm, there was Bao Tan. Observing his conduct, it was merely mediocre and no different from that of an ordinary person.

When occasionally questioned about matters concerning his own fundamental self, he could only respond with embarrassment. Both men had been extraordinary beings in their previous lives; why then did they suddenly forget such things?

An ancient saying holds that even Śrāvakas remain dim-sighted upon emerging from the womb, and Bodhisattvas still lose their way when separated from the physical body. Thus, practitioners must be cautious.
"Is this not a lack of care? Furthermore, there was a monk under the guidance of Master Chengxue (誠) who had attained realization through the practice of Chan.

Cheng tested him with the words of the Three Barriers (三關), and his responses were as swift as a drumstick meeting a drumhead. He passed away early. He was born into a commoner family; both his parents had dreams on the same day.
One morning, his father took him into the mountains and met Master Cheng. The Master asked him, 'Do you remember how you answered my three turning-words regarding your previous life?'"
Jin said, "Try to cite one for me. Once it was cited, [Cheong] nodded his head and said, "These are my words. He earnestly entrusted them to his father to protect them.

Because a monk from another temple sought to become his disciple, he studied the *bansui* (Buddhist chanting) of Mount Odae; he received many offerings and alms, and there was no act of arrogance, luxury, or lawlessness that he would not commit.
Cheong, therefore, established three great vows to encourage practitioners. Generally speaking, for those who study Zen...

Within the state of meditative concentration, one attains a sense of joy; this is merely the temporary cessation of worldly afflictions and the slight manifestation of the light of wisdom, not yet the ultimate realization.
The fundamental ignorance within the field of the eight consciousnesses still remains. It is like grass pressed down by a stone; once the stone is removed, it will grow green again. Be on guard!
According to the *Yunqi Fahui*, Master Jie Chan was the later incarnation of Su Shi (Suzi-zhan). — Qingcaotang.
The later incarnation of the monk Ceng was Duke Ceng; the later incarnation of Elder Xun was Minister Li; the later incarnation of the Abbot of Nan’an was Minister Chen Zhongxu;
the later incarnation of the Librarian was Minister Zhang Wending; and the later incarnation of Head Seat Yan was Wang Guilin.
Following them, Master Cheng became the son of the House of Han, and the temple monk became the son of Prince Qi. Furthermore, his...
Next, Shan Shi became the son of Commissioner Si Hu; Haiyin became the daughter of Defense Commissioner Zhu;

and even the monk of Yandang became Qin Gui, who committed various evil deeds. I, the fool, say that while those with great vows and great power, such as Lingshu, were reborn as monks life after life, and Yunmen thrice became kings and consequently lost his supernatural powers, those like Yunmen will appear again ten hundred generations hence.
How many such people are there? How much more so for one beneath a sacred tree? Whether they be commoners, women, or evildoers, their status becomes increasingly inferior.
Even if they were eminent ministers, it would not be a matter of strategic calculation.

Furthermore, it is recorded that among the disciples of the Sramana Huiquan of Liangzhou during the Sui dynasty, there was one individual who was quite coarse and eccentric. Huiquan had never taken note of him, yet he suddenly declared that he had attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
Dajuan was ill. The man went straight to the bedside; the door remained closed as before. He said to Dajuan, "The Master has passed away and is destined to be born into a Brahmin family.

Dajuan asked, "I have spent my entire life in seated meditation; for what reason am I to be born there? The man replied, "The Master’s faith in the Way was not yet profound, and his study of external teachings was never severed.
Although he possessed meritorious karma, it could not lead him to transcendence. Nowadays, among the monks, there are those who study the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi."

If, while encountering the *kōan*, views and thorns should arise, one changes the case that cannot be resolved and makes it the *kōan*.

With a resolve to risk one’s very life, one investigates through various rules and regulations that are in no way different from those of a renunciant. This is taught for those of the highest faculties; thus it is known.
Afterwards, he strictly observed the precepts of the householder, adorning himself with the myriad practices. He was thus ranked among the fourfold assembly of the Buddha’s disciples;
it would not have been beyond his capacity to guide and lead future generations who shared his affinity.

However, when lay officials and gentlemen are preoccupied with the bustle of worldly affairs, how can they be like the Chan practitioners who devote their whole hearts to practice? It is only those whose minds and wills long for the Way and who are determined to pursue it [who can do so].
He has attained the insight and vision of the Supreme Vehicle and, moreover, holds office within the government. Thus, he is caught between the court and the provinces;
he cannot remain with a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in one place for three or five years.

Since he possesses the necessary affinity, and observing that his intent in practice is sincere and his insight already correct, I have privately permitted him the use of carriage and horse. I have opened a single thread of opportunity so that he may savor the flavor of Prajñā.

From this point forward, one must exert oneself with fierce diligence to seek the ultimate, lest one achieve nothing at all, or even lose everything entirely due to some other circumstance encountered on another day.

These methods may also be applied as a model for those who, though weak in temperament for the monastic life, possess a sincere resolve. This, however, depends entirely upon the clear-eyed master of the lineage.

This is how it functions. As for ordinary men and women who resolve to seek the Way, those among the male practitioners must bear the burden of supporting a household, while those among the female practitioners face the hardships of domestic interference; both require exceptional compassion and understanding.
Even if they investigate with such intense earnestness that they ultimately fail to glimpse the gateway, they too must be granted some slight concession.
Discuss this with straightforward sincerity so that you may understand the path ahead and not fail the intent of those who have come to you.
However, you must possess right view and right knowledge before I can provide you with instruction. This applies to one who can enter the Buddha-dharma but cannot enter the realm of Māra;
it applies to one like Huìtáng’s “I have nothing hidden from you”; and it applies to one like the Patriarch of the Western Heaven who recognized [the nature of] what is called "calling."

If one fails to recognize Buddha-nature and calls it the "vital spirit" (*jinghun*), that may be permissible; however, to go further than this—to claim anything less—is absolutely and categorically unacceptable.

The ancients, in their reception of people, possessed various methods and perspectives, each of which was distinct. Here, I shall briefly cite one or two instances to illustrate the general principle.

In the School of the Patriarchs, the lamp is passed from one to another in succession; it is of vital concern to the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and thus constitutes the very burdening of the Buddha-dharma.
This was the foremost matter. Formerly, when Shoushan had passed away, Master Fenyang Zhao closed his door and slept with his pillow high.

Qichong reproached him, saying, "The great matter of the Buddha-dharma is more important than the minor detail of retiring in quietude. Fengxue feared he would fulfill the prophecy, and thus worried that the fundamental teaching would fall into extinction."
"Fortunately, there was our former teacher, but he has now passed away. You possess the strength to shoulder the Great Dharma; when then would you wish to lie in high repose?
Zhaorong started in alarm and rose, grasping Daocong’s hand and saying, "Were it not for you, I would never have heard such words. Hurry and prepare my luggage; I am going.
Thus, those whose eye of the school is perfectly clear must urgently consider taking up the responsibility of the Buddha-dharma and exert their full strength for the sake of others.
How can one sit idly by while the ancestral style is being swept away, without supporting and championing it?
A monk asked Fenyang, "What is the phrase for receiving a beginner? He replied, "You are a wandering monk. The monk asked, "What is the phrase for discerning a patch-robed monk?
He replied, "The sun rises in the east at dawn. The monk asked, "What is the phrase for the true command being put into effect? He replied, "Traveling a thousand miles specifically..."
He came forward to present his old face. [Zhao asked: "What is the phrase for establishing heaven and earth? He replied, "In the continent of Uttarakuru, there is long-grained rice;
those who eat it have neither anger nor joy. Zhao said again, "I have finished using these four turning phrases to test the monks of the world.
Dayu Zhi said, "The former master used this to test monks; consider it carefully. He took it up.
These four phrases were, in their entirety, scrutinized and penetrated at once by the monks of the world.
Miaoxi said, "Do you all wish to recognize Dayu? To not alter the way of one's father for three years may be called filial piety.
Yian said, "Is there any master today who uses these four words to test people? If the ancestors did not settle it, the calamity will reach their descendants."
This serves as an illustration of how the Buddhas and Patriarchs receive and guide people; it consists of straightforward, practical discourse, which is to say, using words to manifest the wordless.

Its essential instructions have already been partially revealed in various sections concerning the thorough investigation of the source of Chan, cultivation and training, and entry into the state of sagehood. However, for those of beginner’s capacity...
Awakening: everywhere one encounters the source. When the ancient worthies upheld this teaching, every fragment was brocade.

Regarding all matters that open the gate of awakening and instruct on the cultivation of merit, I have briefly excerpted them here from this section. The World-Honored One showed a mani jewel that reflected the colors of its surroundings;
the inhabitants of the five directions each described it as being a different color. The World-Honored One hid the jewel and raised his hand, asking: "What color is this jewel?"

"Color," the deva said. "If there are no pearls in your hand, where is there any color? The World-Honored One sighed and said, "I show the world pearls, yet they speak of the existence of colors such as blue and yellow.
When I bring forth the true pearl, they know nothing at all. The deva then attained full realization.

A brahmin held two stalks of flowers and offered them to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Put them down. After the brahmin had placed the flowers from his left and right hands down, the Buddha spoke again.
The Emperor issued an edict for him to let go. Huizhi said, "Both hands are already empty; what more is there to let go of?

The Buddha said, "You should let go of the six external objects, the six internal sense organs, and the six intermediate consciousnesses all at once. When there is nothing left to abandon, that is the place where you escape birth and death.
Huizhi then realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). King Vītarāga asked Bodhidharma: "Where does the Buddha-nature reside?"
Dashi said: "The locus of the nature's functioning has eight aspects: when in the womb it is the body; when dwelling in the world it is the person;

in the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing; in the nose it is smelling fragrance; in the mouth it is discourse; in the hand it is grasping; and in the foot it is running and moving.

It manifests everywhere, encompassing all lands as numerous as grains of sand, yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute atom. Those who recognize this know it to be Buddha-nature. Not so? [It is.]
"Consciousness is called the spirit-soul (*sūkṣma-ātmā*). An ancient worthy said differently: "Not recognizing it is Buddha-nature;
recognizing it is the spirit-soul. Miaoxi said: "I dare ask you all: which is Buddha-nature? Which is the spirit-soul? The First Patriarch’s *Dharma-gate of Settling the Mind* says:
"In delusion, the person pursues dharmas; in awakening, dharmas pursue the person. In awakening, consciousness subsumes form; in delusion..."
Thus, form subsumes consciousness; yet all that is conceptually discriminated and reckoned by the mind as being the manifestation of one's own mind is entirely a dream.

When consciousness and mind are stilled and extinguished, such that there is no locus for any thought, this is called perfect awakening. Question: What is meant by "the manifestation of one's own mind"? Answer:

One perceives all phenomena as existing, yet their existence does not exist inherently; it is the mind that calculates and constructs them as existing. One perceives all phenomena as non-existent, yet their non-existence does not...

It is non-existent by itself; one conceives it as non-existent through mental calculation. Furthermore, if a person has committed all manner of offenses and yet personally beholds the Dharma-King, they immediately attain liberation.
One who attains liberation through phenomena possesses great power; one who perceives the Dharma within phenomena does not lose mindfulness in any situation.
One who attains liberation through words and letters possesses weak power. That which is both phenomenon and Dharma is profound; even if one leaps and bounds about, nothing exists outside of it.

The Dharma-realm. If one enters the Dharma-realm by means of the Dharma-realm, one is a deluded person. Whatever activities one performs do not transcend the mind of the Dharma-realm, because the essence of the mind is the Dharma-realm.
Question: Why is it that people of the world, despite their various studies and learning, do not attain the Way?
Answer: It is because of seeing the self that one does not attain the Way. "Self" refers to the ego. The Perfected Person (zhiren) does not grieve over suffering nor rejoice in pleasure;
it is because they do not see the self that they do not perceive suffering or pleasure. Because they have extinguished the self, they reach the state of non-being (xuwu).
If even the self is extinguished, what else could there be that is not forgotten? Question: Since all phenomena (dharmas) are empty, who is it that cultivates?
The Way replied: "If there is someone who must cultivate the Way, then cultivation is required. If there is no one, then cultivation is not required. This 'someone' is none other than the self.
If there were no self, then upon encountering things, one would not give rise to right or wrong. When something is 'right,' it is simply that I am right while the thing is not right;
when something is 'wrong,' it is simply that I am wrong while the thing is not wrong. Thus, the mind is without mind; this is what is called penetration."

To realize the Buddha-way is to have no views arise regarding phenomena; this is called realizing the Way. Encountering things directly and penetratingly, one knows their fundamental source. Such a person’s eye of wisdom is opened.

The wise entrust themselves to things and do not entrust themselves to their own selves; thus, they are free from grasping or rejecting, from opposition or compliance. The ignorant entrust themselves to their own selves and do not entrust themselves to things;
thus, they possess grasping and rejecting, as well as opposition and compliance. Not seeing a single thing is called seeing the Way. To not perform a single [action]...

The name of things is "practicing the Way. This means that in all places there is no place; thus, in the place of action, there is no place of action. When the dharma of non-action is realized, one sees the Buddha.
If one perceives signs, then in all places one sees ghosts. Because of grasping at signs, one falls into hell; because of contemplating the Dharma, one attains liberation.
If one perceives recollections, thoughts, and discriminations, one will undergo such matters as the boiling cauldrons and burning furnaces. This is seen in the present.

The characteristics of birth and death: if one perceives the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, one perceives the nature of *nirvāṇa*. To be without recollection, thought, or discrimination is itself the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Because the mind is not form, it is not existent; because its function is never abandoned, it is not non-existent. Furthermore, because its function is eternally empty, it is not existent;
because it is empty yet its function is ever-present, it is not non-existent. Master Ke said: "To claim that the past is different from the present, and the present [is different from the past]..."

It differs from antiquity. Furthermore, apart from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is additionally the Dharma-body. At the moment of realization, the present five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the mind are themselves the perfectly pure *nirvāṇa*.
This mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices and is correctly termed "Great Samādhi. The four marks [of birth, abiding, change, and extinction] are quiescent and extinguished.

Now, one who wishes to recognize the concentration of the mind should know that while sitting upright, this very sitting is the mind; know that when delusion arises, it is the mind; and know that when delusion does not arise, it is the mind.

The mind: knowing that there is neither internal nor external is the mind. All principles ultimately return to the mind. Since the mind is already pure, purity is the original nature which has no exterior;
this single mind is the mark of wisdom. Being clearly aware and unmoving, it is called "self-nature concentration. The Third Patriarch said:
If you wish to know the essential point of the Dharma: the mind is the root of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
There is only the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna). That which is the Single Vehicle is precisely the one mind. Simply maintain this one mind; this is the gate of the True Suchness of the mind.

No phenomenon exists outside of one’s own mind; it is known only by the mind itself. The mind has no form or color. The Patriarchs have transmitted only the mind to the mind. Those who attain realization grant their seal of approval. Furthermore...
There is no separate dharma. It is further said: "All things arise from the mind; whether one is in error or correct depends on oneself. Not thinking of a single thing is itself the original mind;
it can only be known through wisdom, and there is no other practice. Quoting the *Sixin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) by the Third Patriarch:

"The ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Simply do not harbor likes or dislikes, and all will be transparently clear. Do not pursue that which has conditions, and do not dwell in emptiness."

Patience. The preceding transformations of emptiness all arise from deluded views. Do not seek the Truth; you need only cease your views. When the two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them.
As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses the mind. When the One Mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.

To bind one's thoughts is to deviate from the Truth; dullness and torpor are undesirable. If you find such states undesirable, do not weary your spirit. What use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the intimate? If you wish to grasp the One...

Mount [the vehicle]. Do not revile the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). If you do not revile the six sense-objects, you will return to the same state as perfect enlightenment. Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once.
If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness. To achieve immediate resonance, speak only of non-duality.

One thought-moment is ten thousand years; ten thousand years are one thought-moment. The wise of the ten directions all enter this school. The Sixth Patriarch asked: "For what reason did you hear [this]?"
The Dharma does not awaken itself; this is because one’s obstacles of false views are heavy and the roots of affliction are deep. The wisdom of *prajñā* has neither small nor large dimensions.
When the deluded mind looks outward and practices seeking a Buddha, failing to awaken to one's own nature, this constitutes a small root.

If, however, one awakens to the Sudden Teaching, one does not cling to external cultivation; rather, one’s own mind constantly gives rise to right view, such that the dust and toil of afflictions can never defile it.
This is the realization of one's nature. The *Verse on Signlessness* says: "Within the dark house of afflictions, one must constantly give rise to the sun of wisdom.
When the false arrives, afflictions come; when the correct arrives, afflictions are removed. When neither the false nor the correct is employed, purity reaches its ultimate limit.

Awakening (bodhi) originally has no inherent nature; to give rise to a mind [of grasping] is itself delusion. If the pure mind remains amidst delusion, simply being correct ensures there are no three obstacles. This is called Right View.
Transcending the world: that which is called "the world" consists of false views; when both the false and the correct are completely cast aside, the nature of Bodhi remains as it is.
This verse belongs to the Sudden Teaching; awakening occurs in a single instant. This Dharma-gate takes non-thought as its school, formlessness as its essence, and non-abiding as its foundation.
Non-abiding is the original nature. Regarding the worldly—good and evil, beauty and ugliness, enemies and kin, speech, and the thorns of sensory contact—it remains unshaken.
In times of deception and contention, one regards both as empty and does not contemplate returning harm for harm. Within every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*), one does not dwell upon prior objects.

If the preceding and succeeding thoughts continue in succession without interruption, this is called being bound by all phenomena (*dharma*). If each thought-moment does not abide, there is no bondage. This takes non-abiding as its foundation.
To be externally free from all marks (*nimitta*) is called "marklessness" (*animitta*); this is the purity of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This is...

Taking formlessness as its essence, it is called "non-thought" (wunian) because it is unstained by any objects. It means that one’s own thoughts are constantly detached from all objects, such that no mind arises toward them.
If you merely do not think of any things and try to eliminate all thought, then at the moment a single thought ceases, you would die and be reborn elsewhere—this is a great error.
How can non-thought be established as the fundamental principle? Deluded people have thoughts regarding objects; [the teaching of non-thought] is for them...
Wrong views arise; all afflictions and delusive thoughts are born from this. In its own nature, not a single dharma can be obtained.

If one perceives anything as obtainable and falsely speaks of calamity or fortune, this is precisely affliction and wrong view. Furthermore, it is said: "As for 'non-existence,' what is non-existent? As for 'mindfulness,' what is being mindful of?
'Non-existence' means the absence of dualistic characteristics and the absence of all characteristics of affliction. 'Mindfulness' means mindfulness of the Truth."
Suchness is the essence of mindfulness, and mindfulness is the function of Suchness. Mindfulness arises from the self-nature of Suchness.
Although the six sense faculties possess seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad objects, and the true nature remains eternally sovereign. Thus, the Sūtra says:
One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

What is meant by "sitting in meditation" (*zuo chan*)? This dharma-gate is without obstruction or hindrance; when no mental conceptions arise toward any objects, whether wholesome or unwholesome, this is called "sitting.

To clearly perceive one's own nature as immovable is called "meditation" (*dhyāna*). What is called "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*)? Being free from external signs is called "meditation"; being undisturbed internally is called "concentration."
If one clings to signs, the mind becomes distracted; if one is free from signs, the mind is not distracted. One’s original nature is inherently pure and inherently settled;

it is only because of perceiving objects and thinking about objects that the mind becomes distracted. If the mind remains undistracted when encountering various objects, this is true concentration (*samādhi*).
In every thought-moment, one spontaneously perceives the purity of one's own nature, spontaneously cultivates practice, and spontaneously realizes the Buddha-way. Thus, Shizhi (示智) constantly said:
Not seeing a single dharma, yet maintaining a view of non-existence, is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun.

Not maintaining a single dharma, yet guarding a knowledge of emptiness, is like lightning flashing within the vast void. When such a perception suddenly arises, you have mistakenly failed to understand the skillful means.
You should, in a single thought-moment, recognize this as wrong; your own numinous light is constantly manifest. — Yongjia Xuanjue (Yongjia Jue)

"Enter," [the Master said]. [Nanyue] circumambulated the Master three times, shook his mendicant’s staff, and stood there. The Master asked, "Virtuous One, from what direction have you come? You have given rise to great arrogance.
Huairang said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Master said, "Why do you not realize non-birth and understand that there is no swiftness?
Huairang said, "Realizing is itself non-birth; understanding is fundamentally without swiftness. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. Huairang...
Just as he was about to prostrate, Huairang took his leave. The Master said, "Are you returning too soon? Huairang replied, "Since it is fundamentally non-moving, how could there be 'soon'?
The Master asked, "Who knows it is non-moving? Huairang said, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who gives rise to discrimination.

The Master said, "You have deeply grasped the meaning of non-arising. Huairang said, "If it is non-arising, how can there be 'meaning'? The Master said, "If there is no meaning, who would engage in discrimination?"
He said, "Discrimination is also not the mind. The Master said, "Excellent! This is called 'Awakening in a Single Night.

Xuancè told Zhīhuáng Dàdìng, "What my Master has taught is that the essence is wondrously profound and perfectly quiescent, while its function is suchness; the five aggregates are fundamentally empty."
The six sense objects do not exist; they neither emerge nor enter, neither fixed nor chaotic. The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is the stillness of dhyāna that is free from abiding.
The nature of dhyāna has no arising; it is the thought of dhyāna that is free from arising. The mind is like empty space, yet even empty space has no measure.

Huang went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Master said, "It is truly as you have said. You need only let your mind be like empty space, without clinging to the view of emptiness, and apply it accordingly."
There is no obstruction. In movement and stillness, there is no mind; ordinary and sage are forgotten; subject and object both vanish.
Nature and appearance are suchness (tathatā); there is no time when one is not in samādhi. The Master said to Xue Jian: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi.
If one uses wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, that is the view of the Two Vehicles. Ordinary people perceive clarity and ignorance as two; the wise understand them as one."
The nature is non-dual. This non-dual nature is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As for this true nature: it does not decrease in ordinary beings, nor does it increase in sages.
It is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions, nor is it quiescent while dwelling in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it neither comes nor goes;

it is not in between, nor within, nor without. It is neither born nor extinguished. Its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); it is eternally abiding and immutable. This is called the Way (*mārga*). I—

Regarding that which is said to be neither arising nor ceasing: it is originally without birth, and now likewise does not cease. If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not engage in any deliberation regarding good or evil;
you will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, yet possesses wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

The verse says: "Sentient beings are characterized by movement; insentient things are characterized by non-movement. If one practices the path of non-movement, one is the same as the non-movement of insentient things.
If one seeks true non-movement, there is non-movement within movement. This non-movement is [itself] non-movement; insentient things lack the seed of Buddhahood.
One who is well able to discern these characteristics sees that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is non-movement. To have such a view is itself the truth."

Regarding its application, it is further said: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without arising, ceasing, departing, or coming. Relying on this for cultivation, one does not lose the essential purpose.
A verse states: "Stolidly, do not cultivate good; Leisurely, do not commit evil. In stillness, sever seeing and hearing;
In vast openness, let the mind be without attachment. Master Si of Jizhou said: "These very words are your own mind; this mind is the *dharmakāya* Buddha of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*)."
It shares its lifespan with emptiness. If one enters the gate of samādhi, there is nothing that is not samādhi; if one enters the gate of signlessness, everything is signless.
Wherever one stands, one fully attains the essence of the school (zongmen). Whether in speech, weeping, laughing, bending, stretching, bowing, or looking up—all proceed from the ocean of nature;
therefore, they receive the name "essence" (zong). Buddhas of marks and characteristics are Buddhas of cause and effect; they are the Buddha of true reality (dharmatā).
In daily life, at all times, there is not a single further dharma to be practiced. This is the attainment of the Dharma; it is not that by means of attainment one attains further.
Therefore, the Dharma does not know the Dharma, and the Dharma does not hear the Dharma. Equality is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself equality.
One does not, by means of equality, further practice equality. Thus, it is solitary and peerless. When deluded, one is deluded regarding awakening; when awakened...

Awakening occurs within delusion. Delusion is itself delusion; awakening is itself awakening. There is not a single dharma that does not arise from the mind, nor one that does not cease with the mind.
Therefore, both delusion and awakening are entirely contained within the one mind. Nanyue Huisi said: "A student must first master the mind.

Once the mind is mastered, all dharmas will be simultaneously and completely understood upon hearing them explained. When stillness does not give rise to thoughts of stillness, [this is true mastery]."
This is fundamentally quiescent. Hearing of emptiness, one does not grasp at emptiness; it is like a bird flying through the sky:

if it were to dwell in the sky, there would inevitably be the danger of falling. Non-dwelling is the foundation. That the essence of self-nature is tranquil yet gives rise to the mind is its function of illumination.

This very tranquility is self-nature concentration (*samādhi*); this very illumination is self-nature wisdom (*prajñā*). Concentration is the essence of wisdom; wisdom is the function of concentration. Apart from concentration, there is no separate wisdom.

Wisdom (*prajñā*). Apart from wisdom, there is no separate concentration (*samādhi*); at the very moment of concentration, it is wisdom, and at the very moment of wisdom, it is concentration. At the very moment of concentration, there is no concentration;

at the very moment of wisdom, there is no wisdom. This is because their nature is suchness (*tathatā*). It is like a lamp being the substance of light and light being the function of the lamp. Thus, concentration and wisdom are cultivated together, never separated.
From the *Niutou Rongjueguan Lun* (The Treatise on the Absolute Severance of Contemplation by Niu-tou Rong). Question: What is this?
Regarding this mind: the answer is that all that is observed by the six sense organs is the mind. Question: What is the nature of the mind? Answer:

The mind has the cessation of stillness (*śānti*) as its essence, its principle, and its foundation. That the nature of the mind is quiescent is concentration (*samādhi*); the constant understanding of this quiescence is wisdom (*prajñā*). Question: What is knowledge (*jñāna*)? Answer:
The response of understanding when an object presents itself is knowledge. Question: What is the object? Answer: One’s own mental nature (*cittatā*) is the object.
Question: What is meant by "unfolding" and "rolling up"? Answer: The functioning of illumination is unfolding; the mind’s quiescence, being without coming or going, is rolling up.
When unfolded, it pervades and wanders through the *dharmadhātu*; when rolled up, its traces vanish and are difficult to find. Question: What is the *dharmadhātu*? Answer:
That which has no boundaries or defining marks is called seeing the *dharmadhātu*. Master Jue said: "The eyes see all forms, yet the eyes do not belong [to them]."
"All forms are liberated by their very nature. Master Yuan said: "Suppose there is a stone upon which one usually sits or lies down;
yet if it were made into a Buddha image, one would fear committing an offense and dare not sit upon it. This is merely the conscious mind being busy and confused;

within the stone itself, there is fundamentally no sin or merit. Master An said: "The straightforward mind is the Way. With straightforward thought and straightforward application, one does not further contemplate emptiness, nor does one..."

Seeking skillful means, the Sūtra says: "Looking directly, one does not see; thinking directly, one does not conceptualize; receiving directly, one does not act; speaking directly, one is not troubled.
Master Zhida’s Verses on the Mind and Objects state: "When objects are established, the mind arises; when the mind is empty, objects do not arise.
If you bind the mind to objects, both mind and object become blind. When mind and objects each abide in themselves, both mind and object are clear. Awakening.
The object and mind do not arise; it is the deluded mind that functions together with the object. If the deluded mind creates the object, then the mind and object become chaotic and disordered.

When one awakens to the fact that the object and mind are originally still, one knows that the nature of the mind and object is fundamentally pure. One realizes that the mind has no objective nature, and understands that the object and mind have no form.

The object is empty and the mind is silent; the mind illuminates and the object is cool and clear. Master Ganquan said: "To give rise to the aspiration for the Way and enter the Path, one must first..."
Recognize the fundamental mind. For those who have not yet recognized it, take faith as the priority. Faith means believing that one's own mind is Buddha.

This beginningless saṃsāra exists only because we do not dare to believe that our own mind is Buddha. Outside the mind, there is no other Buddha. Who else is it that performs every movement and action?
One who understands in this way is called a Buddha when their single thought-moment accords with reality. The Patriarch Shitou said: "Your mind..."
Its substance is free from annihilation and permanence; its nature is neither defiled nor pure. It is profoundly still and perfect, equal for both ordinary beings and sages.

Its application is without fixed direction; the three realms and six paths are manifested solely by the mind. Are there arising and ceasing in the moon reflected in water or images in a mirror? You should know that there is nothing not fully contained therein.
When the various sages set forth their words, they desire to reveal that the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally quiescent; all return to the same root. — *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source)
Question: How does this school correspond [to reality]? Answer: To approach it is to turn away from it; to draw near is to distance oneself from it.
To enter deeply through a single gate and forget all conscious awareness—this is the Dharma-gate of self-realization within the mind. As the former masters said:

"The various patriarchs have together transmitted the pure, self-awakened, sagely wisdom of the Buddhas, the wondrous mind of True Suchness (Tathatā), which is not something obtained through worldly words and letters. Cao Shan said: "From..."
By relying on conditions, attaining correspondence is swift; by returning to the substance, achieving stability is slow. A thought that flickers up has no original location from the start;

my teacher spoke of this briefly as the inconceivable. Thus we know that all sages employ this single thought-moment, which at the very moment it arises is utterly ungraspable—this is true inconceivability.
Apart from this, there is certainly nothing else; there is nothing superior elsewhere. Is this not indeed "swift"?
Question: How can this be so? Answer: To say it is, it would be a second head; to say it is not, it would be a third head.

When the pathways of the mind and intellect are severed and sensory perceptions dissolve, one dwells in this state and naturally attains penetrating insight. Question: If seeing and hearing are cut off, how does one achieve awakening? Answer:
It is simply because forced awareness and deluded cognition obstruct the Way. One must only detach from external attachments and settle within, so that [the innate nature] may manifest of itself.

Spiritual awareness (*lingzhi*). Once the sense organs and their objects have dissolved, radiant light suddenly manifests. Now, for those who are mired in ignorance and bound by the literal text, I shall employ verbal explanations as a skillful means to reveal this truth.
I shall directly point out that the ever-present, unarisen, and undying nature of the six sense faculties in their current functioning is no different from that of a Buddha.
This can be personally realized and known in the present, clearly and without delusion. For now, I shall first point to the two natures of seeing and hearing. When seeing—
"This moment is itself the intrinsic nature. The Patriarch said: "The eye-gate emits light, illuminating and shattering the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

Furthermore, when the eye is active for even a few moments, the myriad phenomena cannot escape their shadows and forms. Thus we know that while light and darkness come and go, the numinous light never becomes obscured.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha told King Bimbisāra: "When you were three years old and saw the river, until you reached the age of thirteen, its..."
"What about water? The King replied, "It was as it was when I was three years old; even now, at sixty-two, there is no difference.
The Buddha said, "Though your face has wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never wrinkled. That which wrinkles changes; that which does not wrinkle does not change.

It is fundamentally without birth or extinction. How could birth and death be experienced within it? This was spoken because the King had raised a doubt, and [the Buddha] used it as an occasion to refute the view of annihilation."

This is the vision of skillful means. To differentiate between the two natures of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing, yet not cling to the views of annihilationism or eternalism, means that all are the true mark (dharmatā) without arising or ceasing;
thus, the phenomenal marks are eternally true, which alone is called the ultimate. Regarding the nature of hearing, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
For example, when a person sits in stillness and drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they hear them all at once; this is the reality of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*).
When one listens to sounds through a wall, they can be heard both near and far; this is the reality of penetration (*vyāpti*), which the five sense organs cannot achieve equally.

The nature of sound is movement and stillness; within hearing, it appears as existence or non-existence. When there is no sound, it is called "no-hearing," yet this is not truly a state where hearing lacks its own nature.
Since sound is absent, there is no cessation; since sound is present, there is no arising. Being perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the eternal reality.

Thus we know that while the object of sound exists or does not exist of its own accord, the nature of hearing is neither born nor extinguished. Furthermore, it is not only the nature of hearing that is without birth;
looking back at the object of sound, it too is without birth or extinction. Because it arises from conditions, its own essence is entirely non-existent.
The Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it? Ānanda replied, "I hear it. When the bell had ceased and there was no sound, he asked again.
"Did you hear it? He replied, "I did not. Again, he was struck and asked, "Did you hear it? and again he said, "I heard it. The Buddha said: "When the sound has vanished, there is nothing to hear.

If there truly is no hearing, the nature of hearing has already ceased. When the bell is struck again, how do you know it? Whether the object of sound exists or does not exist is a matter for the sound itself;
how could the nature of hearing be subject to existence or non-existence for you? If hearing were truly non-existent, who would be there to know that it is non-existent? It is like a dream."

Within [the chamber], you hear the sound of pounding grain; the nature of hearing does not become dull. Even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of your life-force were to pass away, how could this nature be extinguished?
Furthermore, if you abandon arising and ceasing to maintain the true and eternal, and the light of eternity manifests before you, then your Dharma-eye will be purified at that moment.
How could you fail to achieve unsurpassed awakening? Therefore, if you understand the nature of hearing, it is precisely...

Thus one attains perfect enlightenment. Is this not, indeed, awakening to the Way through words? Now, following the teachings of the Patriarchs, there is yet another approach that is most concise and essential:
namely, "no-mind" (amūrccha). Why is this? If there is mind, there is unrest; if there is no-mind, there is spontaneous joy.
The ancients said: "Do not take the mind as your companion; when there is no mind, the mind is at peace. If you take the mind as your companion, movement will cause you to be deceived by it.
When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. If you simply attain the state of no-mind, objects will naturally not appear.
Since there is no longer any duality of opposition, how can adversity or favor arise? One gives rise to vexation by welcoming objects, and one is drawn into attachment by favorable objects."

This causes the mind to become restless and uneasy. Now, if one is without mind and remains composed and free from affairs, yet does not understand the essential principle of being without mind, then even though one employs antidotes to subdue it, the signs of unease will constantly manifest before one. Furthermore, there are two ways of being "without mind": first, making it non-existent through clarity and stillness;

this involves concentrating the thoughts to eliminate applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), gradually reaching a state of subtlety. Second, realizing that it is fundamentally non-existent in its very essence; this is...

It is directly realized as non-arising, because the point of origin of a single thought-moment cannot be apprehended. The Sūtra says: "When a single thought first arises, there is no characteristic of 'first arising';
this is true mindful protection. Question: Since it is fundamentally non-arising from the beginning, from where does delusion arise? Answer:

It is called "delusion" because one does not understand that the fundamental nature is originally without mind. Once one knows that the fundamental nature is without mind, then delusion has nowhere to arise; this is true non-attainment. Question: [Continues]...

Why is it that having a mind constitutes delusion, while being without a mind constitutes the absence of delusion? Answer: Because the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is empty and quiescent, devoid of a sovereign master.

To have a mind is to have a sovereign master, which entails the existence of limits and divisions. To be without a mind is to be without a sovereign master, which entails the absence of limits and divisions.
Being without limits and divisions means there is no question of birth and death. [Question: Is "being without a mind" something distinct from the mind, or is it attained through the mind itself?
Question: There is no mind. Answer: It is precisely by means of the mind that one attains the state of no-mind. Question: Since the mind itself is "having a mind," how can one attain no-mind? Answer:
Without destroying the characteristics of the mind, one is without conceptual discrimination. Question: Is it not the case that there is still discerning cognition? Answer:

It is precisely because discerning cognition is devoid of subject and object that it is no-mind. How could it be utterly useless? Only when it is thus is it no-mind. It is like a mirror reflecting objects; how could it have a "mind"?

Yes. You should know that sentient beings are always inherently without mind. The essence of the mind is fundamentally and eternally quiescent; it is both eternally active and eternally quiescent. Its true nature is naturally so;

it is not that the mind first begins to function only when there is a "having of mind. It is simply because sentient beings do not understand that their own minds are eternally quiescent that they falsely conceptualize the existence of a mind.
When the mind thus becomes an object, it is because the mind is itself no-mind; therefore, the mind is eternally the principle (li). It is not...
The characteristic of mind is that sentient beings are unborn. This is because there is neither principle nor non-principle; principle is eternally mind.
The unmoving characteristic of mind is itself the Buddha, who is also unborn. Thus, the sacred and the ordinary are always equal within the *dharmadhātu*.
Furthermore, regarding "no-mind," one must not form views of existence or non-existence. To take the mind as being "non-existent" is itself to establish it as existent. If, in all places...
A mindless state like earth or wood would likewise result in annihilation; both belong to deluded consciousness.

Therefore, that which is called the "Inconceivable School" (Acintya-pada) exists because it is beyond the reach of views concerning existence and non-existence. Question: Since one must not interpret this in terms of existence or non-existence, what is the correct realization of the "mindless"?
Answer: Tigers fight before the mountain; reeds sink beneath the water. Question: All sentient beings possess [this nature]. [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "眾生皆有".]

"Buddha-nature—why is it not realized? He replied, "It is like water, whose flavor is always neutral. When mixed with licorice, it becomes sweet; when mixed with yellow lotus, it becomes bitter. The water of the mind is likewise:
when deluded thoughts and defilements arise, one is an ordinary person; when merged with true emptiness, one is a sage. The nature itself never undergoes change."

Furthermore, because they do not awaken, they do not know that [the Buddha-nature] exists; because they do not believe, they do not accept it. They merely give rise to ignorance, and their emptiness becomes inverted conceptualization. Question:
Since both ordinary beings and sages attain Buddhahood by means of the true nature of the one mind, why is there a perception of sequence?
Answer: Although there is a sequence in perception, the nature remains undiminished. Sentient beings have not yet shattered the dream of ignorance, nor have they awakened to the power of the Path.
If [the qualities] are complete, then the Buddha-nature has not yet manifested and the Dharma-body is not yet perfected; does this mean that one does not possess the Tathāgatagarbha?

Question: What is the characteristic of bodhi? Answer: With respect to ultimate bodhi, its essence is eternally dark and quiescent. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Quiescence is bodhi, because it is free from all characteristics.
If one considers it through the characteristic of non-characteristic, it is not that it is not manifested within the gates of skillful means.

This is shown so that those who have first resolved to attain Bodhicitta may understand clearly and be free from doubt. As it is said: "The non-duality of quiescence and illumination is the characteristic of Bodhi.

Just as a mirror has no-mind as its essence and reflective illumination as its function, their union constitutes its characteristic. Thus, one knows that in the Chan school, this is the function inherent in the essence;
and that the essence inherent in the function is eternally quiescent. Knowing that quiescence and illumination are non-dual is the characteristic of the mind. Question:
Where there is thought, there is birth; where there is no thought, there is the Buddha. Why, then, are the holy and the ordinary equal? Answer:

Although sentient beings give rise to thoughts, they do not know that the essence of thought is originally non-thought, which is equal to the non-thought of the Buddha. They falsely fall into the midst of having thoughts, whereas the Buddha has attained non-thought.
Know that thoughts are fundamentally non-existent. Although sentient beings dwell within the midst of thought, the Buddha knows that thought is itself non-thought;

thus, the Buddha’s state of non-thought is identical in meaning to the non-thought of sentient beings. Furthermore, because sentient beings do not know that thought is empty, they give rise to phenomena within thought as if there were distinctions.
If one realizes that thought is empty, then one does not cling to the objects of suffering and pleasure, for these objects arise from thought. [The mind...]

If all is empty, how can there be objects? Since objects do not exist, the bonds of appearances are naturally severed. When both subject and object are empty, who could give rise to grasping and attachment?

Without grasping and attachment, birth and death naturally cease. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To know that these are but flowers in the sky is to be free from the cycle of transmigration."

Furthermore, there is no body or mind that undergoes birth and death therein. A question is asked regarding the school of attaining Buddhahood through the very mind (*citta*), which is the original intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Yet nowadays, people lack faith in this; they claim it cannot be realized in the present life. The answer is: If one sees directly, there is not a single person who is not a Buddha.
If one does not believe, there is not a single Buddha who is not a person. In delusion, one is always a sentient being who is a Buddha; in awakening, one realizes it in the present.
The Buddha within sentient beings appears as diverse through deluded perceptions; its fundamental nature is eternally one. Question: What is the Buddha of this very moment? Answer:
When a single thought arises now, it is fundamentally ungraspable and has no location. This is the Buddha of the past. Since the past does not exist, the future is likewise empty.
This is the Buddha of the future. That which dwells not for even a single moment in the present is the Buddha of the present. However...
Do not grasp, do not sever; do not take up, do not discard. Then the three periods of time leave no trace. In a single thought-moment, one is perfectly endowed with the ten dharma-realms.
These are the laws of cause and effect, yet they are neither cause nor effect. Thus, moment by moment there is resonance; moment by moment one attains Buddhahood.
Ordinary beings and sages are entirely equal. Therefore it is said: "To know the mind thoroughly—this mind is Buddha. If you wish to achieve success quickly, the precept-mind is [the means].
Vinaya: Apart from this mind-king, there is no other Buddha. The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states: "It is not like a single thought-moment of dependent origination without arising;
it transcends the provisional views of those who study the three vehicles. Question: If one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment, one merely enters the gate of faith.
How can one see [the Buddha] clearly and distinctly right before one's eyes? Answer: When there is nothing before one's eyes, that is the true seeing of the Buddha. This is because...

Because the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is quiescent, one penetrates this truth accordingly: that whatever is encountered by the six sense faculties is none other than the seeing of the Tathāgata, suchness itself.

This is called the Path of True Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and true worship. To accord with the mind that conforms to reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), being without the conceptualization of "seeing the Buddha" and realizing one's own *dharmatā*—this is true worship. As the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "To reflect according to reality is itself worship."
To nurture all Tathāgatas means that all [mental] deliberations are non-deliberation; it is through the sudden awakening to the one mind that there is no dharma to be conceptualized.
Question: How does one personally realize and manifest this, so as to see the Buddha of one’s own mind? Answer:

If one seeks by means of wisdom, that wisdom becomes a conceptual understanding, and such understanding turns its back on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). If one gives rise to a mind of illumination, that illumination establishes an objective realm.

To follow appearances while losing the essential meaning is entirely a matter of shadows; it does not accord with this school. If one realizes the true mind, one naturally becomes mindless and merges with the Way.
When Wondrous Virtue opened his mouth to inquire about non-duality, he forgot words to enter the principle and manifest the True School.
He asked of the Chan school: "One must now know the place where all Buddhas emerge—how is this? The answer was: "A stone ox gives birth to an elephant cub; a wooden woman conceives an infant."
All Buddhas emerge from within this. At the moment of their initial attainment of the Way, they see it immediately upon seeing it;
it does not depend on mental deliberation. A person asked Damei, "The divine nature stands alone; why do students not recognize it? He replied, "Who taught you to ask such a question?

He was asked again, "Is it not the case that the one who does not ask is precisely it? He replied, "If it were not so, then who is it that asks such a question? He was further asked, "The divine nature is neither sound nor form."
Regarding the divine nature shown by the Master, the student recognizes only sound and form, yet fails to recognize true nature.
The answer is like the Great Treasury of Space, wherein all jewels are contained. Those with merit see it and directly grasp the bright moon-jewel; those with little merit see it as copper or iron.
It is not that there are no jewels within the treasury, nor is it that the keeper of the treasury refuses them. When I speak to you of nature, you—

One merely perceives sounds and forms. Now, the raising of eyebrows, the movement of eyes, the snapping of fingers, the clearing of the throat, and the murmuring of questions and answers—all these are this very nature;
it is called the Great Way and is ever-present before one's eyes. Although it is ever-present, it is difficult to behold.

If those of superior capacity hear of it, they understand immediately and no longer commit various evils; this is called "once received, eternally tranquil. Those of middling capacity must hear it explained repeatedly.

[The Master] said, "You understand. Even if I were to explain it for ten million people of inferior capacity, they would fundamentally not understand. Though they might memorize a little, it would be like a pearl inside a tattered cloth;

once they leave the door, they will lose it again. Do you know? When asked about 'this very mind is Buddha' (*cittam eva buddhaḥ*), which the Patriarchs and Buddhas equally expound, why do you not speak of 'neither mind nor Buddha' (*na cittaṃ na buddhaḥ*)?
He replied, "'This very mind is Buddha' is a positive definition (*paryudāsa*). It causes one to personally realize the self-mind with complete clarity."

"Seeing one's nature" is a negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*)—that is, it is a method of refuting attachments and stripping away emotional views based on intellectual understanding and false recognition.
Since "mind" and "Buddha" are ultimately unattainable, this is established as a provisional gate of the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*) for the purpose of total cessation and non-reliance;
it is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. It is also a gateway for those of a certain capacity. As for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), however:

This is the dharma of the total exposure of the essence when this emotion is exhausted; it possesses both concealment and manifestation, is neither identical to nor separate from [its essence], and its substance and function encompass one another such that principle and phenomena are unimpeded.
In the present age, people place excessive weight on words of negation and denial, failing to perceive the principle of perfect permanence.
Therefore, the Patriarch said: "This mind is Buddha, like a cow having horns; 'neither mind nor Buddha' is like a rabbit having no horns. These are spoken in response to [the dualistic views].

This is merely a provisional designation for the limits of phenomena. If one attains a sudden awakening to the fundamental mind, right and wrong are instantly stilled. It is not a matter of total detachment, for that would give rise to a view beyond words;
nor is it a matter of total identity, for that would give rise to the ridicule of grasping at the finger [pointing at the moon].

If one truly realizes one’s own school, there is still no cognizing wisdom-mind or a wondrous principle to be realized—how much less could there be any further conceptual understanding? Question: Having entered this gate through faith, does one...

"Is there regression or not? He replied: "Faith is of two kinds. If one’s correct faith is firm and stable, if one understands the truth clearly without doubt, if one’s contemplation of principle is distinct, and if one regards both the precepts and the Dharma-vehicle with equal urgency, then it can be accomplished within a single lifetime; who then would speak of regression?

However, if one relies on a superficial faith where the power of contemplation is coarse and floating, and where habitual tendencies are heavy and external conditions strong, one will regress as soon as one encounters such circumstances. This applies even to those who have merely planted the seed of faith within the Buddha-dharma."

The mind is humble and free from pride; it respects and complies with the virtuous and good. Toward those who are evil, the mind is always compassionate. Toward those superior to oneself, one seeks out and receives what has not yet been heard.
Regarding the sublime Dharma one has heard, one practices it without forgetfulness. All that is false and delusive is eliminated in accordance with the teachings.
One is constantly diligent and never ceasing on the path to *sambodhi*. Indeed, such is the way for a person in life; it is in accord with the Dharma.
If evil does not arise because it is not prolonged, why worry about falling back? Believe that afflictions are themselves bodhi;
they are fundamentally the Buddha, and there is nothing further to advance toward. It is like being in empty space: where could one fall back to? Question:

Since this is the path beyond words and the reality transcending all marks, how can it be expressed through pervasive speech and explained extensively through the characteristics of practice? Answer: Without words, how could one know that [the truth] is non-existent?
It is said: "How can non-characteristics (animitta) be manifested by characteristics? The *Avataṃsaka* states:

"To realize that dharmas do not reside in words is to skillfully enter the realm of wordlessness, yet one can still manifest verbal expressions, like echoes pervading the world. The *Vimalakīrti* says: "As for those who preach the Dharma, there is no preaching and no demonstration.
It further states: "There is no liberation apart from words. All of these use words to manifest the wordless. The *Avataṃsaka*...
Yan said: "The physical body is not the Buddha; sound and voice are likewise so. Yet, without departing from sound and form, one perceives the Buddha’s supernatural powers.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. These passages all use marks to reveal the markless. Question:
Since sentient beings and Buddhas share the same essence, why is there a distinction between suffering and joy? Answer: It is because of Buddha-nature and Dharma-nature.
Having personally realized the source of the mind, delusive thoughts do not arise; one does not lose right mindfulness, and the sense of "mine" is extinguished.

Thus, one no longer undergoes birth and death, and attains ultimate, eternal quiescence. Because of this quiescence, one always joyfully takes refuge in oneself. Sentient beings, however, are deluded regarding their own nature.
Failing to realize the fundamental mind, one gives rise to various delusive thoughts that do not follow right mindfulness; thus, there is love and hatred.

Because of love and hatred, the vessel of the mind is destroyed, and one immediately undergoes birth and death, where all sufferings manifest of themselves. If you wish to know the essentials of the Dharma, guarding the mind is foremost.
If a person who does not guard the mind were to attain Buddhahood, such a thing is impossible. Quoting Yangshan, he says:

"To suddenly awaken to one's own mind as being without marks, like empty space, and for its manifestation through the sense organs to be the inherent nature possessing the wondrous functions of the sands of the Ganges—this has nothing else to support it and nothing else to establish it;
it is the original ground, it is the original land. Quoting Anguo, he says: "It is like the good and evil in a dream."
Knowing that one is sleeping peacefully upon the bed, there is absolutely no anxiety or joy. This is precisely what it means to recognize the mind and see the nature.

Now, hearing that one will become a Buddha brings joy; hearing that one will enter hell brings sorrow. Failing to realize that the nature of the mind rests peacefully upon the bed of Bodhi, one falsely gives rise to anxiety and joy.
Quoting Damei, he said: "Each person must clarify the mind and reach the source. Once the root is attained, the branches follow naturally. The mind is the root; it is simply that the mind..."
It arises concomitantly with all good and evil; thus one knows that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). The *Zongjing* commentary explains:

As the Sixth Patriarch said, "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the essence of the mind. It is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, yet its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
This is because Buddhas represent the extreme limit of goodness, while sentient beings represent the extreme limit of evil; thus, they are encompassed by good and evil.
Because all phenomena are exhausted, it is said that if one does not engage in discursive thought, everything returns entirely to the substance of the mind. As Hanshan said:
"When the myriad objects have all vanished as traces, only then does one see the person of original nature. It is not strictly necessary for them to vanish;

rather, it is because sentient beings do not realize that empty flowers arise and perish, and thus fail to return to the source of the single mind, that they are instructed to bring them to cessation. Once one enters the substance of the mind, there is only profound stillness.

It does not fall into annihilation; naturally, function arises from the essence. This function pervades as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, drawing forth clouds across a thousand acres.

Even the dharmas of the ten evil acts and the five heinous crimes all manifest from within the *tathāgatagarbha*; they are fundamentally Buddhas. It is only because sentient beings give rise to conceptual thoughts that they are so designated.

This torrential flow continues to the present day. Therefore, the Buddha commanded that one should extinguish the faculty of the mind and sever all discursive discrimination; through a single moment of resonance, one immediately transcends to perfect enlightenment.
How could he have taught that extensive knowledge and understanding would disturb and agitate the body and mind? You should now simply sever seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

Do not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding sensory objects. Put on your clothes and eat your meals according to the occasion. The ordinary mind is the Way. This Dharma is extremely difficult. Someone asked:
"When there is no lamp after nightfall, what then? The answer was: "For one who has realized the Way, the constant light is ever-present;
what distinction is there between day and night? Quoting Yunju, he said: "The mundane and the supramundane both arise from the single thought of deluded mind. Thought itself is [the source]."
Regarding the objective realm: the seeing is itself the mind. When one contemplates that a single thought-moment moves, then worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges move simultaneously.

When one contemplates that a single thought-moment is eternally still, then all sentient beings of the six realms are eternally still. If one realizes the essence of a single thought-moment, then worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constantly manifest as one's own mind.
Due to delusion regarding the One Mind, the objective realm and wisdom become as far apart as Hu and Yue. Furthermore, the *Zongjing Lu* states:

Although the preceding citations and subsequent proofs are extensive in text and manifold in meaning, why weary yourself with repeated explanations? As the *Mahā-śāstra* says: "It is like shaking a tree;

those fruits that are ripe fall first, while those that are not yet ripe require further shaking later. Again, it is like catching fish: what was not exhausted by the first net is caught by the subsequent one.
Through various such causes and conditions, there is no fault in repeating the teaching. Question: How can one accord with this essential principle? Answer: The object...

When both wisdom and [its object] are forgotten, how can one speak of "accordance" (*yiqie*)? Question: If this is so, then speech and thought are severed, and the paths of mind and intellect are cut off.
Answer: This too is merely a forced expression; though one wishes to conceal the form, the traces have not yet vanished. Question: How can one attain the forgetting of both form and trace?
[Question: Originally there were no tracks or traces; how can you wish to eliminate them? [Question: It is just as when a person drinks water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself.
Only upon attaining great enlightenment will one finally accord with this principle. [Answer: Within this, there is likewise no principle of delusion or awakening, or of accord or non-accord.
"Casting off your hands, it is as if you possess nothing; in vain you labor to speak of thousands of varieties. An ancient worthy said: "Exhausting the ten..."
I searched throughout the worlds for a single person to be my companion, but could find none. It is further said: "There is but one person who inherits the ancestral seat; there can never be two.
If you have not yet personally arrived at this, your mental exertions are in vain. This Dharma is the place where all ordinary beings and sages utterly relinquish body and life;
anything that does not enter this school is not ultimate. Question: How does one practice it? Answer: Who would you have practice it?
Liu asked, "Is it not the case that everything is ultimately annihilated? The Master replied, "Since even 'permanent abiding' cannot be attained, how could there be annihilation?

Liu asked, "I beg for one final word. The Master replied, "A conjured person questions an illusory man; an echo answers the sound of a spring. If you wish to grasp my fundamental principle, [look here]."
"A mud ox walks upon the water. Ouyang Xiu asked: "When eminent monks face life and death, they shed them with laughter and conversation;

by what path do they achieve this? He replied: "It is through the power of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*). He asked: "Why is it that these are not found today? He replied: "In the past, every thought-moment was in concentration."
How could one be disturbed at the moment of death? Now, if every thought is scattered and distracted, how could one attain stability at the moment of death? [The Master] asked Yunju Deng:
"For what reason are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not constrained by birth and death, while ordinary beings alone are entangled in this suffering? [Yunju] replied:

"Within the nature of purity, if one calculates the existence of subject and object, one immediately falls into birth and death. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas skillfully know that within the nature of purity..."
Not falling into existence or non-existence, subject and object are not established. Question: "In that case, there must be people who have realized [it] and those who have not. Answer:

"Since even 'realization' cannot be found, how could there be a person who realizes? You should reflect that within the pure nature there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, nor are there people who realize or do not realize.
Both 'ordinary being' and 'sage' are merely names. If you give rise to understanding by following these names, you will fall into birth and death. If you know..."
Provisional names are not real; thus, there is nothing that should be named. This is the ultimate, most profound state.
To say, "I can comprehend this, but I cannot comprehend that," is a great illness. To perceive purity and impurity, or ordinary beings and sages, is also a great illness.

To form the understanding that there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, yet still cling to the negation of cause and effect, is likewise a great illness. To perceive a pure nature in which one may take refuge is also a great illness. To form [the view of] non-...

To dwell in liberation is also a great illness. Yet, although there is no movement within the pure nature, one does not destroy the application of skillful means, nor does one cease from giving rise to kindness and compassion.
Such kindness and compassion are themselves the present pure nature; this may be called "seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha.
Question: "Great Pearl, how does one attain Great Nirvana? Answer: "By not creating the karma of birth and death. Question: "How so?"
"What is the karma of birth and death? Answer: "Seeking great *nirvāṇa* is the karma of birth and death.
