The Patriarch said, "This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I too—"

"Thus it is. A foal shall emerge from beneath your feet and trample the people of the world to death. Master Daoyi of Mount Heng was sitting in meditation when Nanquan Puyuan asked him, "What are you aiming for?
Daoyi replied, "I am aiming to become a Buddha. Nanquan took a brick and began to grind it. Daoyi asked, "What are you grinding?
Nanquan said, "I am grinding it to make a mirror. Daoyi said, "How can grinding a brick produce a mirror? Nanquan said, "How can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha?"
[The Master asked: "How does one become a Buddha? Yangshan said, "It is like an ox pulling a cart that will not move.

Is it the cart that should be struck? Is it the ox that should be struck? Yangshan remained silent and gave no answer. [The Master] asked, "How should one apply the mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*)?
Yangshan said, "Your cultivation of the mind is like sowing seeds; my preaching of the Dharma essentials is like the rain from heaven. Because your conditions have converged, you shall see the Way."
A questioner asked, "Since the Way is not a form or characteristic, how can it be seen? Huairang replied, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way;
the same is true for the signless samādhi. The questioner asked, "Does it have arising and ceasing? Huairang said, "If you view it in terms of arising and ceasing," [he would not be seeing the Way].
This is not the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). The verse says: "The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When it meets with moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless;
What could be destroyed, and what could be formed? A wild duck flew past. Mazu asked, "What was that? Baizhang replied, "A wild duck flew by.
Mazu grabbed Baizhang by the nose and twisted it until he cried out in pain. Mazu said, "You just said it flew by!"

Dazhu had an awakening. He returned to his quarters and wept. A fellow practitioner asked him, "Master Ma said this was his realization; why do you weep? Dazhu replied, "I myself am asking him. The fellow practitioner asked, "Master, why are you laughing so loudly?
The next day, as soon as the Patriarch (Baizhang) ascended the seat, Dazhu stepped forward and rolled up the sitting mat. The Patriarch immediately descended from the seat.
Upon reaching the abbot’s quarters, the Patriarch asked, "I have not yet spoken a word; why did you roll up the mat? Dazhu said, "Yesterday, my nose was twisted."
"Yun said, 'It was painful then, but now it is no longer painful. Mazu said, 'You have deeply understood yesterday's matter. Baizhang attended him; Mazu looked at the whisk in the corner of the bed.

Baizhang said, 'Is it used right here, or is it apart from this? Mazu asked, 'In the future, when you open up that two-piece skin..."* *(Note: The sentence regarding Mazu's final question is left incomplete as the source text provided ends there.)*
"What do you take to be a person? Baizhang took up his whisk and held it upright. Mazu said, "This very thing is its function; apart from this, what is its function?
Baizhang hung the whisk back in its original place. Mazu let out a roar of such intensity that Baizhang was deaf for three days straight.

Huangbo went to visit Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Majestic and imposing as you are, from where have you come? Huangbo replied, "From Lingnan. Baizhang asked, "For what purpose have you come? Huangbo replied, "Not for any purpose."
This was another matter. Baizhang prostrated himself and asked, "How does the ancestral school of the Dharma transmit its instructions?
Mazu remained silent for a long time. Baizhang said, "I must not allow future generations to sever this lineage. Mazu said, "I thought you were someone of substance.

One day, Mazu brought up the story of his second visit [to Huangbo] and said, "When I was struck by that one shout, my ears were deaf for three days straight. Baizhang involuntarily stuck out his tongue and said, "Now..."
The Master raised this case, saying: "One may see Mazu’s great capacity and great function, yet one does not recognize Mazu himself.

If you succeed Mazu, your descendants will later lose their own selves. Baizhang said: "If your vision is equal to that of the teacher, you have lost half the teacher's virtue; if your vision surpasses that of the teacher, [you have attained his full virtue]."
Only then was he fit to receive the transmission. Your son possesses a vision that far surpasses his master. When Linji asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, Huangbo struck him;
this occurred three times in succession. Linji then informed Muzhou, saying, "I shall now take my leave. Muzhou said to Huangbo: [...Muzhou said to Huangbo... (The text provided ends here).
Later, he became truly extraordinary. In time, he grew into a great tree that provided shade for all people under heaven.

When Nanquan Jie took his leave, Huangbo said, "Go to Dayu; he will surely explain it for you. Jie went to ask Dayu, but after being beaten three times, he did not know whether he had committed an offense or not.
Dayu said, "Huangbo’s grandmotherly heart has exhausted himself on your account; why have you come here again to ask about having an offense?"
Daguang asked, "Is there a transgression or not? Huangbo replied, "There is no transgression. Jie Daowu said, "So it turns out that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma consists of nothing more than this.
Yuyuan grabbed him by the collar and said, "You bed-wetting ghost! Just now you were asking whether there was a transgression or not, and now you say the Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this.
What principle have you seen? Speak quickly, speak quickly! Jie struck Yuyuan three times under the ribs, and Yuyuan let go.
Yangshan said, "Your teacher Huangbo has nothing to do with me. Yangshan turned back. Huangbo said, "This fellow comes and goes; when will he ever have an end?
Yangshan said, "It is precisely because his compassionate heart is so earnest. He recounted the previous conversation. Huangbo said, "Dagui is too talkative."
"I will wait until he comes and give him a thorough beating. Linji said, "What do you mean by 'waiting until he comes'? He immediately slapped him. Huangbo said, "This madman!
Coming here to pull at a tiger's whiskers. Linji then shouted. Huangbo called to his attendant, "Take this madman away to attend to the hall duties.
Later, Linji said to Puhua and Kefu, "I wish to establish the school of Huangbo's teachings here, but—"
"Accomplish me! The two men respectfully descended. Three days later, Puhua asked, "What were you saying three days ago?
Linji struck him. Kefu asked, "Why did you strike Puhua? Linji struck him again. This is the great outline of the lineage transmitted through the generations of this branch of Linji.
Linji said: "Sometimes I take away the person but do not take away the environment."
Sometimes the object is taken away but not the person; sometimes both the person and the object are taken away; and sometimes neither the person nor the object is taken away.
Kekfu asked, "What is it to take away the person but not the object? Linji said, "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade;
the infant’s hanging hair is as white as silk. He asked, "What is it to take away the object but not the person? Linji said, "The imperial decree has been issued and has spread throughout the world."
"The General has cut off all smoke and dust beyond the frontier. [Linji] asked: "When both the person and the environment are taken away"?

Jie said: "Wang has ascended the precious throne; the village elders sing songs of joy. [Linji] asked: "When neither the person nor the environment are taken away"? Jie said: "The General has cut off all smoke and dust beyond the frontier.

These are what the various quarters call the "Four Kinds of Discernment" (*si liaojian*). Linji further said: "If those of middling or inferior capacity come, I take away the environment but do not eliminate the dharma. If those of middling or superior capacity..."
The faculties, objects, dharmas, and the person are all simultaneously stripped away. When one of superior capacity comes, the faculties, objects, dharmas, and the person are all stripped away.
It is like a person of extraordinary insight who arrives and acts with their entire being; they do not pass through the various levels of faculties and capacities.

At this point, there is no passage for where the student exerts effort. A spark of stone or a flash of lightning passes by in an instant. To conceive of it in the mind is already an error; if the eyes stir or blink, there is no connection.
For those who understand, it is not apart from what is before one's eyes. Dahuai Gaofeng said: "This matter certainly does not reside in words and speech.

If it were in words and speech, why did Bodhidharma instead speak of the 'single transmission of the mind-seal,' of 'not establishing written words or language,' and of 'directly pointing to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha'?
Why did he not say he was transmitting the profound mystery or transmitting words and speech? The matter cannot be avoided."

Enough! Having spoken of the nature of mind, it has already become a mess. If you wish to uproot the source of birth and death, even if you can recite an entire collection of the teachings, it is called "carrying in dung.
This will instead obstruct your right knowledge and vision from manifesting. To do nothing but manage and understand the "Zen of the nature of mind" is to waste your spirit in vain.
The ancients, with a single word or half-sentence, established the "thorny chestnut" (liji pong) to teach one how to penetrate through it. If...
O noble spirit! The acorn burr is merely a toy for a monkey. It is because you cannot realize in a single thought that conditioned arising is unborn;
instead, you have been preoccupied with the realm of consciousness, seeking the mysterious and the wondrous from the mouths of the masters, only to be turned upside down by them.
Consequently, you still do not know where your own original life-spirit resides. At that time, Ke-fu asked Linji: "No..."
"Where could one find such idle talk? Do you understand? The phrase 'radiant sun' is the environment; the phrase 'infant' is the person. The verse says:

"To take away the person but not the environment—this condition naturally carries a paradox. What kind of paradox is there? If you attempt to seek the profound principle, your deliberations will only lead to self-reproach.
To falsely accuse another is a crime. The light of the dragon pearl is brilliant; the shadow of the immortal cassia tree..."
Vasubandhu, why did you not speak thus sooner? To meet face-to-face without deviation—would this not still be to remain caught in the net?

Furthermore, being blown by the wind into another tune, it likely resides within the two lines concerning the dragon pearl; those who conceptualize miss the mark. Face-to-face, they are ensnared by the net of words;

thus, while preserving the objective realm (*viṣaya*), they rob the person. The King’s command-line robs the realm; the General— (Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "General" [將軍], leaving the sentence incomplete.)
The phrase preserves the person; it accords with the verse. To seize the object but not the person—searching for words, where is the truth?

One must also prepare defenses in times of leisure. Asking about Chan, Chan is a delusion; investigating principle, the principle is not intimate. A good thing is no better than nothing. The sun shines, the cold light is faint;
the mountains sway, the verdant colors are fresh. The poor child thinks of old debts. Even if one were to attain a profound realization, it is still but the eye.

The middle dust arises and collapses of its own accord. The two lines beginning with "The sun shines" refer to the objective realm. The two lines beginning with "Even if one were to... take this away as well.
The two lines beginning with "Pingyuan and Fen" take away both person and realm. This verse states: "Both person and realm are taken away; from the outset, the true command has been exercised.

Once it has already fallen into the second [category], there is no longer any question of Buddhas or Patriarchs, nor can one speak of the sentiments of sages or ordinary beings. To buy a stone and receive more clouds is to attempt to violate [the truth].

The "Blow-Off-Hair Sword" is like encountering a blind man in the woods; those who recognize the Dharma tremble before it. Advancing forward to seek the wondrous meeting, it suddenly severs the vital spirit.
The first arrow was light, but the second arrow is deep; once the true command is executed, neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs are spared.

Like the blow-off-hair sword, its edge cannot be met. The two lines beginning with "The King Ascends" accord with the verse: "When both person and environment are not wrested away," this is the meaning of contemplation.
Not partial. Do you understand? This Dharma abides in its own place; host and guest speak without divergence. The characteristics of the world are eternally present;
question and answer are complete in principle. One cannot add or subtract even a hair’s breadth. Having trodden through the moon in the clear pool, there is still this very thing remaining.

Piercing open the azure void of heaven, one exerts effort in vain and achieves no merit; unable to clarify its wondrous function, one errs at the slightest movement and sinks into the state of non-conditioning, remaining as before.
If you wish to attain clarity, simply look toward the point where it is revealed. Sometimes the person is taken away but not the environment;
sometimes the environment is taken away but not the person; sometimes both person and environment are taken away; and [sometimes] both person and environment are...
Do not seize upon it. Suchness is it. If you try to understand it, it is no longer so. Do not say that none of you can understand it; even Miaoxi cannot understand it.
I grant you that you may hear it, but I do not grant that you may understand it. Having provided the commentary above, you have all heard it and all understood it together.
Is Linji’s intent truly like this? If it were merely like this, how could Linji’s fundamental teaching ever reach such a state?
Now, if you attach to even a single word or character, that is the very first grade of malicious speech and the root of birth and death.
Truly, even if you practice Zen for a hundred years, you will not understand it; you must come with an empty mind to investigate it together with me.
Linji said: "Sometimes I first illumine and then act; sometimes I first act and then illumine; sometimes illumination and action occur simultaneously; and sometimes..."

When illumination and function do not occur simultaneously, there is someone who illuminates first and then functions; (Sanshanlai says "someone" refers to the student. When function precedes illumination, there is a method present;
(Sanshan says this refers to the method of the master. When illumination and function are simultaneous, it is like driving the ox of the plowman and snatching the food from the hungry man;

it is like breaking the bones to extract the marrow and striking with needles and awls with painful force. When illumination and function do not occur simultaneously, there is questioning and answering, establishing the guest.
Establishing the master, blending water with mud to meet the needs of beings and engage them: if one is a person of great capacity, one should "lift up and go" even before the staff is raised;
this is still somewhat better. Fenyang said: "First illumination, then function"—let us deliberate on this together.
"First function, then illumination"—only then can you be considered a true person. As for "illumination and function simultaneous," how will you withstand it? Illumination and function...
"If they are not simultaneous, how can they be brought together? Sanshan said: "When a monk comes, one asks, 'Where are you from? or 'Where have you come from?
This is the initial illumination (*zhào*). One waits for him to react; then, whether using a staff or a shout, this is the subsequent application (*yòng*).

"When a monk comes, one immediately strikes or shouts—this is the initial application of a single method—and then follows it by saying, 'Do you understand? What do you say this means? This is the initial application followed by the subsequent illumination (*hòuzhào*)."

When a monk approaches, [the Master] uses the staff or shouts to see how he receives the response. This is "function" (yòng) and "illumination" (zhào) applied simultaneously. When a monk approaches, [the Master] says, "You have come," or strikes him with a blow, observing how he manages the situation and responds.

One should deliberate further; there is no fixed pattern. This is illumination and function occurring at different times. Linji said: "If a man who cannot be deceived comes, I say... (Jingshan Daoyuan continued): "There is a fellow who will not be hoodwinked.

When he comes, [the Master] says: "You have come. Or he strikes a blow. Observe how he handles it and answers. Deliberate on this again; do not be bound by a single form. This is illumination and function occurring at different times. Jingshan Daoyuan said: "If a man who will not accept being deceived comes, I say—"
In this place, what grounds are there for speaking of illumination and function, or of guest and host?
To drag them down and give them a blow with the mallet—this cannot be blamed. Linji said: "Sometimes a shout is like the Vajra King’s precious sword;
sometimes it is like a crouching lion; sometimes it is like a probe-stick or a blade of grass; sometimes a shout does not function as a shout."
"How do you understand this? Sanshan said: "The words of the sword are swift and sharp, difficult to withstand; they sever the intellectual views of students. 'Lion' means not falling into old molds;
with one roar, the brains of all beasts are split open. Should one err even slightly, one is immediately devoured by its claws and fangs.

This is a probing pole used to test whether a student's realization is deep or shallow, correct or false. It is a deception right before one's face; it does not employ shouts, yet it manifests in a thousand transformations."
The myriad transformations are most profound and most wondrous. Only when one can turn the body here within this state does one see the point of Linji’s application.
Linji said: "When guest and host meet, the student presents a bowl of glue. The master fails to discern the situation and merely puts on a show;
he is then met with a shout by the student and refuses to let go. This is called 'the guest looking at the host,' where the teacher follows the student's inquiry."
He immediately seizes it. When the student is seized and refuses to let go, the master looks at the guest; the student should then look at a single object.
If the teacher can discern this and fling it into a pit, the master looks at the master. The student is already wearing a cangue and shackles; the teacher adds yet another layer.
The student rejoices, and neither side can discern the other. This is "the guest looking at the guest. This is the discernment of demons as they are raised.
To know what is deviant and what is correct: when the Guest looks at the symbol in the Host’s position, he says, "Habitually breaking off the horn on the head of the black horse;
the student has nostrils. When the Host looks at the symbol in the Guest’s position, he says, "Driving the ox to seize the food; it depends on the occasion; the student has no nostrils.
When the Host looks at the symbol in his own position, he says, "The game meets its match; both houses have nostrils. When the Guest looks at [the symbol in] the Guest’s [position],...
In the *Weizhong* (Within the Ranks), it says: "The blind meet the blind; both houses have no nostrils. This is entirely the same as Linji.
A monk asked about the "guest within the guest," and Kefu said: "Leaning on the gate or by the door, as if intoxicated"—this too refers to the student having no nostrils.
Regarding the "host within the guest," Kefu said: "Blind eyes, the spirit of the pupils does not emerge from the head; those who bury their heads do not recognize it."
This refers to the student having nostrils. When asking about the "guest within the host," Ke Fu said: "Highly holding the ancestral seal, benefiting beings with compassion.
Here, the word "guest" points to the side of benefiting beings; it does not mean the teacher lacks nostrils. When asking about the "host within the host," Ke Fu said:
"Horizontally grasping the Mo-ye sword, fully maintaining the correct command. Here, the word "host" refers to the teacher’s inconceivable functioning of spiritual means. The monk—
Questioning "the guest within the guest," Xuedou says, "A face covered in dust. Here, the upper "guest" refers to function (*yòng*); the lower "guest" refers to that which cannot be used.
Questioning "the host within the guest," Xuedou says, "Xuan Sha’s fierce tiger. Here, the "host" refers to that which can be used.

Questioning "the guest within the host," Xuedou says, "The moon bears a double halo," and also says, "By warming to the old, one knows the new. This is the simultaneous manifestation of essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*).
Questioning the Lord of Lords, Dou said: "The great trichiliocosm is squeezed into a single point; here, both essence and function are simultaneously extinguished.

This accords with the Caodong school’s principle that being able to maintain continuity is called being the "Lord of Lords. This particular exchange between guest and host can be explained by both masters and students.

Tianmu Huihong has a "Discrimination of the Four Guests and Hosts" (*Sishibinzhuan*). Within the *Guishi*, he provides a detailed examination; study it carefully. A monk asked Zhenfo: [The text continues with the dialogue].
"True Dharma and True Way. Linji said: "The Buddha is the purity of mind; the Dharma is the luminosity of mind;
the Way is the unobstructed pure light everywhere. These three are one; they are all empty names without reality. This is my own perspective."
This is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you can realize the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If you realize the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to humans and devas. If you realize the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself. Now, ask about the first phrase.
Ji said: "The seal of the three essentials opens; the vermilion dot is narrow. There is no room for deliberation; host and guest are distinguished. He was asked about the second phrase. Ji said:

"How could wondrous understanding fail to admit the question of Wuzhuo? How could Upagupta fail to match the power of cutting off the stream? He was asked about the third phrase. Ji said: [He remained silent].
Ji said, "Just look at the puppeteers on the stage; their pulling and manipulating depend entirely upon those inside the puppets.
He then continued, "In general, when chanting the *zongcheng* (the core lineage), one must possess the three mysteries within a single phrase, and each mystery must possess the three essentials.
There is the provisional and the real; there is illumination and function. How do you all understand this? Nan-yuan then asked about the first.
Regarding the three essential phrases: when Fengxue responded with a shout upon hearing the first phrase, [Zhaozhou] asked about the second phrase, the "wondrously understood" speech;
Fengxue said, "Before you even asked, you were already wrong. When he asked about the third phrase, the "eavespeak," Fengxue said, "If it is exposed by clarity, it is no longer fit.
Zhaozhou approved of this. Shending Yin said, "If I were asked the first phrase, I would say, 'Blue sky! Blue sky! For the second phrase, what would there be?"
"You fellow! Third phrase: Come closer and I will tell you. As soon as he drew near, [Shoushan] struck him.
"If you understand it thus, you do not fail the meaning of the Westward Journey. The Buddha-dharma is not a principle of smoothing edges or fitting seams;
one must truly detest the Buddha for not acting and detest the Dharma for not speaking. Take care! A monk asked Shoushan about the first phrase, and he replied: "Great!"

If you do not raise your eyebrows when using [the staff], you must see blood under the blow. Question: Where is compassion? Answer: Sent out beyond the mountain gate. Question: What is the second phrase? Answer:
I will not strike such a donkey-like fellow. Question: How do you receive people? Answer: When it is like this, what can one do? Question: What is the third phrase? Answer:
There is no one to answer your question. Question: Who is the one facing you? Answer: Do not let it be so.
The outsider knew. He asked, "Which phrase did the Master realize? The Master replied, "The moon sets at the third watch as it passes through the marketplace.
A monk asked Fenyang, "What is the place where the student exerts effort? He replied, "Striking the Great Elephant at Jia Prefecture.

He asked, "What is the place where the student turns? He replied, "Watering the Iron Ox at Shan Prefecture. He asked, "What is the intimate point for the student? He replied, "Playing with the Teacher in Xihe."

The Master then said: "If a person understands these three phrases, they have already mastered the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan). Yet there remain the words of the Three Essentials (Sanyao); you must earnestly seek to realize them. The verse says:
'The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; When one attains the meaning, one forgets the words, and the Way becomes easy to approach.
A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena; On the Double-Ninth Festival, the chrysanthemums are fresh. He further said: 'Do you understand the Three Mysteries? "
At such a time, you must directly realize the meaning of the ancients; only then will your own mind become clear.
Furthermore, you will attain mastery in adaptive transformation, enjoying inexhaustible freedom. This is called the Buddha of Self-Enjoyment Body, who does not rely on the teachings of others.
Thus, you recognize your own livelihood. Question: What is this livelihood? Answer: Two water buffaloes, their twin horns unconfined by a pen.
He spoke again: "If you wish to attain clear realization herein, you must directly grasp the essential purport of the Three Mysteries; only then will you be able to employ them without obstruction.
The verse says: The First Mystery: The Dharma-realm is vast and boundless; the myriad phenomena and all things are entirely contained within the mirror, perfectly complete.
The Second Mystery: The World-Honored One asked Ānanda; with extensive learning, he answered according to the matter, responding to the capacity and shape of the vessel."

The third mystery directly issues forth before the ancient sovereigns; it lies beyond the four propositions and the hundred negations. When Layman Lu asked Fenggan about this, he spoke these verses on the Three Mysteries.
What is the essential meaning of these three mysteries? I shall provide a clear and decisive resolution for you.
Do not falsely claim that you have personally attended upon a master and been told [the truth] by me; do not deceive others. There will come a day when you eat iron rods!
It is also said: Within a single phrase, one must possess the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials, with the roles of guest and host clearly distinguished.

Thus it is said: "To grind one's bones to powder would not suffice as recompense; a single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds. Regarding the "Three Mountains" [case] concerning the transmission of the Linji lineage:
when Linji struck him three times, he was called "the one who encountered the mysterious staff. Three Mountains said: "It is like a master setting up a command, yet the student does not understand."

1. Avoiding: To evade and thus offend the very head [of the matter], thereby fragmenting the profound intent. The Master strikes; this is a "punishment staff. 2. Responding to the occasion according to the primary staff:
When a patriarch receives a person, he strikes when it is appropriate to strike; this is called "responding to the primary. 3. Relying on the profound to harm the primary staff:

Students strive for the extraordinary and rely upon the mysterious and subtle, which conversely harms the correct principle. The Master strikes; this is also a "punishment staff. 4. Sealing and conforming to the school.

1. The Staff of the Essential Principle (*zhìbàng*). When the Master reveals the essential principle and the student responds accordingly, the Master then strikes him; this is the "seal" that confirms the student's capacity, and is called the Staff of Reward (*shǎngbàng*).

2. The Staff for Testing Reality or Falsity (*qǐyàn xūshí bàng*). As soon as the student arrives or utters a word, the Master strikes him; this is to test whether [the student's understanding] is real or false, and it does not belong to the category of reward or punishment.
3. The Staff of the Blind Man’s Noose and the Sightless Stick (*mángjiā xiàbàng*). Without discerning the student's capacity, the Master strikes indiscriminately; this is the practice of the Master.
Seven: The Staff of Chastising Ignorance. When a student does not understand clearly and is ten times ignorant, the Master strikes him repeatedly.
Eight: The Staff for Sweeping Away the Mundane and the Holy. Mundane sentiments and holy understandings are swept away together; whether one speaks the Way or not, all are struck.
This severing of the student's life-root is the supreme holding-up [of the Dharma]; the most wondrous use of the staff is called the "Correct Staff."
Yulin Xiu said: "First, one must be authentic in the arousal of the resolve; it must be solely for the sake of birth and death.
Second, one must be authentic in one's practice; investigate a single *huatou*. If you do not penetrate it in this life, you will investigate it in the next life.
Third, one must be authentic in one's realization; do not mistake it for the consciousness of the spirit, nor fall into a blank void."

One doubts birth and death, yet does not doubt the past and present. One does not forcibly assume the role of a sovereign master. One does not take a superficial acceptance as being possessed of power.
One does not take forced arrangements as being free from doubt. One does not take coarse and reckless madness as being the great function of great capacity.

One does not take a state of blank indifference as being a complete and thorough penetration. If one should advance further along the tip of the staff but fails to do so, these are merely words and phrases.
One should have participated but did not participate; one needlessly engaged in forced interpretation when there was no need for it; one suppressed what should not have been suppressed.

To stumble at the very first step of entering the gate is truly a cause for bitter lamentation. Fourth, one must ensure that the lineage transmission is authentic: have you failed to miss the point where the Master acted for your sake?
Have you failed to repay the Master by enduring the deep piercing of the hammer behind the head? Have you not thoroughly clarified the fundamental principles of the ancestors? No.

Does the practice of giving not tend to blind the eyes of people? If there is no authentic master to strike out the eye at the crown of one's head, then even if one possesses genuine realization, calamity will arise when one attempts to teach others.
This is especially true if one’s own view is already biased and the teacher one has approached is likewise mistaken.

When deviant poison enters the heart, it is like oil soaking into flour; yet some, failing to recognize this, recklessly claim "I have attained self-acceptance" (*ziken*) and refuse to undergo ultimate realization, asserting that they "cannot be turned by others.
Such people are hardly worth mentioning. Fifth, one must be precise and authentic at the very end.
Without having penetrated the final barrier, to speak of attaining great capacity and great function, or of possessing the fodder for the fundamental state—this is rare indeed.

Do not act like a coarse and reckless person who fails to recognize this ultimate barrier. Among the ancients, those who did not shift their prior understanding after attaining realization and instead re-examined it with renewed doubt—those who pointed to what they had previously taken for enlightenment as being delusion—are rare.
To slander the ancient sages and mislead future generations stems entirely from failing to understand this barrier that points toward the Ultimate;
should one not stand in awe of this? Sixth, one must properly cultivate the Truth of the Path. One’s own...

He said: "The Dharma-body also has two kinds of illnesses. First, having attained the Dharma-body, one fails to forget the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), and one's own views still persist;
to remain seated within the precincts of the Dharma-body is one illness. Second, even if you manage to penetrate through the Dharma-body, it is not permissible to let it go."
If one examines this closely, what trace of it remains? It too is a sickness. Miaoxi said:
"This is Yunmen speaking according to reality. To pass through the Dharma-body is considered the ultimate by people today; Yunmen, however, regarded it as a sickness."
It is not known through the *dharmakāya*. How can one act? Reaching this point is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
There is no need to ask others; to ask would be a calamity. This is Yunmen’s "Single-Word Barrier. Question: "If one kills one's father and mother, one repents before the Buddha.
Where does one repent if one kills a Buddha or a Patriarch? Answer: "Exposed (*lu*). Question: "Once exposed, what then? [Answer: "An obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*)."

"Empty. Regarding the Second Patriarch’s [question], "Is this understood or not? the answer was definitive. It is not recorded in full. Whenever Yunmen saw a monk, he would look at him and say, "Jian" (Mirror/Reflect).
If the monk wished to respond, he would say, "Ei. This became his constant practice; hence it is called "Guan-Jian-Ei" (Looking—Mirror—Ei).

Master Mi removed the "Guan" (Looking) and composed verses only on "Jian" and "Ei," which are known as the "Chou-Guan-Song" (Verses Extracting the Looking). The verse says: "Meeting face-to-face, no brow is raised. You go East..."
"I too am heading west. Crimson clouds pierce the azure void; the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. Juefan said: "Nowadays, descendants have lost the essential meaning.
To stare with angry eyes is taken as 'not recognizing sound and form,' and to 'recommend [the student] at the very moment of raising the question' is called for.
This is truly lamentable and painful! Yunmen said: "The seal covers heaven and earth; the eye weighs every grain. Without involving worldly conditions, how can one act?"
He accepted it. On his own behalf, he said: "A single arrowhead breaks through the three barriers. Master Mi classified this into three phrases: first, the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth;
second, the phrase that cuts off all streams; third, the phrase that follows the waves and rides the currents. Yuanwu said: "The fundamental reality is fundamentally empty;

it is a single color and a single flavor. It is not that there is no wondrous essence; it is transparently clear and bright—this is the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth. Fundamentally, it is not something to be understood..."
Meeting. To bring them all together, not a single word is needed; the myriad functions cease at once—this is the "sentence that cuts off the stream.

If one allows for mutual recognition, discerning the ground from the sprouts—this is the "sentence that follows the waves. Shoushan cited the "sentence of the container and its cover" as "pervading heaven and encompassing the earth," the "sentence that cuts off the stream" as "not passing through for ordinary or holy beings," and the "sentence that follows the waves" as "having a question, there is an answer. A monk asked:
"What is the Way? Ba Ling Jian said: "A man with clear eyes falls into a well. Question: "What is the 'Blow-Off Sword'? Answer:
"Coral branches, branch after branch, support the moon. Question: "What is the School of Deva? Answer: "Snow served in a silver bowl. Jian did not compose a letter of succession.
He presented these three turning words to Yunmen. Yunmen said, "On the anniversary of my old monk’s death, it will suffice to recite these three turning words as an offering.
The Verse on the Essential Principles of Yunmen says: Kang’s circular form remains stagnant and unilluminated.

The Māra is profoundly empty and lost, struck by the cold ice. When the phoenix’s feathers unfold, it soars beyond the azure Milky Way. Against the eightfold array of sharp points, what can one rely upon?
(1) This mechanism is paired with its counterpart; through the counterpart, the mechanism is deluded. To open the dust of the mechanism, one must travel far away from the dust where it settles.

At sunset and at midday, who has anything to hang upon? By means of this very basis, this very matter, one parts from the delusion of dust. (2) One loses the light of time; the forest of vines falls into ruin. To schematize the intentions of others—what use is this?
(3) Stagnant flesh and emaciated. *Du du du*. Liǎngkǒu xī. Chanzi ya. Zhōngméi chuí. (4) Above, one sees not heaven;
below, one sees not earth. The throat is choked; where can one breathe? Many laugh at me; few smile at me.
(5) This verse is the Great Compassion Perfect Dharani. From the *Zǐfù jí*, "The Eye of Humanity and Heaven."
The middle section is omitted for the sake of explanation. This resembles an awakening that arises from the *Chuanglun* (Treatise on the Creation) school of the Fayan lineage.

When Xuefeng simultaneously threw out three wooden balls, Xuansha made a gesture as if brandishing a wooden shield. Xuefeng said, "Only when you were personally present at Vulture Peak could you act like this.
Xuansha replied, "This too is my own affair. One day, as Xuefeng rolled out a wooden ball, Xuansha seized it.
*Anjuchu* (Resting in the Old Place). Xuan Sha asked, "Is there Buddha-dharma where the bamboo fence is?
Feng shook the fence once. Xuan Sha said, "I do not say it is so. Feng asked, "How is it? Xuan Sha said, "It passes right through the ends of the bamboo strips.

Because those of superior capacity were rarely encountered, Xuan Sha established the three phrases as the fundamental principle (*gangzong*). He said: "The first phrase: For now, take responsibility for yourself. [Manifestation]

It is fully accomplished; it is entirely the work of your mind-king, which completely becomes the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). Regarding the fundamental principle, this still clarifies what precedes but not what follows;
it is of a single flavor, level, and real, representing the measure of partial realization of the *dharmakāya*.

If one knows how to transcend the ordinary and turn [the mind] as soon as it reaches the hand, one does not fall into the view of a settled disposition. This is called the "First Phrase" of the fundamental tenet. It does not cling to the commonplace.
Whether relinquishing or grasping according to what is appropriate, both principles are clearly elucidated; unmoved by either extreme, wondrous function manifests before one.
This is called the topical outline of the second phrase. It is to know the fundamental nature and characteristics of great wisdom and to penetrate its measureless vision.
Its application is without fixed direction; it is used in its entirety, or not used at all. This expedient means is called the gate of the Samādhi of Compassion.
This is what is termed the essential principle of the third phrase. Attendant Lohan Chen was serving as the attendant Sha Ling.
[The Master] closed the door and asked, "How will you get out? Chen said, "What do you call this 'door'? Dizang asked Fayan, "Mountains, rivers, and the great..."
Dizang asked, "Are the earth and the self the same or different? Xuedou said, "Different. Dizang held up two fingers. Xuedou said, "The same.
He also held up two fingers and then rose to depart. When Xuedou took his leave of Dizang, Dizang said, "Ordinarily it is said that the three realms are but mind.
Pointing to a piece of stone, he asked, 'Is this within the mind or outside the mind? Xuedou said, 'Within the mind. Dizang asked, 'What does a traveling monk have to do with such things?'"
Regarding the origins: Fayan was placing a flat stone upon his heart when his vision failed him. He opened his bag and sought a resolution, presenting his understanding day after day.

Fayan said, "The Buddha-dharma is not like this. Fayan said, "I am at my wits' end; my reasoning has reached its limit. Fayan said, "If one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, everything is already fully accomplished.
At these words, Fayan attained great enlightenment. This is the general outline of the lineage transmitted through the Fayan school. Fayan was the Third Patriarch.
The Verse on Mind-Only states: The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Consciousness-only and mind-only—eye and sound, ear and form.
Form does not reach the ear; how could sound touch the eye? Eye, form, ear, and sound—the myriad dharmas are thus accomplished. The myriad dharmas do not exist apart from conditions.

How could one not observe that the great earth, mountains, and rivers are like illusions? What is solid and what undergoes change? The *Verses on the Meaning of the Six Characteristics in the Avataṃsaka* states:

"The meaning of the six characteristics in the *Avataṃsaka*: within identity there is still difference. If difference were distinct from identity, it would entirely fail to accord with the intention of the Buddhas."

The intentions of all Buddhas—whether general or particular—have never possessed identity or difference. When entering meditative concentration within a male body, one does not fix the mind upon a female body.
Not fixing the mind means transcending names and words; the myriad phenomena are luminously clear, yet devoid of principle or substance. The Eye and Mind of Humans and Gods says:
"When the single mind gathers and encompasses all dharmas, it receives the name 'general'; when it gives rise to various conditions, it forms 'particular' designations. Dharma after dharma...

All are equally characterized by the mark of sameness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Because they follow after marks that are not equal, they are called "different aspects" (*nānā-mukha*). Because they establish objects of perception, they are called "accomplishment.
Without moving from its own position, it acts as destruction. A monk asked, "What is one drop of water from the Cao source? Nanquan said, "This is one drop of water from the Cao source.
When Master Shao heard this, he attained great enlightenment and rolled his eyes upward. Nanquan said, "In the future, you shall serve the state."
The National Teacher Shao’s Fourfold Selection: Hearing the Hearing. (Open) Three Mountains’ Verse: Myriad pipes transmit their sounds;
neither there nor here. Open wide the gates of the ears; all are contained within. Hearing the Non-hearing. (Close) Three Mountains’ Verse: Monkeys howl and birds sing;
falling flowers and flowing water. Is it sound? Is it not sound? Returning to the Truth is likewise so. Not Hearing the Hearing. (Clarify) Three Mountains.
Verse: Just arrived beneath the tall pines, again passing by the secluded ravine. Wandering among springs and rocks, at every spot he expounds the Mahāyāna.
Not heard, not heard—(blind! Three Mountains Verse: From all quarters, people ask the Way; face-to-face, there is no penetration of wind.
A light snore (pronounced *gan*) as heaven and earth age; on one pillow, dreaming of Duke Zhou. Song of National Teacher Shao’s Patriarchal Style: Tongxuan Peak.
The Summit. It is not of the human realm. There is no dharma outside the mind. Green mountains fill the eyes.
The preceding records of the essential tenets and words of the Five Houses have briefly demonstrated their school styles; do not, however, become mired in them.
A lion cub takes what it holds and uses it immediately, treading upon the summit of Vairocana. How could a single wedge be considered simplistic? Who would say a general store is fragmented? Herein—
There is none. How could there be five families? All emerge from within this; how could it be limited to five families alone? When employed, one vies in wealth with the Dragon King of the Sea;
when not employed, it is not worth half a coin. To manifest transformation according to the occasion, its application is boundless.
Until the end of the future, I entreat you to take these words to heart.

I shall now demonstrate that our Buddha is the Dharma King of this entire era. The Buddhas and sages of the past were either those who served as the primary recipients of his teaching (*dharmabhājana*) or those who acted as his echoes and influences (*praticchāyā*).

They manifested through provisional means or through reality; they appeared as correct or as erroneous; they manifested the perfect or the partial; they manifested compliance or opposition. Their skillful means are like a vision.
Mañjuśrī, [those who oppose you] are like Sunakṣatra and Devadatta; they are as heterodox as Dīrghanakha and Aṅgulimāla; they are as partial as the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas;

and they even manifest as the ninety-five kinds of external paths, displaying their perverse wisdom to challenge the Buddha. It is because of them that our Buddha’s perfectly sudden and orthodox teaching has been able to be propagated and disseminated through the five periods of exoteric and esoteric revelation.
These individuals are all... [not... (Note: The final phrase "其人皆不" appears to be incomplete or truncated in the source text.)
One may thus hold a Dharma assembly on reality; the various patriarchs of the Chan school were likewise so.

Therefore, at times it was said, "The very mind is Buddha," and at times, "Neither mind nor Buddha. At times, every verdant bamboo is entirely True Suchness (Tathatā); at times, the yellow chrysanthemums are certainly not Prajñā.
All of this is nothing other than untying attachments and removing fetters, pointing the way back to the correct track. Previously, there were six [disciples] converted by the First Patriarch.

As for the school, there have subsequently been various judgments differing across the ages. For instance, regarding the *Three Mysterious Essentials*, there are the partial words of the "Ancient Stūpa" faction and the "picking-up" phrases (*niangu*) of the Sanfeng faction.
Furthermore, the commentaries and songs of the various patriarchs concerning the Five Ranks of the Dongshan lineage differ;

the Master Wumeng’s approach and the "picking up" and "raising" methods of the two houses of Linji and Dongshan each vary. Although these differences involve disparities in quality, the essential point is...

All [these manifestations] are appearances made through the power of vows; they are not partial. If there were no partiality, how could their perfection be revealed? They are not disparate; if there were no disparity, how could their excellence be revealed?

Those of future wisdom must perceive the profound intent behind these manifestations. One must not harbor the impulse for aggressive or boastful speech. Let there be no fixed teacher in learning; let that which is virtuous be the master.
In this way, may the seal of the patriarchs be held high and the wondrous mind be thoroughly penetrated. Thus it is said—Han.
The *Moon Treasury* (*Candragarbha*) states: "Since the time of Aśvaghoṣa was formless, the 'One' (I) has been the progenitor of ten million Buddhas.
Thus, the Seven Buddhas [transmitted] the double-headed single-knot, with the four dharmas interlaced, forging the unlettered secret seal (*guhyamudrā*).

For twenty-eight generations since Kāśyapa, there has been nothing other than taking the Dharma-seal as the mind. The gravity of this Dharma’s inability to perish is profound."—Dharmatrāta, the sixth [patriarch].

Regarding the transmission of the Dharma thereafter, those who branched off as peripheral followers excavated intellectual pathways from within the Dharma-verses; thus, the secret essence became permeated with leakage.

Master Mazu extracted a single pivot and a single realm, utterly severing all side-gates and holding up only that which transcends [the ordinary]. Therefore, the direct manifestation was held as paramount.
Consequently, there arose the "Wild Fox" shaking its door three times and Baizhang’s final "Great Roar. These were the seals of the mind-dharma transmitted from the past.
It is settled here. Huangbo had three "painful blows," but I have never heard of the principle of two or four blows.
These are Linji’s Three Mysterious Essentials (San Xuanyao), which were revealed to elucidate the secrets of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

they were established as a Dharma for ten thousand generations to distinguish [the authentic] from the "one-stump" [view] and the similar "fox-slobber. Tiantong rebuked this, saying: "This Han-yue uses the 'three shakes' as the 'three [blows]."
"Sudden" serves as the basis for Linji’s Three Mysterious Essentials. Let me ask you: if there were a majestic sound (*vīṇā*), one could not say it was without form;
yet if there were none, from whom did this [circle] ◎ come to be drawn? Furthermore, the Seven Buddhas had only gāthās; we have never seen them with double-headed seals or single-knotted seals.
Nor have we heard that Śākyamuni employed the four dharmas in a crisscrossing manner. Since he did employ the four dharmas in a crisscrossing manner, how could it be...?
This may be called the "Seal of the Absence of Words. Han Yue’s *Lianhua* (Plucking the Flower) at Lingzhi Hermitage says: "The root of this Dharma is that originally there is no Dharma.

Is 'no Dharma' not itself something? It is fundamentally the existence of Dharma. To transmit it as 'no Dharma' is precisely the existence of Dharma. What is this 'Dharma of dharmas'? It is precisely no Dharma.
This is existence within non-existence, and non-existence within existence; it cannot be categorized as either existence or non-existence."
This is untenable. Is this not simply Han Yue drilling out a logical path from the Dharma-verses and arranging them into four dharmas?
When has he ever dreamed of Master Ma’s single pivot and single scene, or Baizhang’s single shout that deafened the ears?
Xuedou’s verse on Yunmen’s response to “One” concludes with: “Distinct, distinct! The old man of Shaoyang attained one peg. Now, what is this “one peg”?
Head! How could there be anything else such as being hard or not hard, or being similar or not similar? Han Yue has slandered me;
when has he ever even dreamed of my single staff pointing directly to the fundamental portion of all people—the very matter of holding up the supreme truth?
Master Zang’s *Origins of the Five Schools* says: "The painting of the Seven Buddhas begins with... [the beginning].

Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja: he alone first manifested the single "ten" (一○) sign. Thereafter, the seven Buddhas each possessed their own verbal explanations, yet the purport of their verses did not transcend this circular sign.
Now, "awe-inspiring" (威) refers to that which lies beyond form; "sound" (音) refers to that which lies beyond voice.

Since no record exists of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja having appeared in written accounts, this is the supreme matter prior to the emergence of letters. It is as if it were manifested by Nāgārjuna, and thus we look up to it in reverence.
"Mountain" refers to the samādhi of signlessness; this was the case prior to the time of Dīpaṃkara.
The "round symbol" (yuanxiang) originated with the various patriarchs of India, and its transmission from the Seven Buddhas' verses by Bodhidharma has a clear source.

Let us examine this: the round symbol already embodies the essential tenets of the Five Houses. Tiantong criticized it, saying: "How can the origins of the Five Schools be based on a painter's diagram? This...
Hanyue fabricated [this] and suppressed the account of the appearance of King Awesome Sound (Vaiśvānara) in the *Lotus Sūtra*, falsely claiming it does not exist;
he merely drew a single circle (○). Furthermore, the original *Wu xiang sanmei* (Samādhi of No-Form) did not speak of this, but only of "not departing from the Samādhi of Hiding the Body.
Later, when Wang Changshi sent a letter drawing a single circle (○), Muzhou said, "There is one at a thousand li away."
Zhiyin looked up and said, "He is also just a worldly fellow. He drew a circle on the ground, wrote the character for "sun" inside it, and then wiped it away with his foot.
Guishan laughed heartily. It is clear that various circular signs do not go beyond the *antar-hita-samādhi* (the samādhi of invisibility).
Is wiping it away with one's foot not, in fact, a reversal of the previous case of invisibility? Han Yue speaks thus in delusion; he arbitrarily creates the sign of a circle and claims that...

"Before the lamp. Since it is "before the lamp," how can one say that the circle-symbols (yuanxiang) originated from the patriarchs of the Western Heaven? If they originated from the patriarchs of the West, they all followed Śākyamuni;

by what logic, then, could they be said to exist "before the lamp"? Furthermore, you claim that the circle-symbols already possessed the essential tenets of the Five Houses, and that each house emerged with its own particular aspect.
You assert there was a "True Lineage" (zhengzong) that first produced the Linji school, and thus this circle symbol was cast forth.

It emerges. As for "directly cutting off the life-root of a person": since it is said that each of the five houses presents its own aspect, one should take the single circle (○) and open it into five aspects.
Now, since these five aspects are opened from the single perfect circle, then when they are correct, they are all equally correct.
If one side is biased, both are biased. Why, then, should Linji alone be considered the orthodox lineage?
Furthermore, how could it be said that this ○-mark is fully present in Linji’s casting it forth to directly sever people’s life-roots?
This view—that Han Yue established a single ○-mark as the source of the five schools—is unreliable; how much less can it be said to grasp the essential principles of the five schools? Han Yue said:
Within the "One" (一), guest and host roll on and roll on, entering directly into the eye of Śiva (Maheśvara).

As for that so-called "single verse of unceasing following the current," it is all the more laughable. Linji said, "Who knows that my treasury of the true Dharma-eye has been extinguished by that blind donkey?
If even the true Dharma-eye is extinguished, how much more so names such as "the One," "phases," "guest and host," or "the eye of Śiva"?
"Are you not causing harm to future generations? Furthermore, fearing that you might take names and marks as the ultimate reality, I used the 'blowing-hair sword' to sever those names and marks.
Yet, fearing still that you might take even the blowing-hair sword as the ultimate reality, I said, 'One must urgently polish it.
Thus, Han Yue has not yet reached the fundamental point; therefore, he does not see King Weyin Buddha. 'King Weyin' refers to all Buddhas."

All sentient beings receive this [Dharma] together; it is clear at a glance, requiring no deliberation or verbal explanation. This is what is meant by the statement that "sentient and insentient beings preach the Dharma inexhaustibly.

If one does not take the realization of the Five Houses as the fundamental principle, but instead establishes divergent extremes as the "Five Houses School," then it will lead to later generations fabricating strange anomalies, engaging in groundless and baseless exegesis, and falling into false extravagance. From...
Han Yue began [his critique], and Tan Ji subsequently composed the *Wuzong jiu* (Rescue of the Five Houses). Tiantong [Zhuo] wrote the *Bawang jiu* (Refuting the False Rescue), stating:
"Tan Ji claims that after Linji’s 'three segments and two blows' (the two blows referring to those struck at Kefu and Puhua), he clarified [the teaching] through the 'Four Methods of Examination.

Thereupon, the fundamental tenets such as 'Profound and Essential,' 'Guest and Host,' and 'Illumination and Function' were established. It is evident that [Tan Ji] has lost his own head; he does nothing but force names together.
Regarding the "Phenomenal Signs" (xiàng), there are generally three; these are cited as the essential basis for the Three Mysteries (sān xuán).

For instance, such acts as the three strikes and three shakes, or the verse concerning Baizhang’s soy sauce jar which says, "The pestle was struck, the three jars were passed down," as well as Xinghua’s presentation of incense, are all likewise reduced to the number three.
(Linji, Sansheng, and Daqiao) have bewitched later generations. As for the "three blows of the staff," Han Yue claimed that he had never heard of the principle of "two blows" or "four blows.
Yet how could Tan Ji dare to speak of "two strikes"? To call them "blows" is already like chasing after a clod of earth;
how much more so to take the "three segments and two strikes" as a fixed formula and attempt to clarify them through the "Four Kinds of Selection"? Furthermore, he cites a verse by Han Yue:
The Verse of the Seven Buddhas says: "The formless body and mind are both existence and non-existence; existence and non-existence are both severed, like reeds entwined in secret.
A sudden clap of thunder cannot reach to cover both ears; the dream is broken, and the moon alone is solitary in the distant sky.

Furthermore, this manifestation and that which is called "neither existent nor non-existent, for existence and non-existence are both impossible" are all like the *Hsi* (Commentary) on the *Ten Wings*, intended to clarify the principle of the single zero (一○). It is not...
Once you have realized that [the previous view] was already mistaken, what further need is there to discuss the words regarding its "binding"? It is just like a dream being severed in the vast void;
it does not go beyond being like hearing the verse on thunder while sitting silently in a public hall with the source of the mind unmoving.

When the sound reaches the crown of the head and awakens what is one's own, it is worlds apart from the groundless talk of existence and non-existence. — *Wujia jiuzhu* (The Rescue of the Five Houses)

It is said: Huangmei likewise used the *kāṣāya* to encircle the Sixth Patriarch and examined his prior realization. Upon the Great Enlightenment regarding "the mind arising from non-abiding," he entrusted the robe and bowl to him.
Our former Master remarked that every stitch of the *kāṣāya* clearly manifests the numerical principles of the Dharma; it is not merely for show.
From one stripe to twenty-five, each stripe consists of five sections, each being four spans long and one span short, opening and closing [in this manner].
Through transformation, one silently seals the vast essence of the mind; through the perfect fusion of the integrated and the sequential, one does not stagnate in any single partiality.

Only then does one fully exhaust the profundity of this mind and this Dharma. It is not that there is some so-called "esoteric transmission" existing apart from the mind. This is like the Sixth Patriarch’s verse on the Bodhi tree having no tree:
is it not the case that he remained stuck in the realm of purity, such that his realization of the mind-Dharma was not yet perfect? If this were the ultimate, [it would be incomplete].
When the third drum sounded and [Huineng] entered the room, there could have been no further "great penetration" (da che). Thus, the meaning of the verse would have been partial;

even if Master Lu had emerged again, he would surely have nodded in agreement. Now, because his realization did not reach this point, he concluded that the First Patriarch had fixed the essence of the school (zongzhi) upon the robe.

This clearly demonstrates that Tanji was unwilling to reflect deeply. Previously, he cited the threads of the robe as a demonstration of the number of transmissions, claiming it was no mere formality.

Later, [Hanshan] said, "The essential meaning does not reside in the robe. Thus, they have become mutually confused and self-contradictory. Han-yueh falsely accused the Sixth Patriarch’s verse of being a view of annihilationism;
Tan-jih altered it to say that the mind-dharma was not yet perfected because he remained attached to purity. This refers to the World-Honored One’s verse: "The Dharma originally has no dharma..."
"Is it not also because you are still stuck in the realm of purity and have not yet attained perfection? Furthermore, there is a verse by Kāśyapa: "All dharmas are from the beginning the Dharma;
there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Is this not 'originally not a single thing'? Where, then, could dust and grime settle?

Han Yue Tanji, speaking of the mysteries of this mind and these dharmas outside of the "original state," conversely disparaged the verse of the Sixth Patriarch as being stuck in the realm of purity. He has not even dreamed [of its true meaning].
"To see that in every place and in every speck of dust there is entirely the person of original nature. [The critic] says:
"The Fifth Patriarch’s statement that he had not yet seen his nature is crystal clear; it is laughable for later generations to claim he intentionally withheld permission.
Tiantong says: "The *Platform Sūtra* records the Fifth Patriarch saying: 'I considered your insight to be usable, but fearing that evil people might harm you, I did not speak with you.'"
Later, upon seeing the verse, he took his sandals and wiped them clean, saying, "Even so, you have not yet seen your nature. Thus the doubts of the assembly were dispelled.

Therefore, when [Huineng] met the Fifth Patriarch, he said to his disciples, "Moment after moment, do not depart from your own nature," and later, "All myriad dharmas are not separate from one's own nature;
how could it be that one's own nature gives rise to the myriad dharmas? Although these statements differ in their brevity or detail, their underlying principle is no different. How can one...

To say that "not seeing one's nature" is the truth is precisely the meaning of "originally there was not a single thing. This is entirely the self-nature (*svabhāva*). How could there be another thing apart from this self-nature?
To falsely claim otherwise would be to fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and to slander by clinging to the extreme of purity;

I fear such an error of slandering the Dharma will persist through all future kalpas. Tiantong said: "A single phrase contains the three mysteries; a single mystery contains [the three gates of liberation]."

Regarding the "Three Essentials": they correspond to the Three Mysteries and Nine Essentials. Since one cannot rigidly assign them to these three characters, how could one take the Three Mysteries and Essentials as the ultimate reality and claim that one has personally realized the Three Mysteries and Essentials? Before Linji, there were no such terms as "Mysteries" and "Essentials.

This does not mean that from the World-Honored One down to Linji, there was absolutely no one who attained realization. If there were indeed such realizations, what connection do they have with the [Three Mysteries and] Essentials?
How profound and essential! Although Juefan delivered the same shouts in both halls, the distinction between guest and host remained perfectly clear.

Yet, those who see this and mistakenly take it to be the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials cannot avoid being ridiculed by the wise. However, there is a point where he surpasses you: he says that "to look closely at it is the trap for the tiger.
Does this not prove that the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are not substantial dharmas? Furthermore, in his "Rescue," he also speaks of "seizing and presenting" the Mysteries and Essentials.

Nor would it be so. You have mistaken the subject of the verse. Have you not recited the verse on the "Guest and Host" from within the words of Dongshan?
Cuiyan’s Verse: Guest within guest, The words spoken do not correspond; Without careful and thorough reflection, One rides an ox across Mengjin. The Commentary states:
This verse shows that the eye of the student of the Way is not yet clear. Mengjin is deep and vast, yet one wishes to ride across it. Host within guest: They pull each other until noon.
To expand upon this, one is naturally incapable; thus, one must pass through the gates of others. The commentary says: "The verse speaks of the practitioner possessing the eye.

Northwest. Like Han Shan and Shide meeting and laughing "He-he. If you hesitate to deliberate, the year of the Rabbit (Yimao) becomes the year of the Tiger (Jiatin); the black bean has been swapped.
The Master of Masters sits right at the head; one must be awestruck. Having traversed ten thousand li across the shifting sands, who would say there are Buddhas and Patriarchs?
The commentary states: "The Master of the Verse has firmly grasped [the essence]; even the Buddhas and Patriarchs have no place to lodge.

Awakening. The school of the Buddha’s direct realization of Buddhahood in this very standing place (Zhengli Dizhi Chengfo Zongcheng) shares the same track as the six aspects (liu xiang), the three mysteries (san xuan), the five positions (wu wei), and the three phrases (san ju).
Fayen composed verses to establish these as the fundamental tenets. As for the compiler of *Juren Tianmu*, he included the discourse on the six aspects from the *Zongjing* within the school of Fayen.

"Now, I shall clarify this through the gate of causes and the illumination of wisdom by means of an analogy. For example, a house is the whole, while the rafters and so forth are its parts.
