I now ask Rui to feel his eyebrows for me. Let us inquire: when Rui first took his initial step, was there a master?
This refers to the "initial step with a master. Where did he go at the end? This refers to the "final function without a master.

Furthermore, have your eyebrows ever been told whether there is a master or not, or whether there is presence or absence at the beginning and the end? Is this like a stone woman striking a bell? This is the work of a young girl.
The mind immediately seizes upon the eyebrows and pulls them. A barren woman strikes a bell;

she then proceeds to paint descriptions of words upon the space outside the eyebrows, yet the eyebrows remain fundamentally serene from the beginning—how could they ever be defiled? This is "the cave of the eyebrows. To understand the eyebrows themselves is to understand the master.
Once the cave has dispelled the master, there are no eyebrows. Thus, the cave not only fails to recognize the master, it does not even recognize what the eyebrows are.
Wu: How can you say that this verse was produced without being valued? Yulin said:
When Rui Bai asked Elder Duzhuan, "Who dragged your corpse here? and "Who is it that asks this question?", he misunderstood.
He wanted to recognize this spirit-like inquiry that drags the corpse along, yet he spent several days acting in blindness. Then, it is said, there was a sudden "pulling up" with the hand.
This has been mentioned there and brought up here. To understand this "questioning while dragging a corpse" is to recognize it as one's own self.

Yet, people falsely claim that this is like the initial awakening of Yunmen. The verse says: "With a master, one takes the first step forward; the pillow falls from the peak as if leaping out of a net.

Only when one speaks in disorder can one truly leave behind consciousness and merge with emptiness, such that even the master is no more. The false verse says: "Without a master, this is the final work. This is merely a false recognition.

The spirit (the subject) is taken as the master of awakening; thus, by asserting there is a "master," one first establishes the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), which you yourself know has been condemned by the ancients.

Furthermore, by linking the emptiness of consciousness to this "master" and failing to let go of it, you mistakenly claim this is the final stage of practice, thereby establishing the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

You yourself also know this is not yet accurate, so you separately say, "liberation from both existence and non-existence"—this is like a barren woman striking a bell. If that were so, the Peak would have had a third stage of awakening.

Furthermore, he became a deceptive and confused outsider. At night, startled by an omen, he claimed to have awakened to the "Master. At dawn, having encountered a corpse being dragged past, he asked questions about it and maintained a state of "clear spiritual efficacy" (*zhāolíng*).

Therefore, he was criticized for his view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Later, during a seven-day retreat, his body and mind suddenly fell away; even the "Master" could no longer be found, leading him into a state of falling into emptiness and nihilism.

Therefore, he was criticized for his view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). He then again employed the deception of claiming that "neither existence nor non-existence is itself existence or non-existence."
This jumble of verses at the end may deceive people; by answering haphazardly according to whatever is asked, one might say that birth and death are of no use.
Once one has fallen asleep, they are indeed of no use. It even goes so far as to claim that all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are merely manifestations of one's own mind without distinction.
This leads people to commit murder, debauchery, and falsehoods without limit. They talk of Chan while satiated with meat, hoping for [the robes of a monk].
Those possessed by demonic influences who have not yet invited retribution should each exercise vigilance and repent early; do not wait until it is too late for regret.

Now Rui has died, and his demonic son Liyan, deluded and deranged, has even dared to slander what was recounted on the Hall platform for the purpose of instructing students—spreading perverse and distorted interpretations that must not be taken as the true Dharma.
This is the "Parting from Words and Severing Attachment" (Liyan ge'ai ci).

My dear friend, for what reason exactly? If you wish to treat consciousness as the "external path" (cittabāhya), you need only rely on the five sections and six volumes of the *Avatamsaka Sūtra* (Wéijìng Jīng).
To perversely cite such phrases as "that which is in the eye is called seeing" and gather together the discourse of demons—what need is there to falsely claim this belongs to the Chan school?
Furthermore, you take the "consciousness-spirit" (shénshí) that asks questions while dragging a corpse as your primary principle. Since the fundamental basis is already mistaken, and furthermore...
One becomes attached to demonic realms and falls into a state of indeterminate emptiness. Standing precariously for half an incense stick’s duration before the Buddha, one gradually awakens;
yet within the mouth, chaotic clouds of thought cannot be settled. This is merely like those suffering from alcoholism or fever: when in a state of stupor, there is no master;
one loses heart and forgets the body, remaining ignorant of all matters. Even if struck, one feels no pain, only awakening after a long time—it is just like that. One wishes to subdue these demons...

Externally manifesting, you have erroneously interpreted the essence of the lineage (zong-cheng), defiling the High Peak (Gao-feng). Your false alterations and misalignments have rendered your views utterly untenable.
Before the Peak has even fallen from his pillow, you have merely split the state of "no-thought" into two separate parts.

Yunyan’s stone woman dancing and the stone woman striking the bell—these words of deceptive confusion are worlds apart [from the truth]. Do not say that your teacher annotated his own errors; at the very end...

"Kung! This is the realization of the 'pillow-fall' [koan]. To be 'without' or 'with' [conceptualization] regarding striking it off is to say that a practitioner must not take 'being' or 'non-being' as their livelihood.
Various external views can ultimately never escape [this truth]; what is the use of forced sophistry? It is further said:
'The evil poison of the various demons of the central realm brings about bad fruits from good causes. First, he cites the case of a monk and a layperson from Huzhou, mentioning Gui'an."
There was a layman of abundant and auspicious fortune who, in the prime of his youth, turned toward the Way.

He observed the precepts and maintained the fasts, yet he felt remorse for the weight of his habitual lust and sought liberation from birth and death. By mistake, he fell into the net of the demon Rui.

The son of the Lord of Death, Liyan, took him by the hand and enlightened his spiritual consciousness, causing him to recognize the dragging corpse as the awakened master. Although he still knew that lust and delusion were wrong, Rui then said: "Just now—"
When one penetrates and participates in these conditions, there is immediately a path of entry. Furthermore, it is said that all habitual tendencies are entirely manifestations of one’s own mind;
what differentiation is there? What fetters are there? He teaches them to gain faith in this ultimate point: that there is nothing which is not you, and nothing that is not liberation.
Yet he falsely drags in the myriad phenomena as being the solitary manifestation of the body, indulging their arrogance and causing them to become self-conceited.

Having awakened to the Way, he examined the monastic community; though he broke his fasts and violated the precepts, he encountered no obstacles whatsoever. Who would have known that the Buddha-dharma possesses such great spiritual efficacy?
In the seventh month of last year, half of his body became as cold as ice, and he was unable to turn over. He then gathered his father, elder brother, and relatives together.
Suddenly leaping up, he could not be restrained; he went straight before the hall and said: "One Bodhisattva holds a scroll, upon which his transgressions are written;
another great heavenly general holds a massive iron hammer, ordering him to confess each one."
If even a single word is concealed, it is as if struck by a great hammer. Alas! When the retribution for a lay practitioner has not yet arrived, they refuse to submit to the good;
their tone and appearance become even more defiant. Now, among those whose demonic influence is at its peak, who knows that when birth and death arrive, there will be no further room for pretense?
One must willingly submit at the gate of death and testify according to reality: "The first grave offense was claiming to have attained what one had not attained. This is the second lash.

He interrogated the śramaṇa. Third, he falsely fabricated a record of his sayings. Fourth, he broke the fast and violated the precepts. Having recounted his transgressions, he then described the retribution for suffering.
He spoke of receiving retribution in such-and-such hells, immediately creating their visual forms. Having finished describing the features of the hells, he said, "This is the karmic fruit.

First, one must undergo the "flower-retribution" (the preliminary signs). Having enumerated the various animal forms and sounds constituting this flower-retribution, he suddenly said, "One should first..."

He transformed into a pig and proceeded to grunt like one. He rushed into the bedroom, stripped away the bedding, and lay down upon the straw. His family members took the bedding and grass; he insisted on removing the bedding, saying, "Only the straw brings me peace.
His compassionate father felt heartache, and his kind elder brother shed tears of blood; though they wished to save him, they had no means to do so.
Yet the lay practitioner (upāsaka) explained the offenses and their characteristics with complete clarity. His father and elder brother then ordered him to recite the repentance rites.
When [the younger brother] was addressed by his name, he was suddenly dazed and knew nothing. Alas! When it came to the time for seeking repentance, he was unable to do so.

Why did he not recognize his own error early on, while he still had the capacity to repent, only to reach the point where he bit his own heel with no way to turn back? This may serve as a solemn warning for those today who mistake what they have not attained for what they have attained.
His elder brother personally told me this, and I said, "Your younger brother is truly a 'Seal of Auspiciousness' (Ruìyìn). He replied, "Indeed he is. And: ...he said, "Certainly. And:
Liyan obtained [the robe] by departing; he specifically requested to leave and arrived at his home. His younger brother glared at him with angry eyes.
Seeing that his countenance was unfavorable, Liyan left without uttering a word. His younger brother shouted, "Liyan! Liyan! Three times he called out this name before passing away.
This matter was known to everyone in Huzhou. My aunt recounted it to her elder brother. Furthermore, there was the Zen practitioner Baiyan, who formerly attended the late master...
The Master knelt before the couch and said, "If you, O Monk, would grant me your seal of approval, I would assist you in establishing the monastic community and raising funds and provisions.
He was then severely rebuked by his late teacher, and feeling he had no face to leave, he eventually received the Dharma transmission at Mount Bian. Wu Xunweng remarked:
"When Bairyak saw someone being struck, he asked, 'Do you understand? He wanted people to realize that what is being demonstrated is the very movement of striking; it is not done haphazardly."
He accepted [the transmission], and it was thus certified as enlightenment. His younger brother’s wife was also certified. Recently, she experienced retribution in this life:

she suffered from a strange ailment, her abdomen swelling like a gourd. She encountered many demonic disturbances; the entire house was filled with ghosts who appeared in broad daylight, striking and shouting in disorder.
Thus, this present retribution occurred just before death, known to both the monastic and lay communities. White Rock’s present retribution was like this;

as for its karmic flowers and fruits, they were exactly as described for the layman previously—decisively, not a hair’s breadth off. Until he died from vomiting blood, his present retributions were manifold.

The demonic hordes recognized this as the mind, claiming they had attained what they had not, slandering the Great Prajñāpāramitā. Even if there were no present retribution, [they would still enter...]
"There is no doubt he will fall into hell. Moreover, his retribution is manifest and clear; yet he remains entirely unheeding. What kind of mind is this?
Then the son of Māra remained silent for a long time before saying to his elder brother: "Although my younger brother’s karmic retribution is painful, his philosophical view is excellent.

His elder brother replied: "My younger brother’s view is not good. When his retribution became manifest, he personally claimed that what he had not attained, he had attained—furthermore, he was a prince."

In this family, those who indulge in their desires are many. Why is the retribution so immediate and severe? He has long remained silent, yet still claims that his younger brother has "penetrated" the barrier of the Patriarch.
Such demonic delusion—how could its calamity be small? Because of this, one knows that among his elder brother’s circle, there are many who have been poisoned from without;
how much more so for those of other surnames! Furthermore, his elder brother recounted that a certain person came to Liyan’s place and promised to attain enlightenment within three days.
The Way. On the first day, he gave this instruction: "Look into who it is that raises the hand and moves the foot. On the second day, he told them to look for themselves.
On the third day, he said, "Today you ought to take responsibility. If you do not take responsibility, come at the third watch and knock on my door.
Indeed, at the third watch they knocked on the door and took responsibility. When asked, "Is this a woman? [he replied], "It is a manifestation of the Great Light."
"In this land under the sun, there are such demonic spirits. How lamentable! There was a layman who asked Master Liyan, 'How many days of practice does it take for one to attain realization?
He replied, 'It can indeed be pointed out, but as for realization, one must realize it for oneself.
Bianshan could point it out, but he required people to recognize the *shen* (consciousness). The layman said, "He says that movement constitutes it."

As for the patriarchs of the West who said, "When it is before the eyes, it is called seeing," and so forth, I say: those were skillful means to indicate that when the King [of the Mind] manifests from the eight gates, the nature of seeing is revealed;
they did not point to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as being the nature itself. To cling to such words and misrecognize them is an error.
This would constitute taking cognition as an external path. To explain it apart from words is to labor in vain, for it is a distant recognition of activity.
Layman Li said, "I have spoken clearly; you still do not accept it. Tang replied, "I dare not accept it; I am terrified by the sight of the manifest retribution.
Li said, "If one says that the layman was not good, then nothing can be done about it. Alas! (The text ends with "Di").
"Prison is no small suffering; how could one allow oneself to be possessed by demonic spirits?

When Master Rui gave his instruction, there was none who did not teach that what is directly encountered through opening the mouth and moving the tongue—what is seen with the eyes and heard with the ears—is precisely the original source. Yet Yinyi remained deluded, saying:

'I have received your detailed instructions and believe them most deeply. How lost is his mind! Nevertheless, Yinyi still harbored doubts regarding the continuous flow of discursive thought. Rui said:
In the end, he does not fear falling into hell for eternity. He habitually uses the "poisonous pit" to trap laypeople, saying:

"What do you call 'delusive thought' (*vikalpa*)? To understand it erroneously is to become its victim. He says: "It has never been anyone else. He asks: "Who is it that gives rise to and extinguishes [delusion]?
It should be known," he says, "that the entire substance of delusive thought is none other than one's own self. This is a heterodox person speaking of the orthodox.

The Dharma; even the True Dharma becomes perverse. Therefore, I have raised this matter in general for two reasons: first, to hope that the demonic hordes will repent; second, to allow all quarters to debate it together.
Thus, the sons of Māra do not realize their own defeat and downfall. Is hell something to be taken lightly? To lead people astray into hell—how grave!

How can this be treated as mere child’s play? Why inflict such suffering upon infinite good people by sending them to hell? A monk asked Kōngtóng about the verse on Gāopīng: “Gāopīng was certainly not right,” [the monk said].
Bào’ēn remarked, “If Gāopīng had broken through the ‘corpse-sentence,’ he would have attained true enlightenment;
what do you think? Mùyúnmén said, “In the *Yísìshū*, it is asked: ‘Xuěyán, who dragged this corpse for you? This points to Gāopīng’s entire being.”
This is the Master. When Feng saw this, he praised him, saying, "Who is this fellow who stirs up trouble and drags around a corpse? His soul fled and his courage failed;

he was as if dead and then revived again, like one who has laid down a burden of several hundred thousand catties. This describes the state of the ultimate limit of the mind's inquiry and its objective manifestations.

Upon reaching Nanming, he encountered a total collapse and defeat; this was the karmic occasion of their meeting. The details of the correspondence regarding his succession have been omitted for brevity.
This is an introduction. It clarifies that even if one has attained the public case (gong'an), one is not yet free from deception;

and when one opens one's mouth, it is all muddled again. In daily life, one still lacks freedom, like being in debt to someone. This clearly shows that what was previously attained was not yet stable.

When fast asleep and without dreams, where is the master? [The questioner] has no answer. Although he previously understood the "corpse-dragging master," he has not yet realized the "master of the whole body. —Feng.
Do not deceive yourself. When you give rise to indignation and doubt, your pillow may fall from your head as you leap out like a fish from a net.

Recalling those former doubts regarding the enigmatic and paradoxical *gong'an* of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like a long-traveling guest returning to his hometown: it is simply the person of old, with no change in one’s former conduct.

"Securing the state and stabilizing the nation; cutting off the ten directions"—this refers to thorough awakening. When previously questioned by the master, one was茫然 (mángrán—bewildered and ignorant);
now, it is manifest before one's eyes. To have awakened to the place where one stands is to realize that one's conduct remains unchanged:
when unawakened, one eats and sleeps; once awakened, it is the same. "Cutting off the ten directions" means that what was previously vast and expansive is now sleep.
A dream has a master; now, that very master is manifest before you. Without troubling to stir a thought, he is everywhere and has never been hidden.
If you can break through this "dragging the corpse" phrase, you will truly awaken. Even if you must endure a lifetime of stupidity, what was the point of five years of resolute exertion?
When asked about this, Feng said: "Being triggered by the 'dragging the corpse' phrase, it was as if empty space were pulverized and the great earth leveled."

Deeply absorbed, subject and object are both forgotten, like a mirror reflecting a mirror. The "Wild Fox," "Puppy," "Buddha-robe," and "Emerging from Samādhi" anecdotes—when examined, they are perfectly clear.
The wondrous function of Prajñā is truly not deceptive; is this not genuine awakening? Answer:

There is doubt regarding the subsequent letter [of succession], for after failing to penetrate it even in one's dreams, one realizes that what preceded was not yet the ultimate reality. Question: Why did Feng [Shan] ascend the hall and not [speak]?
He brings up the final "finished hand" phrase, yet he also cites the earlier "unfinished" dialogue. It is just like empty space shattering and the earth sinking;
when both are forgotten, what is there that cannot be reached? Answer: This is precisely what you must ask. Fengchufu spoke of the place where one meets the "dragging of a corpse" to others.
He did so to encourage people to investigate in this manner, for there will surely be spiritual efficacy. He never pointed directly to this [specific case].

Regarding the phrases such as "to realize the hand as reality" and "the void shatters," some say these refer to having accomplished the matter, while others say they refer to not having accomplished it.
It is not that there is a difference in the words themselves; rather, there is "accomplishment" or "non-accomplishment" because there are depths and heights in realization.

According to this, one may merely understand the master of the daytime, but has not yet understood the master of the dreamless state. One sees only the void shatter and the earth sink, [yet fails to see] the non-duality of self and object.
Both are forgotten. One has not yet realized that subject and object are entirely the Master. It is like a mirror reflecting a mirror; one has not yet realized the origin of the mirror.

Even if you understand "dragging a corpse," you have not yet understood the corpse itself; therefore, there are no dreams or thoughts. To strike it into two separate pieces is to remain ignorant of where it falls.
The *Sishu* (Book of Succession) states: "To revive after death is also to reach the extreme limit of emotional intensity and find a path of life;

this is not merely a case of casting off the hand and reviving to deceive the world. Only when the pillow falls to the ground is it truly the moment of casting off the hand, self-acceptance, and revival.
The "Wild Fox Emerging from Samādhi" story is also understood clearly according to what one perceives; yet after the summer retreat ends, upon opening one's mouth, one feels it once again.
When the mind is turbid, where is clarity? One should know that although it is called "clarity," it is not a true clarity.
The *Xingzhuang* records his visit to Nanming to meet [him]. Although their spiritual jabs were not yielding, one does not know whether those jabs and turning phrases truly settled the matter or not.
Have you not seen how Dahui was still not yet enlightened when he had not yet met Yuanwu?
However, regarding this critical pivot (*jīfēng*), the *Yísì* does not record it. [Fēng] himself knew that his previous practice was not authentic and thus omitted it;
he also did not record [the case of] Kōngsuì Dìshèn. Is this not because Fēng himself did not regard this as the ultimate? Question:

Fēng was unable to respond to "no dreams or desires," yet he explained it separately by saying, "One's ground of realization has not escaped obstruction; this is right knowledge and vision. This seems similar [to the previous case]. Answer:
It has been five years since I broke through the "corpse-dragging" phrase. Why is it that there is no dream-mind master to confront?

How can one claim to have realized the truth while remaining ignorant of the master? One's correct view is merely empty and not yet substantial; how can this be called having a "ground of realization"?

Though you may shout when it is time to shout, sweep with your sleeve when it is time to sweep, and turn the sharp point of the pivot, your understanding is not yet certain. Master Yan will not let you off the hook.
As for this peak: one may only manage to become the master while dreaming in sleep; yet when questioned about the master who is without dreams, there is no answer. Therefore, I entrust you with this:

where does this master of a single awakening reside? It is precisely because you wish to truly see the place where the master is established that you must take this dragging corpse and break it open as your realization of reality.
Otherwise, will it not lead future generations to have a semblance of breaking open and dragging a corpse, seeing it and then claiming it for themselves?
This refers to true awakening. Regarding the phrase "The high peak rests upon a fallen cliff," every word must correspond to what Xueyan previously pointed out;
every word must overturn what one previously took as one's own master. Xueyan fully presents the master of the whole body, and Wufeng fully embodies the master of the whole body.
This is what is called "the ground of realization not being shed. Is it not so? The ground of realization not...
This is not the correct intent. I personally believe that High Peak’s “breaking the phrase of dragging a corpse” is fundamentally different from Rui’s own view of the "first step with a master.
However, if one does not realize the master who is without dreams or thoughts, then even reaching this point is seeing [the truth] but not yet penetrating it thoroughly.

Baoyuan also said this when speaking to Master Rui, calling it "great awakening" or "thorough awakening. However, when speaking of the state of awakening experienced by Houzhengzi, he simply called it "awakening.

Nevertheless, in the end, Baoyuan’s judgment—that [Houzhengzi] had not yet fallen before the pillow—regarding the statement that "one forms two separate pieces at the hand of the dreamless master," is actually quite appropriate as a measure of Fengxue’s triggering of the "dead corpse" (the ultimate realization). Tian.

The remarks of Mushi Yunmen regarding "the eyes being dark yet possessing discernment" are not recorded here. Ba’en’s judgment on "demons" and Feiyin’s censure of "wild interpretations" are likewise not recorded.
Regarding Tiantong’s judgment of Chaozong’s discourse, it says: "You cite Shimen Zhao, who claimed that all the sages of antiquity possessed the three mysteries and essentials.
I, this old monk, dare say that Zhao himself lacked the eye for discerning the Dharma; he was deluded by the 'mysteries and essentials' of Linji. Linji—

The first phrase of the Way means that one may become a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas; this is based on the fact that the person of original substance is the teacher of the patriarchs and Buddhas.
Thus it is said: "When all sentient beings are saved, there will be Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The second phrase means that one may become a teacher to humans and devas;

this is also based on the fact that the person of original substance is neither human nor deva, yet because they fail to turn their own mechanism back upon themselves, they falsely transmigrate through the realms of humans and devas. The third phrase...

One may attain self-deliverance, yet fail to reach full completion; this also refers to the primordial person who does not themselves turn the mechanism [of awakening], and thus fails to achieve self-deliverance.
This old monk relies solely on the person penetrating the three phrases; he does not perceive the names and words of those three phrases, much less the "Three Essentials" that have come as seals.
As with the first phrase when asked, the Old Monk has already spoken the second. Ji said: "The Seal of the Three Essentials opens; the vermilion dot is narrow.
Referring to the person before him by the vermilion dot, Shoushan’s great function did not involve raising an eyebrow;

under the staff, one must see blood. From the beginning, there was no distinction between self and other; it is only through question and answer that host and guest arise. Therefore, it is said: "There is no room for hesitation or deliberation."
In the "Distinction Between Host and Guest," Fengxue let out a shout as soon as he heard the sound. According to this, the Three Essentials (*sanyao*) allow no room for deliberation or conjecture.

Since there is no room for deliberation or conjecture, everything is clear at a glance; how could one still perceive any distinction between Buddhas, patriarchs, host, and guest, or even the names of the Three Essentials?
It is simply because [the Master] relies upon what each person inherently possesses and has always attained from the very beginning, that he points to each individual as such.

It is but a single phrase. When asked about the second phrase, Linji said, "How can one contend with the mechanism that cuts off the stream? Is this not a reversal of the question regarding cutting off the stream?
What is called "one phrase cuts off the stream" means that ten thousand mechanisms are stilled and eliminated. Shoushan also said, "A single word cuts off the mouths of a thousand rivers;
only at the crest of a ten-thousand-fathom peak does one attain the profound. Nan-yuan said, "Upon the bare flesh-ball, it stands like a wall ten thousand fathoms high. All of these refer to this.
Pointing to this mass of red flesh as the "Mystery" (xuán), it is said that the light has not yet reached the fundamental attainment; thus, one lacks the eye of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

Therefore, it is said that all sages possess the essential purport of the Three Mysteries. If one awakens to the fundamental attainment, one sees that there is no person who does not possess the principle of the fundamentally attained mass of red flesh.
How could one possibly apply some separate dharma to others? [The Master] asked about the third phrase. Jì replied:

To speak of "the person within the lining of the clouds" is precisely to rely upon the person of original nature; therefore, the pathways [of conceptualization] cannot withstand being exposed and broken open.

You claim that the "Seal of the Three Essentials" constitutes the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Path. Furthermore, you reckon that the first, second, and third phrases constitute three gates.
This is your error in attempting to correlate the three gates of the Three Mysteries with these three phrases, as well as with the triad of Buddha, Dharma, and Path.
Therefore, it is said that the third is based on the True Buddha, the second is the Dharma, and the first is the Way.
The Way clarifies both the Buddha and the Dharma; its illumination and function are unimpeded. Thus, it is said that "the One serves as the teacher for the Patriarchs and Buddhas.

Since both the Buddha and the Dharma are clarified, there is a Buddha who can serve as the teacher for the Patriarchs and Buddhas. Furthermore, it is said that the Patriarch is the Dharma itself, yet they are divided into two.
[The Master] said: "The Buddha established three phrases. Now I ask you: within these three phrases, can you save yourself?
You cannot. [The student] replied: "The Buddha’s mind is pure; this is one phrase. The Dharma-mind is luminous; this is one phrase.
The Way is everywhere unobstructed and is pure light; this is one phrase. You say that within a single phrase the three mysteries are complete; thus, a single phrase contains all three phrases."

This is *quan* (expedient means). To maintain the integrity of the correct command lies in the guest. Since you speak of *quan*, how can it be the complete and correct command? You have not yet dreamed of the meaning of the complete and correct command.
Furthermore, it is said: "A single phrase, luminously encompassing the myriad phenomena. This is because you do not understand that Fen-yang himself constitutes this single phrase.
The chrysanthemum is precisely the dust; every speck of dust is entirely Fen-yang. By using this to awaken people, he shows that each person encompasses the myriad phenomena. Dust...
When the dust is cleared away, it is simply the person of original nature. Furthermore, it is said that the three phrases are but one phrase, and the three mysteries are but one mystery;

thus, within a single mystery, the three essentials are complete. Every word does not depart from the fundamental state—this is the reality. To establish the primary essence, it must be perfect and round. Now I ask you:
why do you say that when the meaning is attained, words are forgotten, and that the Way is easy to approach? Does Yangshan [Fenyang] truly fail to forget them as you do?

The terminology of the "Profound" (xuán) and the "Essential" (yào) is indeed subject to reversal and inversion. Furthermore, it is said that the Three Profundities are but one Profundity, and the Three Essentials are but one Essential.
Thus it is said: "The four gates all lead to the one Essential; the one Essential encompasses the three Profundities. This was the teaching of Linji, Shoushan, and Fenyang.

The three essentials (*san yaoyao*) come first, followed by the three mysteries (*san xuan*); these are the real (*shi*) and the provisional (*quan*). Do not slander them. You see that one essential contains the three mysteries;
that is to say, the essential is the real and the mysteries are the provisional. Now, let me ask you where the four gates (*si men*) fall. Only after that can the one essential be judged;
then you will see that this is not a confused discourse. Shoushan said, "Who is it that comes thus? This was like pointing at the ground, and like testing him.
The monk replied, "I am so-and-so. Since the name applies to anyone who comes, he was always on the road and never left his home.
The Head said, "Do not say this is another person," thereby subtly verifying him. The monk prostrated; it can be seen that he knew the proper etiquette.
The Head asked, "What have you seen that you prostrate? This was yet another test of him. The monk replied, "Today it is very much like celebrating a feast. Indeed, he knew the etiquette.

[The Master] said: "As for what you just said, you must spit it out immediately. I fear that others might take these words as their own business, rather than realizing they do not accord with their own reality.
[The monk] replied: "I know, Master, that you have condescended to me. Indeed, I see that I cannot accept such indirect and named expressions.
The Master said: "If someone asks you hereafter, 'What did you say? how will you respond? The monk shook his sleeves and departed. If...
"It does not come forth. To explain it circuitously is also empty talk. He first summoned a monk and tested him again. When the monk turned his head, Shou immediately shouted.
Using the shout as a test for what is not a shout, the monk said, "This old thief! You get a cow and give back a horse. Shou then showed him the "One Gatha of the Four Gates," saying:
"As for that which must be made perfectly complete—how will you explain it? You say that Linji established this teaching."
The opening verse of the *Fen Song* first mentions the Three Essentials (*sanyao*) and subsequently the Three Mysteries (*sanxuan*). This represents the Real (*shi*) within the Expedient (*quan*).
To deliver a single phrase, one must possess the three gates of mystery; each gate of mystery must, in turn, possess the three essentials. Upon what do you rely to establish a single essential?

In the *Fen*, the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish, as both always precede the mysteries and follow the essentials. The initial four gates universally encompass a single essential, according to the opening [verse].

"First, one must understand that the 'Three Essentials' (sān yāo) of Linji are not the same as the 'Three Essentials' of Juefen. Based on the first four gates, the 'One Sentence' of Linji possesses the Three Mysteries (sān xuán);
each Mystery possesses the Three Essentials (sān yāo). If you can first attempt to correlate these so that they fit perfectly, then your explanation will not be erroneous.

Furthermore, it is said that in reality there is originally no sequence; the Three Mysteries are themselves the Three Essentials. It is simply because the Three Essentials are applied to the 'gate and courtyard' (mén tíng) of teaching that they are called 'Three'."
The Gate of the Mysterious (Xuánmén): the four gates all lead to this one. How will you account for this? Furthermore, it is said that one must view the mysterious authority as essential to the real;

the mysterious function as essential to illumination; and the mysterious guest as essential to the host. Since you prioritize authority and place the real afterward, then authority and reality are established merely by following the person.

When the initial question asks, "Who is it that comes here?", this is not a case of the function and illumination being simultaneous. When the monk answers, "It is I," this is likewise not a case of illumination and function.

At the same time, does this not point to the reality that there is no dharma apart from the person? Even when he first shouted, "Old thief! was that not the simultaneous manifestation of the whole body of illumination and function?
Therefore, while the guest is fully present, the host must establish the primary command; the main point must be perfectly complete.
In the dialogue between these two, how could there ever be even a shadow of the two terms "profound" (xuán) and "essential" (yào) to be seen? Among the four gates, there is but one essential.
The Three Mysteries are all termed "names" (*nāman*). Yet you, regarding these names, have perversely fabricated and falsely discoursed upon them. Shoushan said: "You must quickly spit this out!
How could there ever be such a thing as "mysterious essentials" or "names" that could deceive and entrap you? When did he ever say to you:
"If one discerns minutely, within the Mystery there is also 'reality,' 'illumination,' and 'the Host'—this is why the 'Host' is established within the Guest"? [He] sits upon the ground.
The "Lion" is the third phrase; within its essentials, there is both the provisional and the functional, as well as the guest—this is why it is established as the guest within the host.
The "Probe-Pole and Shadow-Grass" is the second phrase; where the profound and the essential are manifested together, this is why it is established as the host within the host.
The "Vajra Jewel Sword" is the first phrase; therefore, it is said at the outset: "Seizing hold of heaven and earth, one acts as the great master."
Without allowing for deliberation or conjecture, he cuts through the entire body; only then can he be called the "Master among Masters. Is this not the very head?

Since he does not allow for deliberation or conjecture when cutting through the entire body, he is precisely based upon the whole body from the outset, never having come from deliberation or conjecture.
The verse on the Guest and Host says: "Having awakened, one awakens from within delusion. Do you dare, within the sphere where awakening and delusion are not two separate persons, to set them apart?"
Xuan and Yao and others have established fixed stages one by one, which confuses people. How can it be said that "delusion and enlightenment have never differed from the beginning"?

Only now do we know that from the origin to the present, and from ancient times to today, there has been no divergent path handed down. Furthermore, when the two houses [of Chan] employ [their methods], they do not yield to the master;

is this not because the teacher is not seen except in the moment of action? Moreover, there is no room for deliberation or conjecture—is this not because one would otherwise cling to conceptualization?
Why do you not rely upon the entire body to demonstrate it to people through such conventional designations as the "Profound" (xuan) and the "Essential" (yao)?

You claim that the "patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) beneath the staff constitutes the "entire guest" (quan bin), and that "not seeing the teacher" when facing the opportune moment constitutes the "entire host" (quan zhu) or the "three essentials" (san yao).

This is most certainly not so. Since the teacher is not seen, there is no distinction between teacher and disciple; each is inherently endowed with the entirety of the universal equality. Who, then, [could be more...]?
I have already distinguished for you the guest and host within the Three Mysteries and the Essential; how much more so regarding the Three Mysteries and the Essential themselves!

Furthermore, as for what is called "the single phrase that fully presents [the truth]," it is because the Three Mysteries and the Essential, along with guest and host, are clearly distinct and inseparable.

Within the Three Mysteries themselves, guest and host are likewise clearly distinct and inseparable. This applies equally to the first, second, and third of the three essentials, which are like the three legs of a tripod. Or...
Whether vertical or horizontal, the cauldron cannot stand upright. This old monk relies solely on the freedom of the whole body;
who would come to divide it for you into vertical and horizontal? It is also said: "If it were merely a vague mass, there would be no standard for the feet and it could not stand.
These three essentials of the mysteries are but a single phrase and are difficult to distinguish. Jieyuan said: "The three dharmas are fused together; since they cannot be discerned, call them..."
The vast expanse of karmic consciousness does not refer to something vague or indistinct. Let me ask you: who told you it was vague? Are you slandering this old monk by calling him vague?
You merely pursue the words of Jieyan and fail to regard your own total embodiment. Furthermore, everyone stands on two feet;
even if you were to grow an extra leg like a tripod, you would still be nothing but a monster. This is not because you lack the capacity for discernment.
Can one obtain the consciousness of karma from sentient beings? Furthermore, you say that the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) can be divided;
how then can they be contained within a single phrase? If the Three Mysteries can be taken as a whole, why does a single phrase contain the Three Mysteries?

This shows that the provisional and the real proceed together, illumination and function manifest simultaneously, and guest and host are clearly distinguished, like a great mass of fire—not merely a fire of a single blade of grass or a single piece of fuel. Now, ask about the Great Prajñā.
Wisdom is like a great mass of fire; those who attempt to measure it risk having their faces scorched.

How many people have shared in this same prajñā, yet claim it is not merely a single blade of grass or a piece of firewood? What is this but slandering the Great Prajñā? Since time immemorial, there has been no secret or essential transmission handed down.
You say that the Three Mysteries and Essentials were not established by Jie, nor were they specially created by Huangbo; they are not mere superficialities.
Would this not defile the former sages? As for how you understand the various people [mentioned], there are the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan).
These are the Guest within a single phrase; they are the provisional means for you, the masters who have penetrated the mysteries. "Descending from the seat" refers to the Three Essentials (Sanyao);

these are the Host within a single phrase; they are the reality. The staff and the shout are necessary according to the occasion. Therefore, a single phrase contains the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials, as well as Guest and Host.
This is perfectly clear. When the old monk speaks of the staff and the shout being applied according to the occasion, how can one understand them as being the same?

To say they are "the same" has no connection to the actual act of putting down the seat. Jie said: "Before the staff is even raised, one should lift it up and go. Therefore, I say that [the shout] is for putting down the seat.
By means of the total body’s solitary liberation, one wipes away the three mysterious essentials. How could this compare to your further dividing and confused matching?

As recorded above, the selection of the heterodox and the demonstration of the correct are deeply related to the single eye of the *zong* (school) vehicle. I have briefly extracted the essentials here to serve as a guide for further inquiry.
Alas! From a transmission that does not rely on words and letters, we have reached a state where various debates arise, with trivial talk and prolix terminology.

Might this not be considered excessive? Nevertheless, were it not for this mutual investigation, how could the cases, principles, sayings, and insights of the patriarchs be so clearly dissected down to the finest detail?
This is not for me, a mountain monk, to indulge in the egoism of "self" and "other. If there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must simply strive for clarity.
The moon in the empty expanse of the azure pool has shone for ten thousand ages; yet, one must still scoop at it again and again.

I hope that those of future wisdom will sift through and clarify this, so as not to辜负 (fail) the compassionate heart of the ancient masters of virtue who manifested through both the provisional and the real.
— *Guànjiào* (Penetrating the Teachings).
Chan is the Buddha’s mind; the Teachings are the Buddha’s mouth. The mind and mouth of the Buddha can never be at variance.
An ancient worthy said: "Chan is the separate transmission outside the teachings; the teachings may likewise be considered the separate transmission outside of Chan. Truly profound are these words!

In the *Zongjing Lu*, one hundred scriptures and treatises are cited as evidence to demonstrate their essential accord, encompassing everything in vast detail; I shall not cite them here exhaustively, but shall merely present [the essentials].
In the Eastern Land, schools of study were established—namely the Tiantai, Xianshou, and Weishi schools—which have been handed down to the present day.
Together with the Chan school, they each raise the banner of the Dharma to propagate it inexhaustibly.

This work specifically clarifies the differences within their commonalities and identifies the commonalities within their differences, so as to unify them within the intent of our Buddha’s One Vehicle, thereby...

When these aspects are mutually attained, they become even more manifest. Let there be no mutual attacks and no clinging to one's own views as the only truth; rather, let the Pure Land be taken as the ultimate goal.

Thus, for both the Chan and doctrinal schools, it shall serve as the correct path—stable, secure, and reliable—for the accomplishment of the Way in a single lifetime. This, indeed, would be a near-perfect achievement.

As for the school of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), after several generations following Master Xuanzang, its sound was nearly extinguished. In recent times, it has been largely absorbed by the Tiantai school.

The Venerable Master Liangjia lectured on both [the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*]. Within the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, five stages of the practice of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) are established;

among these, the third is the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha*). This refers to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) wherein Bodhisattvas abide and penetrate reality as it truly is. The verse states:

"When, with respect to an object of cognition, Cognition finds nothing at all to be apprehended, At that time one abides in Consciousness-Only, Because one is free from the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper. This refers to the ultimate truth...
In the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), with respect to the objective referent and non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*), there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended.

At that time, one is said to truly abide in the ultimate nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). This is the wisdom that realizes *tathatā* (suchness), which is equal and co-equal with *tathatā*.
Because it is free from both the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped, this is called the stage of the True Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) in the Yogācāra school;

in the Tiantai school, it corresponds to the first *bhūmi* (abiding) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), or the first stage of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), wherein one portion of ignorance (*avidyā*) is shattered.

To realize the aspect of a portion of *tathatā* (Suchness) is, when compared to the superior practitioner of Chan meditation, equivalent to "recommending" one's original face and being in accord with one's fundamental nature.
However, within the Teachings (*śāsana*), this constitutes the actual realization of *tathatā*, which is the mark of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood;
whereas in the Chan school, it is a momentary flash of awakening. The difference between them is as vast as that between heaven and earth. Nevertheless, regarding the state of the object realized...
The characteristics of the realized realm are understood to be without differentiation; this is the very source of the non-dual mind of the present Buddha and the Buddhas of the past.
This is what is meant in the Chan school by "sharing the same nostrils with all Buddhas," and it is also what is meant by the statement that "the three realms are mind-only.
Once a follower of the school has attained such resonance, this realm manifests spontaneously from time to time, dissolving [all delusions].

Once the habitual tendencies of the two types of grasping are eliminated—whether in a single lifetime or over the course of several lifetimes—the *prajñā* will mature until it suddenly equals the actual realization described in the teachings.
This depends entirely upon the density of the individual’s own cultivation and effort, and thus cannot be easily predetermined.

Nevertheless, from the moment one first accords with the fundamental nature, progress is as swift as the wind; one need only ensure that *prajñā* is constantly manifest, for there is no need to hope for haste.

It is effective, and there is nothing that it does not effect swiftly. Compared to the fundamental school of Yogācāra itself, from the initial stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*), through the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), up to the third stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha*), one must pass through great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before attaining realization of the Truth.

Furthermore, proceeding to the fourth stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) and the fifth stage of ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), one requires three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in total to ascend to the fruit of Buddhahood; thus, it is slow.
The difference between them is more than that between heaven and earth. Tiantai judges that the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) is subsumed within the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

While it is certainly possible to harmonize the two schools regarding the perfect fusion and sequential arrangement of their names and characteristics (*mingxiang*), their gateways for opening up understanding and initiating practice are vastly different; there is no need for forced reconciliation.
Xianshou judges that the *Vijñaptimātratā* is subsumed within the Initial Teaching (*shijiao*), which is not even the Final or Sudden Teachings, let alone the Huayan.
Regarding the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): since the *Huayan Shuchao* extensively cites the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, one who does not master the *Vijñaptimātratā* cannot expound the Huayan school.
This differs from the approach of the Tiantai school, which established its own specialized tradition and did not require the inclusion of other schools.

For a Bodhisattva seeking to realize the nature of *Vijñaptimātratā*, from the moment they generate the profound and firm resolve for great Bodhicitta, they cultivate the excellence of the six perfections.
The "provisions" (sambhāra) involve entering the path by contemplating that the self-grasping and dualistic grasping of conventional designations are empty;

this is vastly different from the Chan school’s teaching that "a single thought-moment turning the faculty back [to its source] is identical to original attainment," and that "merely being free from delusive conditions, one is immediately a Tathāgata. There is no need to attempt to harmonize these two.
In the *Pramāṇa* treatises, it is established that there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and non-tripartite [cognition].
Regarding the explanation of perception (*pratyakṣa*), it says: "In this context, perception refers to that which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).

When a correct cognition arises with respect to objects such as form, sound, or taste, and functions by directly discerning [the object] while being entirely devoid of seeds of linguistic habituation (*abhilāpa-vāsanā*) and the like, it is therefore called perception. Adherents of the Chan school (*zongmen*) frequently [use] perception...

While the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitutes the fundamental essence [of conventional knowledge], when the manifest sense organs confront manifest objects, there arises the distinction between the manifesting subject and the manifested object.

This is clearly different from the essential principle of the "spiritual light shining alone," which is utterly detached from both sense organs and their objects. One must understand that this is the gate of awakening in the School of the Essential Doctrine (*zongmen*).
It is not the present. It does not fall within the scope of cognition. With a single "thump" of the fist, one knocks over this faceless fellow;
only then is this the true point. This is the position of the Sole Honored One. Do not be reckless; do not mistake ordinary perception (*pratyakṣa*) for your own fundamental share. Consider this:
when you are fast asleep, without dreams or thoughts, and without seeing or hearing—what serves as the measure then? What is it that manifests? The pillow falls.

Regarding the signs of the stages (*bhūmi*): these have not yet manifested and do not fall within the scope of temporal measurement; even the Buddha-eye cannot perceive them. How, then, could one speak of manifestation or measurement?

Generally, one should take the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the Vijñaptimātra school as the point where True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) are directly realized, and it is permissible to cite this as a point of concordance.
The masters of the *Bhadanta*-school take the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as their primary tenet, and they analyze the principle of the Dharma-realm into its phenomena (*dharma*).
The Dharma-realm: the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, and the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena.

In the Chan school, these four Dharma-realms are entirely encompassed as the gate of enlightenment; that is, the entirety of the four Dharma-realms is taken as one's fundamental portion, wherein the four Dharma-realms are utterly extinguished.
It fully encompasses the four dharma realms; it is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases—ineffable and inconceivable.

Its innate truth is revealed in its own right, and is collectively termed the "One True Dharma Realm. This is not like the method of the Xianshou school, which analyzes and dissects [the teachings] into minute fragments.
Therefore, many practitioners of the Chan school take pleasure in the sutras and treatises of the Xianshou school, as their expositions largely accord with the language of the Chan tradition.
Furthermore, Master Xianshou judged this school to be "Sudden" (*dùn*). As it is said: "If for even a single moment no thought arises, one is immediately named a Buddha.

Because it directly expounds this principle without enumerating gradual stages, it is called the Sudden Teaching. It is intended specifically for a class of practitioners whose faculties are free from discursive thought, and thus it accords with the Chan School.
Moreover, according to what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a single stage is all stages, and all stages are a single stage.

Regarding the classification of the stages: based upon the Samantabhadra Dharma-realm, with its infinitely nested Indra’s net and the complete presence of primary and attendant elements, it is established as the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
If one were to judge according to the Chan school as it has been categorized, it would be merely sudden and not perfect; this would not be without words of disparagement.

In my private opinion, it may be acceptable to say that the School of the Gate (Zongmen) accords with the Perfect through its suddenness, but to say that it is merely sudden and entirely lacks the Perfect is not so.
This is acceptable. However, although the patriarchs of the Avataṃsaka school have made such a classification, they also allow that the Chan school is subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

Guifeng said: "If one suddenly awakens to the fact that one's own mind is originally pure, fundamentally free from afflictions, and that the nature of untainted wisdom is inherently complete—this mind is itself the Buddha, ultimately no different [from it]—then practicing in accordance with this is the Meditation of the Supreme Vehicle."
The *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi) is the root of all samādhis. If one can practice it moment by moment, one will naturally and gradually attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
This is the very Chan transmitted within the lineage of Bodhidharma. It is identical to the Buddha-body in an instant;
upon attaining it, one becomes a sage and swiftly realizes *bodhi*. Furthermore, it is said that the Absolute Truth is suddenly perfected through awakening, while delusive emotions are extinguished.
[The afflictions] gradually diminish until they are exhausted. Sudden perfection is like a newborn infant whose limbs are already complete in a single day;

gradual cultivation is like growing into an adult over many years, only after which one’s will and character are finally established. One should know that the nature of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is inherently complete.
The Single Practice Samādhi (*ekavyūha-samādhi*) is the root of all samādhis. Furthermore, such statements as "the true principle is realized and suddenly perfected" [refer to this].

All of these belong to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong). They are not merely the sudden doctrine of "not giving rise to a single thought" or "separation from thought. One must not rashly attempt to pass judgment upon them.

Once one has developed the perfect understanding according to the Huayan school, one should contemplate with precision how phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused and unimpeded, pervading and containing the entire Dharma-realm.
Throughout, ten meanings are opened up, yet they all ultimately converge in attaining the equality of the mind, thereby accomplishing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the phrase "like clouds dissolving into equality": this is intended to cause those who have not yet realized it to understand their own mind. If one knows that all objects encountered are mind, only then does one realize the nature of the mind.
Thus, the *Brahmacarya Chapter* states: "To know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind, one then accomplishes the body of wisdom without depending on another for enlightenment.
Since the mind and its objects are thus like [space], such likeness is equal and unimpeded; this is the realization of the mind.

Regarding the Buddha of the objective realm (*viṣaya*): one perceives within the very realm that the Tathāgata is nothing but mind. While the Buddhas of the mind unfold in successive layers, the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) is one and the same.
Since all these cannot be grasped, both mind and object are forgotten; since they cannot be exhausted by illumination, principle and wisdom penetrate each other. The commentary states:
"People today only understand that 'mind is Buddha' and 'this mind makes Buddha,' but they do not know that the objective realm itself is [Buddha]."
The Buddha. This is the Buddha as an object. When one gathers the object within the mind, one sees the Buddha within the mind; this is the Buddha of the objective realm.
When one gathers the mind within the object, one sees the Buddha within the object; this is the Tathāgata who is solely the mind. Regarding the "repeated layers of the mind-Buddha":

if two mirrors are placed facing each other to reflect a single Buddha, the image of that single Buddha enters repeatedly into both mirrors. When both mind and object are forgotten, this is cessation (*śamatha*). When principle and wisdom are unified, this is insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The mutual penetration of the three contemplations is analogous to the Tiantai school’s notion of the simultaneous operation of cessation and illumination (*zhēzhào*) for the beginner;

it is precisely the most critical point for the diligent application of cultivation and practice. In the Chan school, after one has realized "there is something," there is a spontaneous state of ease where one is simply "mindless" amidst the myriad things, yet what prevents the myriad things from constantly surrounding one?
On the ground of ultimate reality (*jìshí lǐdì*), not a single speck of dust can be admitted.
Within the gate of Buddha-work, not a single dharma is abandoned; practice and realization are in accord.

This is also identical to the vivid, solitary luminosity of the "unreliant person" (wuyi daoren) of the Ji lineage, and the same as the "six doors unbarred and the four crossroads leaving no trace" of the Dong lineage. This is the one path to the gate of Nirvana.
It accords with the seal of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) of the Perfect School (Yuanjiao), which is what is meant by the so-called "constantly contemplating Nirvana while practicing the Way."

Furthermore, as for the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*śaśva-śaśva-apratighāta-dharmadhātu*) expounded by the Avataṃsaka school—wherein the Indra’s net is infinitely layered and the principal and its attendants mutually interpenetrate—it is only at the stage of fruition that one can fully realize and certify this through practice; it seems beyond the capacity of beginners to enter.

Although the Chan school claims that one's own mind is inherently complete and that there is no need to cultivate such understanding or give rise to such contemplation, [the matter remains as stated].
This differs from that of Xianshou. As for Xianshou, based on the Avataṃsaka teachings, he established fifty-two stages of sages and worthies, with their successive ranks clearly ordered;
this is unlike the Vijñaptimātratā system, which holds that one can only achieve Buddhahood after passing through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Qingliang stated that one attains Buddhahood in three lifetimes; thus, the swiftness [of this path] is evident.

Although the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) does not explicitly establish fifty-two stages, one may discern their traces by looking toward the void, and their implicit realization must certainly not be dismissed as non-existent. Furthermore, there is never any regression throughout one's entire life.
One enters the stage of the noble ones; this is the swift realization that is entirely in accord with the [teachings].

The Tiantai school, relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as pure, perfect, and uniquely wondrous, establishes five layers of profound meaning—name, essence, doctrine, function, and teaching—within the title of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Among these, they take the "true reality" (*bhūtatathatā*) within the sūtra as the essence. This is precisely the original face realized by the Chan school.

Apart from the true reality (dharmatā), there is no gateway to enlightenment; apart from the true reality, there is no fundamental portion. What is called the "true object" is without marks, and even the absence of marks is absent.
True wisdom is without conditions, and even the absence of conditions is transcended. Although the object is without marks, it constantly serves as the condition for wisdom;
although wisdom is without conditions, it constantly arises from the object. It is neither real nor unreal, neither marked nor unmarked; negation and illumination occur simultaneously.

This is precisely the correct eye of the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen). However, while the Teaching School (Jiao-xia) manifests through words yet accords with that which is beyond words, the School of the Patriarchs points entirely toward the side of acceding to that which is beyond words. The Tiantai school judges the Buddha’s lifetime teaching into five periods:
first, the Avataṃsaka period; second, the Āgama period; third, the Vaipulya period; fourth, the Prajñā period; and fifth, the Dharma [Nirvāṇa] period.
During the "Flower" period (Huashi), he categorized the four teachings—Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Complete.

Although he did not specifically discuss the School of the Lineage (Zongmen), he judged that the Chan school was subsumed within the Prajñā period, incorporating both the Shared and Distinct teachings while ultimately converging upon the Complete teaching, for those who have attained the essential meaning of the Lineage school.

All are fully integrated within the Perfect [Teaching]. Those who have not yet attained its essential meaning may adhere to either the distinct [teachings] alone, or to both the general and the distinct.
Consequently, there are varying depths of awakening, which result in the integration of doctrine and principle being either pure or mixed.

The Sixth Patriarch’s proclamation and exposition of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and his exhortation to recite the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* serve as proof of this. This is because that which is discussed in the *Prajñāpāramitā* section is identical to that of the Zen School.

This is because the Patriarchal Masters frequently pointed this out as being consistent with the truth. The Tiantai school itself maintains that the *Lotus Sūtra* is uniquely pure, perfect, and wondrous, standing outside the first four periods of the Buddha’s teaching.

This is because the first four periods represent a "perfect teaching" of relative opposition (*duìdài*), whereas the period of the *Lotus Sūtra* represents a "perfect teaching" of absolute transcendence (*juédài*).

One establishes the inconceivable realm of the three thousand worlds within a single thought-moment—emptiness, provisionality, and the middle—and gives rise to the inconceivable contemplation of the three thousand worlds within a single thought-moment—emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.

One contemplates that the realm and the contemplation are non-dual, simultaneously illuminating and simultaneously negating. Thus, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause.
The Buddha-son dwelling in this stage immediately enters the rank of all Buddhas. He realizes that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in their threefold naturelessness.

By simply observing the state of the five aggregates within a single thought-moment of his own mind, he perceives the ten dharma-realms of ordinary and sage beings, the ten suchnesses, the thousand provisional names, the thousand five-aggregate realms, and the thousand lands.
These three thousand phenomena within a single thought-moment are such that when one is empty, all are empty.
One is provisional, and all are provisional; one is the Middle Way, and all are the Middle Way. The objective realm and contemplation thus established are most perfect and subtle.
When adventitious matters come from the Chan school, they are not accepted; being mindless in all places, this accords with the principle that "one is empty and all are empty.

Departing for the state of non-alteration—departing yet remaining unaltered—this accords with the principle that "one is the Middle Way and all are the Middle Way. This is exclusively the Tiantai school.
The Tiantai school enters through observing the false and not observing the true; the Chan school enters through observing the true and not observing the false.
The same applies to the Chan school. Consequently, the Chan school and the Tiantai school are largely unable to reach a common understanding.

This is because the Tiantai school observes that a single thought of the deluded mind contains all phenomena—being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way—whereas the Chan school first requires the total extinction of the deluded mind before one can attain [realization].
The true mind is nakedly revealed; yet, from time immemorial, it has never been free from thought. It is not only the arising and ceasing that is delusion;
even at the moment when there is no arising or ceasing, one is still encompassed by indeterminate deluded thoughts.

Only upon reaching the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching, breaking through a portion of ignorance and realizing a portion of *tathatā*, does *tathatā* begin to manifest fully before one’s face. Prior to reaching these stages, one remains entirely within the state of delusion.
The ground is merely the deluded mind of ignorance; once one leaves this ground-abiding ignorance, there is nowhere else to seek the true mind.
Thus, Master Li said: "Ground-abiding ignorance is precisely the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas.

Consequently, whether the Tiantai school contemplates the deluded or the Chan school contemplates the true, neither goes beyond this ground-abiding ignorance. Therefore, the Tiantai school says: "The mountain..."
Observing the true externally is the same as observing the deluded; observing the deluded within the mountain is, in fact, observing the true.

This is spoken in contrast to the Xianzong (Exoteric) school, yet the Chan school may also be understood through this. For the Chan school reveals the true by departing from the deluded, while the Tiantai school realizes the true within the deluded;

both point to this very ground-of-abiding ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is none other than the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of all Buddhas. To realize this, there is no need for further differentiation.

Whether categorized as Chan, categorized as Teaching, or distinguished as false or true, one need only recognize the *prajñā-pāramitā* of the true mark—which remains unchanging while following conditions.
When mind after mind does not diverge from this, it is the unmoving wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of all Buddhas manifesting before you; you are then walking hand-in-hand with all Buddhas.

This is precisely entering the rank of all Buddhas. The Tiantai school likewise delineates fifty-two stages, wherein one may hope to ascend to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjuzu*) within a single lifetime.
This is identical to the Chan gate’s principle of never retreating for the rest of one’s life until entering the state of sainthood.

Since there has never been a great master of antiquity who did not penetrate the Great Vehicle of the doctrinal teachings (*jiao*), it is said: "To penetrate the essence (*zong*) but not the teachings is to fall into chaos as soon as one opens one's mouth."
How can the Way receive and benefit sentient beings without missing the opportune moment?

I shall now briefly excerpt the essential tenets of the three schools—Weishi (Vijñaptimātra), Xian-shou (Huayan), and Tiantai—and clarify their similarities and differences with the Chan school, thereby harmonizing them into a single thread so that both doctrine and practice are fully integrated.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs have set their seals upon this; though it may not hit the mark exactly, it is not far from it.

Nevertheless, as the fortunes of the Dharma reach their decline and the faculties of people are for the most part dull, there are certainly not a few who vigorously give rise to the Great Mind to bring an end to birth and death. Among them, some have ascended the mountain three times or nine times.
If one does not encounter a true lineage master, one cannot attain true knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

Even if one encounters a true lineage master and attains true knowledge and vision, if it is merely a partial understanding and one has not reached the state of great penetration and mastery, then when the "twelfth month" arrives, one will inevitably suffer a moment of embarrassment and regret.
Furthermore, even if one attains true knowledge and vision, if one's habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are thick and worldly...
Life is short and fleeting. Furthermore, members of both the lay and monastic assemblies may spend their entire lives amidst worldly toil without having attained maturity in practice and realization;
thus, when their karmic retribution comes to an end, they cannot avoid abandoning their path midway.

Although they may not lose right mindfulness at the moment of death and may return in a future life by virtue of their vows—certainly fulfilling those aspirations—the transition between states of existence (the "separation from the corpse") is a source of concern. Doubts may arise that fail to dissipate, thereby robbing them of their right mindfulness.

Consequently, there are those who have lost their way. Now, for the sake of such people, I shall establish a direct and swift path—one that is a thousandfold secure and ten-thousandfold reliable—as a skillful means to enable every person to transcend to the other shore in this very life.
Nothing is more suitable than the single gate of the combined practice of Chan and Pure Land.

This applies to those who have not yet attained the gate of awakening, as well as those who have never practiced Chan, and who instead focus exclusively on the "single-mindedness of affairs" (sixin) in the Pure Land.

This need not be discussed further. Those listed here are solely for the sake of those who have already engaged in Chan meditation and know that [enlightenment] exists, yet whose strength and capacity are weak and thin, such that they cannot purely rely on their own power to transcend and ascend to the ranks of the sages;
though their realization may be correct, residual habits still burn fiercely within them.
Like a solitary lamp beneath the sun, it constantly lacks illumination; how could it ever achieve integration? This is a malady still prevalent among the two groups of householders.
If one does not rely on the empowerment of that Buddha’s power, how can one avoid regret at the moment of death?
Moreover, since ancient times, the Patriarch Yongming You has exerted great effort in advocating this, establishing the "Four Kinds of Discrimination" (*si liao jian*) as the method for cultivation.

The Zen masters urged them to set out on their journey. As for the other patriarchs of successive generations who clarified the Great Matter and made vows to be reborn in the Land of Bliss, they are too numerous to count; this may be verified by consulting the *Jiaohu ji*.

However, the children of our school often take "the Pure Land of Mind-Only" and "Amitābha as Self-Nature" as their ultimate goal. This, however, remains merely the cultivation of self-power and is not...
To harmonize with the primary cause for rebirth is of utmost importance; one error leads to a hundred errors, so it must not remain unknown. As for the primary cause for rebirth:
